05 / RESEARCH NOTES

Einstein's Derivation of General Relativity

This is general relativity's own derivation of its curvature and its field equations, by Einstein's route: from free fall to curvature, from curvature to an equation with matter as its source, and from Newton's law far from the mass to the constant. It is the comparison side. Nothing from this paper is added to it, and nothing in it is changed to bring it closer to Section 4 or further from it. Every assumption that general relativity makes is named as an assumption, in the list of part 1 and again at the step where it enters, so that Section 6 can point to each by its number.

What it assumes. Twenty-one assumptions, A1 to A21 (part 1). The ones that carry the derivation:

  1. One spacetime with one metric, and every observer measures components of this same metric (A1).
  2. The equivalence principle: freely falling bodies fall alike, and in a small freely falling laboratory special relativity holds (A2).
  3. Ideal clocks and rulers read the metric (A3), and free bodies follow its straightest paths (A6).
  4. The equations have the same form in every coordinate system (A4).
  5. Matter enters through one stress-energy tensor \(T_{\mu\nu}\), conserved locally (A7, A8).
  6. The geometric side of the equations is built from the metric alone, is of second order, and has a divergence that vanishes identically (A9). The source side is one constant times \(T_{\mu\nu}\) (A10).
  7. Newton's law holds far from the mass (A11), and the cosmological constant is zero (A12).

What it gets. The field equations, with the constant fixed by Newton's law:

\[ R_{\mu\nu}-\frac12\,R\,g_{\mu\nu}=\frac{8\pi G}{c^4}\,T_{\mu\nu},\qquad R_{\mu\nu}=0\ \ \text{in empty space}. \]

For a still arrangement, with the clock rate \(f\) and the rulers \(h\):

\[ \Delta_hf=\frac{4\pi G}{c^4}\,f\,(\varepsilon+S),\qquad R_{ij}(h)-\frac{D_iD_jf}{f}=\frac{8\pi G}{c^4}\Big[S_{ij}+\tfrac12\,h_{ij}\,(\varepsilon-S)\Big]. \]

For a small ball of free particles at rest relative to one another, in every local inertial frame:

\[ \frac1V\frac{d^2V}{d\tau^2}=-\frac{4\pi G}{c^2}\,\big(\varepsilon+p_1+p_2+p_3\big). \]

To first order, for an arrangement that changes:

\[ \Box\,\bar q_{\mu\nu}=-\frac{16\pi G}{c^4}\,T_{\mu\nu}, \]

a wave equation, with the speed \(c\) and two polarizations.

For a child

Here is the whole recipe that Einstein used to get his equations, every step written out.

It starts by assuming that there is one map of space and time, and that everyone, wherever they are and however they move, reads their clocks and rulers off that same map.

It assumes that inside a small falling room nothing feels the pull, and that things left alone follow the straightest lines on the map.

It measures how the map bends by watching two things that fall side by side drift together or apart.

Then it looks for the simplest rule that ties the bending to the energy of the stuff that is there, and it sets the one number in that rule so that far from a heavy body it gives Newton's old law.

Two things come out at the end: Einstein's equations, and ripples in the map that move at the speed of light.

For a high school physics teacher

The assumptions. Twenty-one things are assumed, listed in part 1. The ones that carry the derivation: there is one spacetime with one metric, the same for all observers; in a small freely falling laboratory special relativity holds (the equivalence principle); ideal clocks and rulers read the metric; the equations have the same form in every coordinate system; free bodies follow the straightest paths; matter enters through one stress-energy tensor \(T_{\mu\nu}\), conserved locally; the equation for the metric is of second order; Newton's law holds far from the mass; and the cosmological constant is zero.

Free fall. In the falling laboratory a free body moves uniformly in a straight line. Written in any coordinates this is the geodesic equation, \(\ddot x^\sigma+\Gamma^\sigma{}_{\mu\nu}\,\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu=0\) (part 3).

Newton's limit of free fall. For slow motion far from the mass the geodesic equation becomes Newton's \(\mathbf a=-\boldsymbol\nabla\Phi\) if \(g_{00}=-(1+2\Phi/c^2)\). A clock at rest then runs at \(1+\Phi/c^2\) (part 4).

Curvature. Two neighbouring free bodies accelerate relative to one another, and the Riemann tensor measures it. Its contractions are the Ricci tensor \(R_{\mu\nu}\) and the scalar \(R\), and they obey an identity of their own: \(\nabla^\mu(R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12g_{\mu\nu}R)=0\) (part 5).

The source. The energy density, the momentum density and the stresses of matter are the components of \(T_{\mu\nu}\), and \(\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0\) (part 6).

The field equations. Among tensors built from the metric with at most second derivatives, the only one whose divergence vanishes identically is \(R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12g_{\mu\nu}R\), up to a constant times the metric. Setting it equal to a constant times \(T_{\mu\nu}\), with no cosmological term: \(R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12g_{\mu\nu}R=\kappa T_{\mu\nu}\) (part 7).

The constant. Newton's law \(\nabla^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho\) far from the mass fixes \(\kappa=8\pi G/c^4\) (part 8). In empty space the equations are \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\) (part 9).

A still arrangement, in clocks and rulers. With the clock rate \(f\) and the rulers \(h\), the equations read \(\Delta_hf=(4\pi G/c^4)\,f\,(\varepsilon+S)\) and \(R_{ij}(h)-D_iD_jf/f=(8\pi G/c^4)\,[S_{ij}+\tfrac12h_{ij}(\varepsilon-S)]\), with \(S\) the sum of the three pressures (part 10).

A small ball of free particles, at rest relative to one another, starts to shrink at the rate \(\ddot V/V=-(4\pi G/c^2)(\varepsilon+p_1+p_2+p_3)\), in every local inertial frame. That statement, for every such frame, is equivalent to the field equations (part 11).

Energy. The energy and momentum of matter are balanced from place to place. The gravitational field itself has no energy density that can be given at a point. A total mass exists for an isolated system that is flat far away, or for one with a symmetry in time (part 12).

Changes. To first order the equations are a wave equation, \(\Box\,\bar q_{\mu\nu}=-(16\pi G/c^4)\,T_{\mu\nu}\). A change of the metric moves at the speed \(c\), with two polarizations (part 13).

For a theoretical physicist

Complete derivation of Einstein's field equations

This section takes Einstein’s route from free fall to curvature, from curvature to a tensor equation with matter as its source, and from Newton’s limit to the coupling constant. Part 7 gives both the trace correction in Einstein’s source-side form and its expression through the contracted Bianchi identity. The four-dimensional uniqueness theorem is identified separately because it came later.

Each numbered step is marked assumption, definition, mathematics, or input from observation. A step marked mathematics follows from its named premises. The distinction matters particularly for the source law in Part 7 and the normalization in Part 8.

1. The setting and the assumptions

  1. A1. Assumption. One spacetime metric. Spacetime is a smooth four-dimensional manifold with one smooth Lorentzian metric \(g\) of signature \((-+++)\). Every observer measures components of this same metric. Choose a time orientation wherever future-directed observers are used. Reference: Einstein, The Foundation of the General Theory of Relativity (1916), and Wald, General Relativity, chapters 2–3.
  2. A2. Assumption. Equivalence principle. Freely falling test bodies with the same initial position and velocity fall alike. In a sufficiently small freely falling laboratory, nongravitational physics takes its special-relativistic form locally. The exact local statement used below is at the central event. Tidal effects across a finite laboratory are calculated in Part 5. Reference: Einstein (1916), §§2–4.
  3. A3. Assumption. Metric clocks and rulers. An ideal clock measures proper time along its worldline. An ideal local ruler measures the metric length of a separation simultaneous in its rest frame. The locally measured speed of light is \(c\). Reference: Einstein (1916), §4.
  4. A4. Assumption. General covariance. The field equation is a tensor equation valid in arbitrary smooth coordinates. Its geometric side is constructed naturally from the metric, with no preferred coordinate system or fixed background geometry. Reference: Einstein (1916), §§3, 12, and the metric hypotheses specified in A9.
  5. A5. Assumption. Metric connection. The connection governing spacetime parallel transport is torsion-free and metric-compatible. Reference: the metric formulation of GR, Wald, chapter 3.
  6. A6. Assumption. Free propagation. A structureless massive test body subject only to gravity follows a timelike geodesic. A freely propagating light ray in geometric optics follows a null geodesic. Proper time is an affine parameter for the massive body. An affine parameter is chosen separately for the light ray. Reference: Einstein (1916), §§9, 13, 22, and Wald, chapters 3–4.
  7. A7. Assumption. Matter source. Matter and nongravitational fields together have a symmetric stress-energy tensor \(T_{\mu\nu}\). Its local components give energy density, momentum density, energy flux and stress. Reference: Einstein (1916), §16, and Wald, chapter 4.
  8. A8. Assumption. Local conservation. When the matter equations hold, total nongravitational stress-energy obeys \(\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0\). Interacting constituents can exchange energy and momentum. The conservation statement applies to their sum. Reference: Einstein (1916), §§16–18.
  9. A9. Assumption. Class of geometric field equations. The geometric side is a smooth, local, natural, symmetric rank-two tensor of the metric alone. It involves derivatives through order two and is linear in the second derivatives, allowing an additive term independent of them. Its covariant divergence vanishes identically for every metric. This last condition is the geometric compatibility requirement used in the uniqueness argument. Reference: the second-order metric construction in Einstein (1916), §§12–16, and the modern uniqueness theorem of Lovelock (1971).
  10. A10. Assumption. Universal coupling. The source side is a single universal constant times \(T_{\mu\nu}\), algebraically and linearly, for every kind of matter. Reference: Einstein, Die Feldgleichungen der Gravitation (1915), and Einstein (1916), §16.
  11. A11. Assumption. Newtonian correspondence. In Newton’s limit ordinary matter obeys \(\mathbf a=-\boldsymbol\nabla\Phi\) and \(\nabla^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho\), with \(G\) fixed by gravitational measurements. Reference: Newtonian gravitation and Einstein (1916), §21.
  12. A12. Assumption. Zero cosmological constant. Set \(\Lambda=0\). This selects the field equations of Einstein’s November 1915 paper. The place where the general metric construction admits \(\Lambda\) is displayed in Part 7.
  13. A13. Assumption. Conditions for the Newtonian calibration. Use an isolated, nearly Minkowskian, stationary configuration with slow test motion, slow source motion and stresses small compared with rest-energy density. Normalize time at infinity and put \(\Phi(\infty)=0\). These are conditions on the calibration calculation in Parts 4 and 8. Reference: Einstein (1916), §21.
  14. A14. Assumption. Vacuum specialization. In a region called vacuum below, \(T_{\mu\nu}=0\), including the stress-energy of nongravitational fields. Reference: Einstein (1916), §14.
  15. A15. Assumption. Static specialization. In Part 10 there is a hypersurface-orthogonal timelike Killing field. Work in its timelike region, with clocks at rest along its flow. Reference: the definition of staticity in metric GR, Wald, chapter 6.
  16. A16. Assumption. Small-ball experiment. Use an infinitesimal ball of freely falling test particles. At the initial event its relative velocity gradient vanishes in the central particle’s inertial frame. The central velocity may be any future timelike velocity. Reference: Baez and Bunn, The Meaning of Einstein’s Equation.
  17. A17. Assumption. Isolated-system boundary conditions. For energy and momentum at spatial infinity, assume an asymptotically flat spacelike end with the falloff and integrability needed for the ADM surface integrals. Reference: Arnowitt, Deser and Misner, The Dynamics of General Relativity.
  18. A18. Assumption. Time symmetry for a Killing charge. Where a time-translation Killing field is used, assume it exists. For the stationary mass at infinity normalize it to unit timelike length there. For a conserved current integrated over a bounded region, specify its boundary flux. Reference: Komar, Covariant Conservation Laws in General Relativity.
  19. A19. Assumption. First-order waves. In Part 13 expand about Minkowski spacetime, retain terms of first order in the metric perturbation, and use a vacuum propagation region to identify the freely propagating polarizations. Reference: linearized GR, Wald, chapter 4.
  20. A20. Assumption. The density of Newton's law. The density \(\rho\) in Newton's law is the matter's rest-energy density divided by \(c^2\). It enters at step 8b. (Named by the check of this derivation.)
  21. A21. Assumption. The chart of Newton's law. The chart's \(t\) and \(x^i\) are the time and the lengths of Newton's law, for observers at rest in the chart. It enters at step 4c and is used again in steps 8a and 8d. (Named by the check of this derivation.)

1a. Definition — notation. Use \(x^0=ct\). Greek indices run from \(0\) through \(3\), and Latin spatial indices from \(1\) through \(3\). Repeated upper and lower indices are summed. A hat denotes an orthonormal-frame component. A comma denotes a partial derivative. A unit timelike vector \(n\) has \(g(n,n)=-1\). A four-velocity \(u=cn\) has \(g(u,u)=-c^2\). Throughout, \(G\) without indices is Newton’s constant.

2. Clocks, rulers and the metric connection

2a. Assumption — apply A1 and A3 to a clock. The metric interval is \(ds^2=g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu\). Along a timelike clock worldline its reading satisfies

\[ \boxed{d\tau=\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{-g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu}.} \tag{1} \]

2b. Mathematics — obtain the local ruler reading. For an observer \(n\), the projection of a displacement \(X\) into the observer’s rest space is \(X_\perp=X+n\,g(n,X)\). Indeed, \(g(n,X_\perp)=g(n,X)-g(n,X)=0\). Expanding \(g(X_\perp,X_\perp)\) gives the observer’s spatial metric

\[ P_{\mu\nu}=g_{\mu\nu}+n_\mu n_\nu. \]

For a simultaneous separation \(n_\mu dx^\mu=0\), A3 therefore gives

\[ \boxed{d\ell^2=P_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu =g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu.} \tag{2} \]

A length along a specified spatial curve is \(\ell=\int d\ell\).

2c. Mathematics — obtain the connection from A5. Write \(\Gamma_{abc}=g_{ad}\Gamma^d{}_{bc}\). Torsion freedom gives \(\Gamma_{abc}=\Gamma_{acb}\). Metric compatibility gives

\[ \partial_b g_{ac}=\Gamma_{cba}+\Gamma_{abc}. \]

Add this equation to the one with \(b,c\) exchanged and subtract the one with derivative index \(a\). Symmetry in the last two connection indices cancels all terms except \(2\Gamma_{abc}\). Raising \(a\) gives

\[ \boxed{\Gamma^\rho{}_{\mu\nu} =\frac12g^{\rho\sigma} \bigl(\partial_\mu g_{\sigma\nu} +\partial_\nu g_{\sigma\mu} -\partial_\sigma g_{\mu\nu}\bigr).} \tag{3} \]

This is the Levi-Civita connection of the one metric in A1.

3. Free fall and the geodesic equation

3a. Assumption — apply A2 and A6 at an event. Choose freely falling local inertial coordinates \(X^a\) at an event \(p\). There \(g_{ab}=\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)\) and \(\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=0\). For an affinely parametrized free trajectory, A6 gives

\[ \left.\frac{d^2X^a}{d\lambda^2}\right|_p=0. \]

3b. Mathematics — express that trajectory in arbitrary coordinates, using A4. With \(\dot x^\mu=dx^\mu/d\lambda\), the chain rule gives

\[ 0=\frac{\partial X^a}{\partial x^\rho}\ddot x^\rho +\frac{\partial^2X^a}{\partial x^\mu\partial x^\nu} \dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu . \]

Multiply by \(\partial x^\sigma/\partial X^a\). At \(p\), the product of this inverse Jacobian with the second derivative is \(\Gamma^\sigma{}_{\mu\nu}\), by the connection transformation law from the frame where \(\Gamma=0\). Since \(p\) was arbitrary,

\[ \boxed{\frac{d^2x^\rho}{d\lambda^2} +\Gamma^\rho{}_{\mu\nu} \frac{dx^\mu}{d\lambda}\frac{dx^\nu}{d\lambda}=0.} \tag{4} \]

3c. Mathematics — check the two normalizations. Put \(v=dx/d\lambda\). Equations (3)–(4) give

\[ \frac{d}{d\lambda}g(v,v)=2g(\nabla_vv,v)=0. \]

For a massive body, (1) permits \(\lambda=\tau\), giving \(g(v,v)=-c^2\). For a light ray, A6 gives \(g(v,v)=0\) initially and the same calculation preserves zero along the ray.

4. Newton’s limit of free fall

4a. Assumption — specialize using A13. In asymptotically inertial coordinates write \(g_{\mu\nu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}+q_{\mu\nu}\), with \(q_{\mu\nu}\) small and stationary in the calculation. Retain first order in \(q\) and the leading acceleration at small \(|\mathbf v|/c\).

4b. Mathematics — convert (4) to coordinate time. Write \(w^\mu=dx^\mu/dt=(c,v^i)\). The chain rule gives

\[ \frac{d^2x^\mu}{d\lambda^2} =\left(\frac{dt}{d\lambda}\right)^2\frac{dw^\mu}{dt} +w^\mu\frac{d^2t}{d\lambda^2}. \]

The time component of (4) eliminates \(d^2t/d\lambda^2\) from its spatial components, giving

\[ \frac{d^2x^i}{dt^2} =-\Gamma^i{}_{\alpha\beta}w^\alpha w^\beta +\frac{v^i}{c}\Gamma^0{}_{\alpha\beta}w^\alpha w^\beta. \]

At the retained order only \(-c^2\Gamma^i{}_{00}\) survives. Stationarity in (3) gives \(\Gamma^i{}_{00}=-\tfrac12\delta^{ij}\partial_jq_{00}\). Thus

\[ \frac{d^2x^i}{dt^2}=\frac{c^2}{2}\partial_i q_{00} \quad\text{at the retained order.} \tag{5} \]

4c. Mathematics — match the acceleration using A11. Set (5) equal to \(-\partial_i\Phi\). Then \(\partial_i(q_{00}+2\Phi/c^2)=0\). The boundary values in A13 set the integration constant to zero. Therefore

\[ \boxed{g_{00}=-1-\frac{2\Phi}{c^2}\quad\text{to first order}.} \tag{6} \]

For a clock at rest, (1) gives \(d\tau=\sqrt{-g_{00}}\,dt=(1+\Phi/c^2)dt\) to this order.

5. Parallel transport, curvature and the Bianchi identity

5a. Definition — parallel transport. Along a path \(x(\lambda)\), parallel transport by the connection in A5 means

\[ \frac{DV^\rho}{d\lambda} =\frac{dV^\rho}{d\lambda} +\Gamma^\rho{}_{\mu\sigma}\dot x^\mu V^\sigma=0. \tag{7} \]

Metric compatibility preserves the inner product of two parallel-transported vectors along the path.

5b. Definition — fix the sign of curvature. Define \(R(X,Y)V=\nabla_X\nabla_YV-\nabla_Y\nabla_XV-\nabla_{[X,Y]}V\). For commuting coordinate directions this compares the two orders of covariant differentiation:

\[ [\nabla_\mu,\nabla_\nu]V^\rho =R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu}V^\sigma . \]

5c. Mathematics — expand the commutator. Apply \(\nabla_\mu\) to \(\partial_\nu V^\rho+\Gamma^\rho{}_{\nu\sigma}V^\sigma\) and subtract the expression with \(\mu,\nu\) exchanged. The mixed second derivatives of \(V\) cancel. The terms with one derivative of \(V\) cancel in pairs. The connection terms for the derivative index cancel by torsion freedom. The coefficient of \(V^\sigma\) is

\[ \boxed{ R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu} =\partial_\mu\Gamma^\rho{}_{\nu\sigma} -\partial_\nu\Gamma^\rho{}_{\mu\sigma} +\Gamma^\rho{}_{\mu\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\nu\sigma} -\Gamma^\rho{}_{\nu\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\mu\sigma}.} \tag{8} \]

5d. Mathematics — derive the algebraic symmetries. Lower the first index. At any chosen event use normal coordinates, so the first derivatives of \(g\) and the connection coefficients vanish there. Substitution of (3) in (8) leaves

\[ R_{abcd} =\tfrac12\bigl(g_{ad,bc}+g_{bc,ad}-g_{bd,ac}-g_{ac,bd}\bigr). \]

Exchanging \(a,b\) reverses the sign. Exchanging \(c,d\) reverses the sign. Exchanging the pairs \(ab,cd\) preserves the expression. In the cyclic sum over \(b,c,d\), each second derivative occurs twice with opposite signs. These are tensor identities, so in every coordinate system

\[ \boxed{\begin{aligned} R_{abcd}&=-R_{bacd}=-R_{abdc}=R_{cdab},\\ R_{abcd}+R_{acdb}+R_{adbc}&=0 . \end{aligned}} \tag{9} \]

The second line is the algebraic Bianchi identity.

5e. Mathematics — derive the relative acceleration of free bodies. Take a family of geodesics with tangent \(u=\partial x/\partial\tau\) and connecting vector \(J=\partial x/\partial s\). The parameter derivatives commute, so \([u,J]=0\). Torsion freedom gives \(\nabla_uJ=\nabla_Ju\). Equation (4) gives \(\nabla_u u=0\). Consequently

\[ \nabla_u\nabla_u J =\nabla_u\nabla_J u =R(u,J)u+\nabla_J\nabla_u u =R(u,J)u . \]

In a parallel-transported orthonormal frame along the central geodesic, \(u^{\hat a}=(c,0,0,0)\). Antisymmetry in the last index pair then gives

\[ \boxed{\frac{D^2J^{\hat i}}{d\tau^2} =-c^2 R^{\hat i}{}_{\hat0\hat j\hat0}J^{\hat j}.} \tag{10} \]

5f. Definition — contract the curvature. The Ricci tensor and curvature scalar are

\[ \boxed{R_{\mu\nu}=R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}, \qquad R=g^{\mu\nu}R_{\mu\nu}.} \tag{11} \]

Pair exchange in (9) gives \(R_{\mu\nu}=R_{\nu\mu}\). Contracting (8) explicitly gives the component formula used below:

\[ R_{\mu\nu} =\partial_\alpha\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\nu\mu} -\partial_\nu\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\alpha\mu} +\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\alpha\beta}\Gamma^\beta{}_{\nu\mu} -\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\nu\beta}\Gamma^\beta{}_{\alpha\mu}. \tag{12} \]

5g. Mathematics — derive the differential Bianchi identity. Differentiate the full expression (8), then evaluate at the origin of normal coordinates. Each derivative of a product \(\Gamma\Gamma\) vanishes there because each summand still contains a factor \(\Gamma\). Also \(\nabla R=\partial R\) at that event. The cyclic sum is

\[ \begin{aligned} &\nabla_eR^a{}_{bcd}+\nabla_cR^a{}_{bde}+\nabla_dR^a{}_{bec}\\ ={}&\partial_e\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db} -\partial_e\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb} +\partial_c\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{eb} -\partial_c\partial_e\Gamma^a{}_{db}\\ &+\partial_d\partial_e\Gamma^a{}_{cb} -\partial_d\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{eb}=0. \end{aligned} \tag{13} \]

The mixed derivatives cancel in pairs. Tensoriality extends (13) to all coordinates.

5h. Mathematics — contract (13) twice. First contract \(a,c\). Using (11) and antisymmetry gives

\[ \nabla_eR_{bd}+\nabla_a R^a{}_{bde}-\nabla_dR_{be}=0. \]

Now contract with \(g^{bd}\). Metric compatibility allows the metric through each derivative, and \(g^{bd}R^a{}_{bde}=-R^a{}_e\). Thus

\[ \nabla_eR-\nabla_aR^a{}_e-\nabla^bR_{be}=0, \qquad \nabla^aR_{ae}=\tfrac12\nabla_eR. \]

It follows that

\[ \boxed{\nabla^\mu \left(R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12g_{\mu\nu}R\right)=0.} \tag{14} \]

Equation (14) holds for every metric in A1 with the connection in A5, before a field equation is imposed.

6. The source and its local conservation

6a. Definition — read the components of the source in A7. In an observer’s orthonormal frame,

\[ T^{\hat0\hat0}=\varepsilon,\qquad T^{\hat0\hat i}=c\,(\text{momentum density})^i,\qquad cT^{\hat i\hat0}=(\text{energy flux})^i,\qquad T^{\hat i\hat j}=S^{ij}. \tag{15} \]

Here \(S^{ij}\) is the flux of \(i\)-momentum across a surface with normal in direction \(j\). Its diagonal elements in principal axes are the three pressures \(p_1,p_2,p_3\). In this frame

\[ T=g^{\mu\nu}T_{\mu\nu} =-\varepsilon+p_1+p_2+p_3. \tag{16} \]

6b. Assumption — apply A8 to the total source.

\[ \boxed{\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0.} \tag{17} \]

6c. Mathematics — expand the conservation law. Let \(g=\det(g_{\mu\nu})\). The determinant derivative and (3) give \(\partial_\lambda\ln\sqrt{-g}=\tfrac12g^{ab}\partial_\lambda g_{ab} =\Gamma^\mu{}_{\mu\lambda}\). Expanding (17) and collecting this trace gives

\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt{-g}}\partial_\mu(\sqrt{-g}\,T^{\mu\nu}) +\Gamma^\nu{}_{\mu\lambda}T^{\mu\lambda}=0. \tag{18} \]

At an inertial origin, the time component reads \(\partial_t\varepsilon+\partial_i(cT^{\hat i\hat0})=0\). Each spatial component reads \(\partial_t(T^{\hat0\hat j}/c)+\partial_iT^{\hat i\hat j}=0\).

7. Einstein’s field equations

7a. Assumption — specify the field-equation problem using A4, A7–A10. Seek a geometric tensor \(H_{\mu\nu}[g]\) such that

\[ H_{\mu\nu}[g]=k\,T_{\mu\nu}. \tag{19} \]

A10 supplies the proportionality to \(T_{\mu\nu}\). A9 requires \(\nabla^\mu H_{\mu\nu}\equiv0\) for arbitrary metrics. A8 then makes the source compatible with this identity on matter solutions. The distinction is between a geometric identity and an equation obeyed by matter.

7b. Mathematics — identify the possible geometric terms under A1, A4, A5 and A9. At an event choose normal coordinates. The metric there is \(\eta\) and its first derivatives vanish. The normal-coordinate expansion gives

\[ g_{ab,cd}=-\tfrac13(R_{acbd}+R_{adbc}) \]

at the origin, with the sign in (8). Thus a natural tensor linear in the second derivatives has a curvature-dependent part linear in the Riemann tensor. Its coefficients at the event must be invariant under a change of orthonormal frame. The orthogonal invariant-tensor theorem reduces these coefficients to metric contractions. Using (9), those contractions are as follows.

ContractionSymmetric rank-two result
Leave two curvature indices free and contract the other two\(R_{\mu\nu}\), up to sign, or zero
Contract all curvature indices and supply two free metric indices\(R\,g_{\mu\nu}\), up to a constant factor
Use the metric with no curvatureA constant multiple of \(g_{\mu\nu}\)

There is no varying scalar made from the value of a metric alone at a point of fixed signature. The coefficients are therefore constants. The possible tensor is

\[ H_{\mu\nu}=aR_{\mu\nu}+bRg_{\mu\nu}+d g_{\mu\nu}. \tag{20} \]

This is the quasilinear case of the four-dimensional metric uniqueness statement. In its usual four-dimensional Lovelock formulation, a symmetric, divergence-free natural metric tensor through differential order two is a linear combination of the Einstein tensor and the metric. The dimension, the metric-only construction, locality, differential order and divergence condition are hypotheses of that statement. Lovelock, The Einstein Tensor and Its Generalizations

7c. Mathematics — determine the relative curvature coefficient. Take the divergence of (20). Equations (3) and (14) give

\[ \nabla^\mu H_{\mu\nu} =\left(\frac a2+b\right)\nabla_\nu R. \]

A9 requires zero for every metric, including metrics with varying scalar curvature. Therefore \(b=-a/2\). A11 requires a nonzero differential gravitational response, so \(a\ne0\). Divide (19) by \(a\) and define \(\Lambda=d/a\), \(\kappa=k/a\). Then

\[ G_{\mu\nu}+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}=\kappa T_{\mu\nu}, \qquad G_{\mu\nu}:=R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12Rg_{\mu\nu}. \tag{21} \]

7d. Assumption — select the 1915 equation using A12. Set \(\Lambda=0\). This gives

\[ \boxed{G_{\mu\nu}=\kappa T_{\mu\nu}.} \tag{22} \]

Taking the divergence of (22) reproduces (17) for \(\kappa\ne0\). The arbitrary constant \(d\) in (20) shows precisely why the divergence identity leaves the cosmological term available.

7e. Mathematics — exhibit Einstein’s source-side trace correction. An equivalent way to do the coefficient calculation is to write the Ricci equation, after A12, as \(R_{\mu\nu}=\kappa(T_{\mu\nu}+b' g_{\mu\nu}T)\). Contraction in four dimensions gives \(R=\kappa(1+4b')T\). Taking the divergence and using A8 gives \(\nabla^\mu R_{\mu\nu}=\kappa b'\nabla_\nu T\). Equation (14) gives a second expression for the same divergence, \(\kappa(1+4b')\nabla_\nu T/2\). Compatibility for general matter therefore requires

\[ b'=\frac{1+4b'}2,\qquad b'=-\frac12. \tag{23} \]

This is the trace term in Einstein’s November 1915 source equation. Equations (20)–(23) give the modern tensor derivation of its coefficient. The later uniqueness theorem supplies the scope of the argument. Einstein, The Foundation of the General Theory of Relativity

8. Fix the constant from Newton’s limit

8a. Mathematics — calculate \(R_{00}\) to the order in A13. In (12), stationarity removes the time derivative and the products of connection coefficients are second order. Equations (3) and (6) give

\[ R_{00} =\partial_i\Gamma^i{}_{00} =-\tfrac12\nabla^2 q_{00} =\frac{1}{c^2}\nabla^2\Phi \quad\text{to first order}. \tag{24} \]

8b. Mathematics — calculate the source of \(R_{00}\) in the same limit. For the slow source in A13, \(T_{00}\simeq\rho c^2\), \(T\simeq-\rho c^2\), and \(g_{00}\simeq-1\) in the source term. Equation (23) then gives

\[ R_{00} =\kappa\left(T_{00}-\tfrac12g_{00}T\right) \simeq\kappa\left(\rho c^2-\tfrac12\rho c^2\right) =\tfrac12\kappa\rho c^2. \tag{25} \]

8c. Input from observation — identify the empirical scale in A11. The \(G\) in Newton’s law is fixed by gravitational measurement. For example, Cavendish recorded torsion-balance scale readings and oscillation times with attracting masses in specified positions. The readings are observations. Extraction of a gravitational coefficient uses the apparatus model and the Newtonian force law. No numerical value of \(G\) is required for this derivation. Cavendish, Experiments to Determine the Density of the Earth

8d. Mathematics — match where the Newtonian source density is nonzero. By A11, \(\nabla^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho\). Equating (24) and (25) gives

\[ \frac{4\pi G\rho}{c^2}=\frac{\kappa\rho c^2}{2}, \qquad \boxed{\kappa=\frac{8\pi G}{c^4}.} \tag{26} \]

Thus the fully normalized field equations are

\[ \boxed{R_{\mu\nu}-\frac12 Rg_{\mu\nu} =\frac{8\pi G}{c^4}T_{\mu\nu}.} \tag{27} \]

Matching in a Newtonian material source fixes the coefficient. In an exterior region with \(\rho=0\), equations (24)–(25) alone give \(0=0\) for every \(\kappa\).

9. Trace reversal and vacuum

9a. Mathematics — take the trace of (27). Since \(g^{\mu\nu}g_{\mu\nu}=4\),

\[ R-\tfrac12(4)R=\kappa T, \qquad R=-\kappa T. \]

Substitute back into (27) and move the trace term to the right:

\[ \boxed{R_{\mu\nu} =\frac{8\pi G}{c^4}\left(T_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12 g_{\mu\nu}T\right).} \tag{28} \]

Taking the trace of (28) returns \(R=-\kappa T\), so the two forms are algebraically equivalent.

9b. Mathematics — apply the vacuum condition A14. With \(T_{\mu\nu}=0\) and A12,

\[ \boxed{R_{\mu\nu}=0,\qquad R=0.} \tag{29} \]

Equation (29) sets the Ricci contraction of (8) to zero. The uncontracted tidal tensor can have nonzero components, as the explicit wave calculation in Part 13 also demonstrates.

10. The static equations in clocks and rulers

10a. Definition — express A15 in coordinates adapted to the static clocks. With \(x^0=ct\), choose

\[ ds^2=-f^2(dx^0)^2+h_{ij}dx^idx^j,\qquad f>0,\qquad \partial_0 f=\partial_0 h_{ij}=0. \tag{30} \]

By (1)–(2), the stationary clocks read \(d\tau=f\,dt\), and their orthogonal spatial slices have ruler metric \(d\ell^2=h_{ij}dx^idx^j\). Let \(D\) be the Levi-Civita derivative of \(h\), \(H^i{}_{jk}\) its connection coefficients, and \(\Delta_h f=D_iD^if\). The unit observer is \(n^\mu=(1/f,0,0,0)\). Define

\[ \varepsilon=T_{\mu\nu}n^\mu n^\nu=T_{00}/f^2,\qquad S_{ij}=T_{ij},\qquad S=h^{ij}S_{ij},\qquad T=-\varepsilon+S. \tag{31} \]

10b. Mathematics — calculate the connection. The inverse metric has \(g^{00}=-f^{-2}\), \(g^{0i}=0\), \(g^{ij}=h^{ij}\). Write \(f_i=\partial_i f\). Equation (3) gives the complete potentially nonzero sets

\[ \Gamma^0{}_{0i}=\frac{f_i}{f},\qquad \Gamma^i{}_{00}=fD^if,\qquad \Gamma^i{}_{jk}=H^i{}_{jk}, \tag{32} \]

and the entries obtained by exchanging the lower indices.

10c. Mathematics — calculate the time-time curvature. Insert (32) in (12). Its second term vanishes by stationarity. Its first, third and fourth terms give, respectively,

\[ \begin{aligned} R_{00} &=\partial_i(fD^if) +\left(H^j{}_{ji}+\frac{f_i}{f}\right)fD^if -2\frac{f_i}{f}\,fD^if\\ &=f\bigl(\partial_iD^if+H^j{}_{ji}D^if\bigr) +(1+1-2)f_iD^if. \end{aligned} \]

The bracket is the spatial divergence of the gradient. Hence

\[ \boxed{R_{00}=f\Delta_h f,\qquad R_{tt}=c^2 f\Delta_h f.} \tag{33} \]

The second component uses \(t\) itself as time coordinate.

10d. Mathematics — calculate the spatial and mixed curvature. The purely spatial connection terms in (12) give \(R_{ij}(h)\). The additional terms carrying a time index give

\[ \begin{aligned} R_{ij} &=R_{ij}(h)-\partial_j(f_i/f) +H^k{}_{ij}f_k/f-f_i f_j/f^2\\ &=R_{ij}(h)-f^{-1}(\partial_j f_i-H^k{}_{ij} f_k). \end{aligned} \]

For \(R_{0i}\), the derivative terms are \(\partial_0\Gamma^0{}_{i0}=0\) and \(-\partial_i\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\alpha0}=0\). In its first product the only candidate is proportional to \(\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\alpha0}=0\). In its last product every term requires \(\Gamma^0{}_{ij}\), \(\Gamma^i{}_{0j}\), or \(\Gamma^0{}_{00}\), all zero. Therefore

\[ \boxed{R_{ij}=R_{ij}(h)-f^{-1}D_iD_j f,\qquad R_{0i}=0.} \tag{34} \]

10e. Mathematics — derive the clock equation. Equations (28) and (31) give

\[ R_{00}=\kappa\left[f^2\varepsilon +\tfrac12f^2(-\varepsilon+S)\right] =\tfrac12\kappa f^2(\varepsilon+S). \]

Use (33), divide by \(f>0\), and insert (26):

\[ \boxed{\Delta_h f=\frac{4\pi G}{c^4}\,f(\varepsilon+S).} \tag{35} \]

10f. Mathematics — derive the spatial field equations. Substitute (31) and (34) in the spatial components of (28):

\[ \boxed{R_{ij}(h)-f^{-1}D_iD_j f =\frac{8\pi G}{c^4} \left[S_{ij}+\tfrac12h_{ij}(\varepsilon-S)\right].} \tag{36} \]

The mixed component gives \(0=\kappa T_{0i}\), so a static metric of the form (30) requires vanishing total energy flux in its static frame.

10g. Mathematics — obtain the spatial scalar curvature. Denote the scalar of \(h\) by \(R(h)\). Contract (36) with \(h^{ij}\):

\[ R(h)-f^{-1}\Delta_h f =\kappa\left[S+\tfrac32(\varepsilon-S)\right] =\tfrac12\kappa(3\varepsilon-S). \]

Equation (35) gives \(f^{-1}\Delta_h f=\kappa(\varepsilon+S)/2\). Adding cancels \(S\) and yields

\[ \boxed{R(h)=2\kappa\varepsilon=\frac{16\pi G}{c^4}\varepsilon.} \tag{37} \]

An independent contraction of (33)–(34) gives the spacetime scalar \(R=R(h)-2f^{-1}\Delta_h f\). Thus \(G_{00}/f^2=R(h)/2\), which checks (37) directly against (27).

11. An initially comoving small ball of free particles

11a. Definition — implement A16 in the central particle’s frame. Carry an orthonormal spatial triad parallel along the central geodesic. Let the columns of \(L^i{}_j(\tau)\) be the three Jacobi separation vectors in units of their initial lengths. Choose \(L(0)=I\). Initial relative rest throughout the ball gives \(\dot L(0)=0\) in every component. Its infinitesimal volume ratio is \(V(\tau)/V(0)=\det L(\tau)\) near \(\tau=0\).

11b. Mathematics — take the initial volume acceleration. From \(d(\det L)/d\tau=(\det L)\operatorname{tr}(L^{-1}\dot L)\), all terms quadratic in \(\dot L\) vanish initially. Equation (10) therefore gives

\[ \left.\frac{\ddot V}{V}\right|_0 =\operatorname{tr}\ddot L(0) =-c^2\sum_i R^{\hat i}{}_{\hat0\hat i\hat0} =-c^2 R_{\hat0\hat0}. \tag{38} \]

The last equality uses (11); the omitted time-index contribution vanishes by antisymmetry.

11c. Mathematics — insert the field equation. In the frame of the ball, (16) and (28) give \(R_{\hat0\hat0}=\kappa[\varepsilon+(-\varepsilon+\sum_i p_i)/2]\). Consequently, for every choice of the central inertial frame,

\[ \boxed{\left.\frac{1}{V}\frac{d^2V}{d\tau^2}\right|_0 =-\frac{4\pi G}{c^2}\,(\varepsilon+p_1+p_2+p_3).} \tag{39} \]

Each pressure and the energy density in this formula are measured in the chosen frame. The pressure sum is the spatial stress trace even when the observer measures an energy flux.

11d. Mathematics — prove the converse for all frames. Suppose (39) holds for every initially comoving infinitesimal ball at the event. Define the symmetric tensor

\[ Q_{ab}=R_{ab}-\kappa\left(T_{ab}-\tfrac12g_{ab}T\right). \]

Equations (38)–(39) give \(Q_{ab}n^a n^b=0\) for every future unit timelike \(n\). In one orthonormal basis write \(n=\gamma(1,\boldsymbol\beta)\), \(|\boldsymbol\beta|<1\). Divide by \(\gamma^2\):

\[ Q_{00}+2Q_{0i}\beta^i+Q_{ij}\beta^i\beta^j=0 \quad\text{throughout the open unit ball.} \]

At \(\boldsymbol\beta=0\) this gives \(Q_{00}=0\). Its first derivatives there give \(2Q_{0i}=0\). Its second derivatives give \(2Q_{ij}=0\). Hence \(Q_{ab}=0\), which is (28), and Part 9 returns (27). The equivalence is pointwise:

\[ \boxed{\text{Equation (39) in every local inertial frame} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G_{\mu\nu}=\frac{8\pi G}{c^4}T_{\mu\nu}.} \tag{40} \]

The quantifier “every” supplies the mixed and spatial components in the reverse implication. Baez and Bunn, The Meaning of Einstein’s Equation

12. Local energy, gravitational energy and total mass

12a. Mathematics — identify the local balance. Lower the free index in (17). Expanding the covariant divergence as in (18) gives \(\partial_\mu(\sqrt{-g}\,T^\mu{}_\nu)=\sqrt{-g}\,\Gamma^\lambda{}_{\mu\nu}T^\mu{}_\lambda\). Insert (3). Symmetry of \(T^{ab}\) cancels the two terms containing derivatives with respect to the contracted indices, leaving

\[ \boxed{\partial_\mu(\sqrt{-g}\,T^\mu{}_\nu) =\tfrac12\sqrt{-g}\,T^{ab}\partial_\nu g_{ab}.} \tag{41} \]

Equations (17)–(18) give the local energy and momentum balance for matter and nongravitational fields. Equation (41) displays the metric term that arises when one attempts to integrate a coordinate component as an ordinary conserved density.

12b. Mathematics — obtain a current when A18 supplies a symmetry. A Killing field \(k\) obeys \(\nabla_\mu k_\nu+\nabla_\nu k_\mu=0\). Define \(J^\mu=-T^{\mu\nu}k_\nu\). Then

\[ \nabla_\mu J^\mu =-(\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu})k_\nu -\tfrac12 T^{\mu\nu}(\nabla_\mu k_\nu+\nabla_\nu k_\mu)=0. \tag{42} \]

Integrating (42) over a spacetime slab by the divergence theorem equates the change of its matter Killing charge to the negative of its outward boundary flux. Vanishing boundary flux gives equality of the charges on its two time slices.

12c. Mathematics — identify the status of gravitational field energy. At any event a choice of normal coordinates sets every first metric derivative to zero. A proposed tensorial local gravitational energy density built from \(g,\partial g\) and calibrated to vanish for the constant Minkowski metric would therefore vanish at that event for every metric. Tensoriality would make it zero in every frame. This rules out a nonzero local gravitational stress-energy tensor of that form. GR permits coordinate-dependent gravitational energy-momentum expressions and invariant charges with specified boundaries. Curvature and the relative accelerations in (10) remain measurable at the event.

12d. Definition — total energy and momentum at spatial infinity, using A17. On an asymptotically Euclidean slice write its metric as \(\gamma_{ij}=\delta_{ij}+O(r^{-1})\), with first and second spatial derivatives of the correction \(O(r^{-2})\) and \(O(r^{-3})\). Take \(K_{ij}=O(r^{-2})\), with the usual integrable constraint sources and admissible asymptotically Cartesian coordinates. Choose \(K_{ij}=-\tfrac12\mathcal L_n\gamma_{ij}\), \(K=\gamma^{ij}K_{ij}\). With \(s^i\) and \(dA\) the asymptotic outward normal and area element, the ADM definitions are

\[ \boxed{\begin{aligned} E_{\rm ADM} &=\frac{c^4}{16\pi G}\lim_{r\to\infty} \int_{S_r}(\partial_j\gamma_{ij}-\partial_i\gamma_{jj})s^i\,dA,\\ P_i^{\rm ADM} &=\frac{c^3}{8\pi G}\lim_{r\to\infty} \int_{S_r}(K_{ij}-K\gamma_{ij})s^j\,dA . \end{aligned}} \tag{43} \]

The energy integrand has a direct geometric origin. For \(\gamma_{ij}=\delta_{ij}+b_{ij}\), the linear part of its spatial scalar curvature is \(\partial_i\partial_j b_{ij}-\partial_i\partial_i b_{jj} =\partial_i(\partial_jb_{ij}-\partial_i b_{jj})\), by (12). Spatial integration gives the surface combination in (43).

For timelike total four-momentum the rest mass is

\[ M_{\rm ADM}=\frac{1}{c^2} \sqrt{E_{\rm ADM}^2-c^2\delta^{ij}P_i^{\rm ADM}P_j^{\rm ADM}}. \tag{44} \]

In the asymptotic rest frame this is \(E_{\rm ADM}/c^2\). The time translation used by ADM is an asymptotic symmetry. The interior can be time dependent. Arnowitt, Deser and Misner, The Dynamics of General Relativity

12e. Definition — stationary mass, using A17–A18. For a stationary isolated spacetime, normalize the time-translation Killing field \(k\) by \(k^ak_a\to-1\) at infinity. With \(dS_{ab}=(s_a n_b-s_b n_a)dA\), the Komar mass on an enclosing two-surface is

\[ \boxed{M_{\rm K}[S]=-\frac{c^2}{8\pi G} \int_S\nabla^a k^b\,dS_{ab}.} \tag{45} \]

Its limit at infinity defines the stationary total mass with this normalization. Komar, Covariant Conservation Laws in General Relativity

12f. Mathematics — evaluate the mass with static clocks and rulers. In (30), \(k=\partial_0\) and \(n=k/f\). Equation (32) gives \(\nabla^ik^0=D^if/f\) and \(\nabla^0k^i=-D^if/f\). Since \(n_0=-f\), contraction with the surface element in (45) gives \(-2s^iD_i f\,dA_h\). Thus

\[ M_{\rm K}[S]=\frac{c^2}{4\pi G}\int_S s^iD_i f\,dA_h . \]

For two nested surfaces bounding a regular static shell \(\Omega\), the spatial divergence theorem followed by (35) gives

\[ \boxed{M_{\rm K}[S_2]-M_{\rm K}[S_1] =\frac{c^2}{4\pi G}\int_\Omega\Delta_h f\,dV_h =\frac{1}{c^2}\int_\Omega f(\varepsilon+S)\,dV_h.} \tag{46} \]

A vacuum shell gives equal masses on its two enclosing surfaces. This calculation specifies both the time symmetry and the boundary surfaces used for that equality.

13. The equations to first order and the two wave polarizations

13a. Assumption — apply A19. Write \(g_{\mu\nu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}+q_{\mu\nu}\) and retain first order in \(q\). In the sourced linear equation \(T^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}\) denotes the source at the same order about the vacuum background. Use \(\eta\) to move perturbation indices. Define \(q=\eta^{\mu\nu}q_{\mu\nu}\) and \(\Box=\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu=\nabla^2-c^{-2}\partial_t^2\).

13b. Mathematics — linearize the connection and curvature. Multiplying \(g_{\mu\alpha}g^{\alpha\nu}=\delta_\mu{}^\nu\) to first order gives \(g^{\mu\nu}=\eta^{\mu\nu}-q^{\mu\nu}\). Equation (3) becomes

\[ \Gamma^{(1)\rho}{}_{\mu\nu} =\tfrac12(\partial_\mu q^\rho{}_\nu+\partial_\nu q^\rho{}_\mu -\partial^\rho q_{\mu\nu}). \]

Its trace is \(\Gamma^{(1)\rho}{}_{\rho\mu}=\partial_\mu q/2\). Drop the quadratic products from (12), differentiate the displayed connection, and contract once more:

\[ \begin{aligned} R^{(1)}_{\mu\nu} &=\tfrac12(\partial_\mu\partial_\rho q^\rho{}_\nu +\partial_\nu\partial_\rho q^\rho{}_\mu -\Box q_{\mu\nu}-\partial_\mu\partial_\nu q),\\ R^{(1)} &=\partial_\rho\partial_\sigma q^{\rho\sigma}-\Box q . \end{aligned} \tag{47} \]

13c. Mathematics — trace-reverse the perturbation. Define \(\bar q_{\mu\nu}=q_{\mu\nu}-\eta_{\mu\nu}q/2\). In four dimensions \(\bar q=-q\), so \(q_{\mu\nu}=\bar q_{\mu\nu}-\eta_{\mu\nu}\bar q/2\). Substitute in \(G^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}=R^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}-\eta_{\mu\nu}R^{(1)}/2\). The derivatives of \(\bar q\) cancel, giving

\[ 2G^{(1)}_{\mu\nu} =-\Box\bar q_{\mu\nu} +\partial_\mu\partial^\rho\bar q_{\rho\nu} +\partial_\nu\partial^\rho\bar q_{\rho\mu} -\eta_{\mu\nu}\partial^\rho\partial^\sigma\bar q_{\rho\sigma}. \tag{48} \]

13d. Mathematics — choose Lorenz gauge using A4. Under \(x'^\mu=x^\mu+\xi^\mu\), the two covariant metric indices contribute \(q'_{\mu\nu}=q_{\mu\nu}-\partial_\mu\xi_\nu-\partial_\nu\xi_\mu\) to first order. Taking the trace reversal and then its divergence gives

\[ \partial^\mu\bar q'_{\mu\nu} =\partial^\mu\bar q_{\mu\nu}-\Box\xi_\nu. \]

Solve \(\Box\xi_\nu=\partial^\mu\bar q_{\mu\nu}\) locally, or with compatible wave-equation data on the chosen domain. This imposes \(\partial^\mu\bar q'_{\mu\nu}=0\). In that gauge (48) and (27) give

\[ \boxed{\Box\bar q_{\mu\nu}=-\frac{16\pi G}{c^4}T^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}.} \tag{49} \]

Taking the divergence gives the first-order compatibility condition \(\partial^\mu T^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}=0\).

13e. Mathematics — obtain the propagation speed in vacuum. Apply A14 in the propagation region. Set \(\bar q_{\mu\nu}=\operatorname{Re}(A_{\mu\nu}e^{ik_\alpha x^\alpha})\) for a nonzero-frequency mode. Equations (49) and the gauge condition give

\[ k_\alpha k^\alpha=0,\qquad k^\mu A_{\mu\nu}=0 . \]

With \(k^\mu=(\omega/c,\mathbf k)\), this is \(-\omega^2/c^2+|\mathbf k|^2=0\). On the positive-frequency branch \(\omega=c|\mathbf k|\). Thus the wavefronts are null and the propagation speed is \(c\).

13f. Mathematics — isolate the independent amplitudes. Choose propagation along \(+z\), so \(k^\mu=(k,0,0,k)\), \(k=\omega/c>0\). Transversality gives \(A_{3\nu}=-A_{0\nu}\). Gauge transformations with \(\Box\xi_\nu=0\) still preserve Lorenz gauge. For a mode of the same wavevector, absorb the derivative’s factor of \(i\) into four amplitudes \(b_\nu\). The change is

\[ \delta A_{\mu\nu}=-k_\mu b_\nu-k_\nu b_\mu+\eta_{\mu\nu}k^\alpha b_\alpha . \]

The four combinations needed here change independently:

\[ \delta A_{01}=k b_1,\qquad \delta A_{02}=k b_2,\qquad \delta A_{00}=k(b_0-b_3),\qquad \delta(A_{11}+A_{22})=2k(b_0+b_3). \]

Choose them to set \(A_{01},A_{02},A_{00},A_{11}+A_{22}\) to zero. Transversality then sets every component with a \(0\) or \(3\) index to zero. The amplitude is traceless, so \(q=\bar q\) componentwise in this gauge. The two remaining amplitudes are

\[ \boxed{ A^{\rm TT}_{ij}= \begin{pmatrix} A_+&A_\times&0\\ A_\times&-A_+&0\\ 0&0&0 \end{pmatrix}.} \tag{50} \]

13g. Mathematics — check the physical displacements. Substituting the transverse, traceless perturbation in (8) gives \(R^{(1)}_{i0j0}=-\partial_0^2q^{\rm TT}_{ij}/2\). Equation (10) yields

\[ \boxed{\frac{d^2J^i}{d\tau^2} =\frac12\,\partial_t^2 q^{\rm TT}_{ij}\,J^j} \tag{51} \]

at the retained order for a central observer at rest in the background coordinates. The \(+\) amplitude produces opposite relative accelerations along \(x\) and \(y\). The \(\times\) amplitude produces the same pattern on axes rotated through \(45^\circ\). Their tidal trace is zero, in agreement with (38) in vacuum.

06 / RESEARCH NOTES

Reconciliation of the Two Derivations

Section 4 derived general relativity from the conservation laws. Section 5 derived it the way Einstein did. This section lays the two side by side the way a code review shows a change: the lines taken away in red, the lines that replace them or are added beside them in green, the lines that stay in grey.

Each box below holds Einstein's derivation first, as it stands in Section 5, and then the same derivation line by line with the changes marked. The child's box carries the recipe, the teacher's box the simplified derivation, and the physicist's box Einstein's assumptions and every step of his derivation.

1. What stays.

For one point mass at rest, outside its event horizon, the two derivations give the same clocks and the same rulers:

\[ F=f^2=1-\frac Lr,\qquad d\ell=\frac{dr}{f},\qquad R_{\mu\nu}=0 . \]

For several point masses they give the same clocks to first order. The mathematics of curvature stays. So does the one input from observation, Newton's law far from the mass, which fixes \(G\).

2. What Einstein assumes and the conservation derivation derives.

Einstein assumesThe conservation derivation derives it from
The equivalence principle (A2)premises 4 and 5, with special relativity at one place: no force, no work, so the same clocks, rulers and mass
Clocks and rulers read one metric (A3)the f dot dr idea for the clock; for the rulers, the f dot dr in the field set equal to the f dot dr needed to generate the motion, with special relativity at one place
Free bodies follow the straightest paths (A6)premise 4, with special relativity at one place, for the fall along the radius; the paths in other directions are not yet worked out in this paper
Newton's law as a limit far from the mass (A11)the counted pull of a point mass is Newton's law exactly, at every strength, once Newton's law far away has fixed \(G\)
Equations chosen from a class (A9, A10)premise 1: the count sets the pull, anything is a point mass, and the integral of f dot dr gives the clock
That the arrangement is the same at every time (A15)the count does not change, which keeps the clocks and rulers outside a round body at rest the same; when bodies move, the clocks change with their places, and the same sum holds at every moment
The mass of the source, defined far away (A17, A18)the complete count inside a closed surface, \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}=E_{\mathrm{enc}}/c^2\)

3. Where the two part.

Three of Einstein's assumptions are not taken over.

One metric for every observer (A1). In Einstein's derivation every observer measures components of one and the same metric, at every distance. When his solution for one body is continued across \(L\), general relativity takes one metric for all observers and continues the same solution, with the same mass, on the other side (Section 9). Nothing outside \(L\) requires that step. It is the step by which general relativity merges the frames' different values into one event horizon, and it is the error that this paper names (Section 18). The conservation derivation does the calculation in one frame with that frame's ruler, scale and clock. Outside \(L\) the readings of the frames held at rest and of the frames that fall fit one line element, as a result (Section 4, statement 6). The continuation across \(L\) is not taken. In its place stand premises 7 and 8:

\[ s_{PQ}=\pm\,i\,\sqrt{\frac{L/r_Q-1}{1-L/r_P}}\ \ \text{across } L,\qquad \Big(\frac{dr}{d\tau}\Big)^2=c^2\Big(e^2-\Big|1-\frac Lr\Big|\Big). \]

What two frames read is real for each from its own frame of reference, an inferred measurement across \(L\) has two solutions, and objects move beyond their event horizon. The observation that decides: anything, light or matter, arriving outside from inside an event horizon (Section 18).

Equations that are not linear (A9). Einstein's equations are not linear: for point masses at different places their solution is not the sum of the solutions for each. In the conservation derivation the counted pull of every point mass is Newton's law in the frame of the calculation, the pulls add, and so do the squared-clock deficits, exactly, with the pull counted through the areas of that frame's grid (Section 4, statement 7 and its premise table):

\[ F(\mathbf x)=1-\sum_a\frac{L_a}{|\mathbf x-\mathbf x_a|}. \]

In Einstein's equations, for bodies at rest on one line and held apart, the clock rates multiply (Weyl's solutions, with each body's rate taken in his coordinates). So for the same two deficits the two give the same clocks to first order and part at the second, by the product of the two deficits: for the deficits 0.25 and 0.0833 the squared clock rate is 0.6667 here and 0.6875 there. The rule for the rulers between two bodies, with the ruler, the scale and the clock updated to the frame of the calculation, is not yet stated in Section 4, and nothing is claimed about it here. The observation that could decide: clock rates measured between two bodies (Section 10, Part 16).

Changes that move at the speed of light (A4, A9, A10; part 13). In Einstein's derivation his equations go on holding while the arrangement changes. To first order (A19) they then give a wave equation for a change of the metric, and a wave of such change moves at the speed \(c\) (steps 13d and 13e). General relativity reads such a wave as carrying energy and momentum away; Section 5 itself gives the pattern of clocks and rulers no local density of energy (part 12). In its place stands premise 6: the rulers are updated instantaneously (not transferred via information carried by light and at the speed of light). The same sum holds at every moment \(T\), with each body's place and count at that moment:

\[ F(\mathbf x,T)=1-\sum_a\frac{L_a(T)}{|\mathbf x-\mathbf x_a(T)|},\qquad \frac{d\mathbf P}{dT}=\sum_i\mathbf F_i(T)=0 . \]

The observations that could decide: whether an instrument takes up energy, or recoils, when a count far from it moves, with no light from the event; and when an instrument registers the change, compared with the light from the same event. Premise 6 says what is seen: the change is at once, and what an instrument registers comes with the light, so a delay that is observed is the light's (Section 3). The mathematics of what a given instrument registers is still to be written in this paper.

4. How Einstein's derivation is reconciled with the conservation laws.

By three changes. Its assumptions about clocks, rulers, free fall and the source become results. Its solution for one body at rest is kept, because the count gives the same. And the three assumptions of statement 3 are replaced: by the exact sum for several bodies, and by premises 6, 7 and 8.

For a child

The recipe, as it stands in Section 5

Here is the whole recipe that Einstein used to get his equations, every step written out.

It starts by assuming that there is one map of space and time, and that everyone, wherever they are and however they move, reads their clocks and rulers off that same map.

It assumes that inside a small falling room nothing feels the pull, and that things left alone follow the straightest lines on the map.

It measures how the map bends by watching two things that fall side by side drift together or apart.

Then it looks for the simplest rule that ties the bending to the energy of the stuff that is there, and it sets the one number in that rule so that far from a heavy body it gives Newton's old law.

Two things come out at the end: Einstein's equations, and ripples in the map that move at the speed of light.

The recipe, redone with conservation, line by line

− red: taken away  ·  + green: replaces it, or is added beside it  ·  grey: unchanged

 

Here is the whole recipe that Einstein used to get his equations, every step written out.

−

It starts by assuming that there is one map of space and time, and that everyone, wherever they are and however they move, reads their clocks and rulers off that same map.

+

It starts from everything inside the bubble, whose total never changes because the lid stays on. Each person keeps their own clock, their own ruler and their own scale, and what each one reads with them is real. The maps of neighbours fit together smoothly, and that is all the recipe needs. It does not need one map for everyone all the way across an edge.

−

It assumes that inside a small falling room nothing feels the pull, and that things left alone follow the straightest lines on the map.

+

It shows why nothing in a falling room feels the pull: nobody is pushing, so no work is done, and the one who falls keeps the clock, the ruler and the scale they started with. Things left alone follow the straightest lines for that reason.

 

It measures how the map bends by watching two things that fall side by side drift together or apart.

−

Then it looks for the simplest rule that ties the bending to the energy of the stuff that is there, and it sets the one number in that rule so that far from a heavy body it gives Newton's old law.

+

It does not look for a rule. The rule is already there: the pull through any closed bubble is set by the total inside it, so anything in a bubble pulls like one small heavy point. Adding up the pull along the way gives every clock, and for many points the effects simply add. The one number is set the same way, by Newton's old law far away.

−

Two things come out at the end: Einstein's equations, and ripples in the map that move at the speed of light.

+

Two things come out at the end: the same clocks and rulers as Einstein's around one body that sits still, and a different answer when there are many bodies or when something moves. For many bodies the effects simply add. When something moves, every clock and every ruler changes at once, and light does not carry the change to them.

For a high school physics teacher

The simplified derivation, as it stands in Section 5

The assumptions. Twenty-one things are assumed, listed in part 1. The ones that carry the derivation: there is one spacetime with one metric, the same for all observers; in a small freely falling laboratory special relativity holds (the equivalence principle); ideal clocks and rulers read the metric; the equations have the same form in every coordinate system; free bodies follow the straightest paths; matter enters through one stress-energy tensor \(T_{\mu\nu}\), conserved locally; the equation for the metric is of second order; Newton's law holds far from the mass; and the cosmological constant is zero.

Free fall. In the falling laboratory a free body moves uniformly in a straight line. Written in any coordinates this is the geodesic equation, \(\ddot x^\sigma+\Gamma^\sigma{}_{\mu\nu}\,\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu=0\) (part 3).

Newton's limit of free fall. For slow motion far from the mass the geodesic equation becomes Newton's \(\mathbf a=-\boldsymbol\nabla\Phi\) if \(g_{00}=-(1+2\Phi/c^2)\). A clock at rest then runs at \(1+\Phi/c^2\) (part 4).

Curvature. Two neighbouring free bodies accelerate relative to one another, and the Riemann tensor measures it. Its contractions are the Ricci tensor \(R_{\mu\nu}\) and the scalar \(R\), and they obey an identity of their own: \(\nabla^\mu(R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12g_{\mu\nu}R)=0\) (part 5).

The source. The energy density, the momentum density and the stresses of matter are the components of \(T_{\mu\nu}\), and \(\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0\) (part 6).

The field equations. Among tensors built from the metric with at most second derivatives, the only one whose divergence vanishes identically is \(R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12g_{\mu\nu}R\), up to a constant times the metric. Setting it equal to a constant times \(T_{\mu\nu}\), with no cosmological term: \(R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12g_{\mu\nu}R=\kappa T_{\mu\nu}\) (part 7).

The constant. Newton's law \(\nabla^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho\) far from the mass fixes \(\kappa=8\pi G/c^4\) (part 8). In empty space the equations are \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\) (part 9).

A still arrangement, in clocks and rulers. With the clock rate \(f\) and the rulers \(h\), the equations read \(\Delta_hf=(4\pi G/c^4)\,f\,(\varepsilon+S)\) and \(R_{ij}(h)-D_iD_jf/f=(8\pi G/c^4)\,[S_{ij}+\tfrac12h_{ij}(\varepsilon-S)]\), with \(S\) the sum of the three pressures (part 10).

A small ball of free particles, at rest relative to one another, starts to shrink at the rate \(\ddot V/V=-(4\pi G/c^2)(\varepsilon+p_1+p_2+p_3)\), in every local inertial frame. That statement, for every such frame, is equivalent to the field equations (part 11).

Energy. The energy and momentum of matter are balanced from place to place. The gravitational field itself has no energy density that can be given at a point. A total mass exists for an isolated system that is flat far away, or for one with a symmetry in time (part 12).

Changes. To first order the equations are a wave equation, \(\Box\,\bar q_{\mu\nu}=-(16\pi G/c^4)\,T_{\mu\nu}\). A change of the metric moves at the speed \(c\), with two polarizations (part 13).

The simplified derivation, redone with conservation, line by line

− red: taken away  ·  + green: replaces it, or is added beside it  ·  grey: unchanged

 

The assumptions. Twenty-one things are assumed, listed in part 1. The ones that carry the derivation: there is one spacetime with one metric, the same for all observers; in a small freely falling laboratory special relativity holds (the equivalence principle); ideal clocks and rulers read the metric; the equations have the same form in every coordinate system; free bodies follow the straightest paths; matter enters through one stress-energy tensor \(T_{\mu\nu}\), conserved locally; the equation for the metric is of second order; Newton's law holds far from the mass; and the cosmological constant is zero.

+

In the conservation derivation none of these is assumed as it stands. It starts from the conservation laws of Section 2 and the premises of Section 3. Special relativity at one place, Newton's law far from the mass and Planck's relation are used with them (Section 4).

−

Free fall. In the falling laboratory a free body moves uniformly in a straight line. Written in any coordinates this is the geodesic equation, \(\ddot x^\sigma+\Gamma^\sigma{}_{\mu\nu}\,\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu=0\) (part 3).

+

Free fall. A frame that needs no force does no work, so it keeps the clock, the rulers and the mass of the frame it left (premise 4). The frame that falls past a held frame is in the motion that the same integral of f dot dr would generate there, \(\gamma=1/f\) (Section 4, statement 4). Special relativity holds in it, a free body moves uniformly in a straight line in it, and its count \(\gamma f\) stays fixed.

−

Newton's limit of free fall. For slow motion far from the mass the geodesic equation becomes Newton's \(\mathbf a=-\boldsymbol\nabla\Phi\) if \(g_{00}=-(1+2\Phi/c^2)\). A clock at rest then runs at \(1+\Phi/c^2\) (part 4).

+

The clock at every strength of the pull. The three steps give \(f_A/f_B=\exp(\int_A^B\mathbf g\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell/c^2)\) with no limit taken, and the counted pull of a point mass is Newton's law exactly (Section 4, statements 1 and 6). Far from the mass the clock rate is \(1+\Phi/c^2\), the same.

 

Curvature. Two neighbouring free bodies accelerate relative to one another, and the Riemann tensor measures it. Its contractions are the Ricci tensor \(R_{\mu\nu}\) and the scalar \(R\), and they obey an identity of their own: \(\nabla^\mu(R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12g_{\mu\nu}R)=0\) (part 5).

+

The same mathematics. In the conservation derivation the curvature between two points is the integral of f dot dr (Section 4, statement 1).

−

The source. The energy density, the momentum density and the stresses of matter are the components of \(T_{\mu\nu}\), and \(\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0\) (part 6).

+

The source. The source is the count: every kind of energy inside a closed surface, counted once in one observer's units, with the mass equivalent \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}=E_{\mathrm{enc}}/c^2\). For a closed system it does not change (Section 2).

−

The field equations. Among tensors built from the metric with at most second derivatives, the only one whose divergence vanishes identically is \(R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12g_{\mu\nu}R\), up to a constant times the metric. Setting it equal to a constant times \(T_{\mu\nu}\), with no cosmological term: \(R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12g_{\mu\nu}R=\kappa T_{\mu\nu}\) (part 7).

+

The equations. No class of equations is chosen. The count sets the pull through every closed surface (premise 1), so anything inside a closed surface is a point mass. In the frame of the calculation the counted pull of a point mass is Newton's law, exactly, and the integral of f dot dr gives \(f^2=1-2G\mathcal M/(c^2r)\). For many point masses the deficits \(1-f^2\) add exactly (Section 4, statements 5 to 7).

 

The constant. Newton's law \(\nabla^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho\) far from the mass fixes \(\kappa=8\pi G/c^4\) (part 8). In empty space the equations are \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\) (part 9).

+

The same input from observation, used the same way. Empty space holds no count, so no constant is added. Around one point mass the result satisfies \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\).

 

A still arrangement, in clocks and rulers. With the clock rate \(f\) and the rulers \(h\), the equations read \(\Delta_hf=(4\pi G/c^4)\,f\,(\varepsilon+S)\) and \(R_{ij}(h)-D_iD_jf/f=(8\pi G/c^4)\,[S_{ij}+\tfrac12h_{ij}(\varepsilon-S)]\), with \(S\) the sum of the three pressures (part 10).

+

The first equation is premise 1 written at a point, and it holds here for any arrangement of point masses. Around one point mass the second holds as well. For several point masses the ruler along the force follows the force at each place, and the deficits add exactly in the grid of the frame of the calculation (Section 4, statement 7). Which frame of the calculation applies between two bodies, for the lengths, areas and light paths there, is not yet stated (Section 4, the physicist's box).

 

A small ball of free particles, at rest relative to one another, starts to shrink at the rate \(\ddot V/V=-(4\pi G/c^2)(\varepsilon+p_1+p_2+p_3)\), in every local inertial frame. That statement, for every such frame, is equivalent to the field equations (part 11).

+

Around one point mass a small cloud of free particles in empty space keeps its volume at first, at rest and in any motion. Here that is a result of the clocks and rulers of Section 4, checked by direct calculation of the particles' paths. The conservation derivation does not start from it.

−

Energy. The energy and momentum of matter are balanced from place to place. The gravitational field itself has no energy density that can be given at a point. A total mass exists for an isolated system that is flat far away, or for one with a symmetry in time (part 12).

+

Energy. The potential energy is in the count, as the clock rate: an energy held at rest counts in A's units at \(f\) times what its own frame reads. The mass of a closed system is the mass equivalent of the complete count inside any closed surface. It takes no condition far away and no symmetry in time, and it is conserved (Section 2).

−

Changes. To first order the equations are a wave equation, \(\Box\,\bar q_{\mu\nu}=-(16\pi G/c^4)\,T_{\mu\nu}\). A change of the metric moves at the speed \(c\), with two polarizations (part 13).

+

Bodies in motion. Premise 6: the rulers are updated instantaneously (not transferred via information carried by light and at the speed of light). At every moment the same sum holds, with each body's place and count at that moment (Section 4, statement 8). General relativity's premise at this step is that its equations go on holding while the arrangement changes. A wave of change in clocks and rulers then moves at the speed of light, and general relativity reads it as carrying energy and momentum away.

For a theoretical physicist

Einstein's assumptions and steps, as they stand in Section 5

A1. Assumption. One spacetime metric. Spacetime is a smooth four-dimensional manifold with one smooth Lorentzian metric \(g\) of signature \((-+++)\). Every observer measures components of this same metric. Choose a time orientation wherever future-directed observers are used. Reference: Einstein, The Foundation of the General Theory of Relativity (1916), and Wald, General Relativity, chapters 2–3.

A2. Assumption. Equivalence principle. Freely falling test bodies with the same initial position and velocity fall alike. In a sufficiently small freely falling laboratory, nongravitational physics takes its special-relativistic form locally. The exact local statement used below is at the central event. Tidal effects across a finite laboratory are calculated in Part 5. Reference: Einstein (1916), §§2–4.

A3. Assumption. Metric clocks and rulers. An ideal clock measures proper time along its worldline. An ideal local ruler measures the metric length of a separation simultaneous in its rest frame. The locally measured speed of light is \(c\). Reference: Einstein (1916), §4.

A4. Assumption. General covariance. The field equation is a tensor equation valid in arbitrary smooth coordinates. Its geometric side is constructed naturally from the metric, with no preferred coordinate system or fixed background geometry. Reference: Einstein (1916), §§3, 12, and the metric hypotheses specified in A9.

A5. Assumption. Metric connection. The connection governing spacetime parallel transport is torsion-free and metric-compatible. Reference: the metric formulation of GR, Wald, chapter 3.

A6. Assumption. Free propagation. A structureless massive test body subject only to gravity follows a timelike geodesic. A freely propagating light ray in geometric optics follows a null geodesic. Proper time is an affine parameter for the massive body. An affine parameter is chosen separately for the light ray. Reference: Einstein (1916), §§9, 13, 22, and Wald, chapters 3–4.

A7. Assumption. Matter source. Matter and nongravitational fields together have a symmetric stress-energy tensor \(T_{\mu\nu}\). Its local components give energy density, momentum density, energy flux and stress. Reference: Einstein (1916), §16, and Wald, chapter 4.

A8. Assumption. Local conservation. When the matter equations hold, total nongravitational stress-energy obeys \(\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0\). Interacting constituents can exchange energy and momentum. The conservation statement applies to their sum. Reference: Einstein (1916), §§16–18.

A9. Assumption. Class of geometric field equations. The geometric side is a smooth, local, natural, symmetric rank-two tensor of the metric alone. It involves derivatives through order two and is linear in the second derivatives, allowing an additive term independent of them. Its covariant divergence vanishes identically for every metric. This last condition is the geometric compatibility requirement used in the uniqueness argument. Reference: the second-order metric construction in Einstein (1916), §§12–16, and the modern uniqueness theorem of Lovelock (1971).

A10. Assumption. Universal coupling. The source side is a single universal constant times \(T_{\mu\nu}\), algebraically and linearly, for every kind of matter. Reference: Einstein, Die Feldgleichungen der Gravitation (1915), and Einstein (1916), §16.

A11. Assumption. Newtonian correspondence. In Newton’s limit ordinary matter obeys \(\mathbf a=-\boldsymbol\nabla\Phi\) and \(\nabla^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho\), with \(G\) fixed by gravitational measurements. Reference: Newtonian gravitation and Einstein (1916), §21.

A12. Assumption. Zero cosmological constant. Set \(\Lambda=0\). This selects the field equations of Einstein’s November 1915 paper. The place where the general metric construction admits \(\Lambda\) is displayed in Part 7.

A13. Assumption. Conditions for the Newtonian calibration. Use an isolated, nearly Minkowskian, stationary configuration with slow test motion, slow source motion and stresses small compared with rest-energy density. Normalize time at infinity and put \(\Phi(\infty)=0\). These are conditions on the calibration calculation in Parts 4 and 8. Reference: Einstein (1916), §21.

A14. Assumption. Vacuum specialization. In a region called vacuum below, \(T_{\mu\nu}=0\), including the stress-energy of nongravitational fields. Reference: Einstein (1916), §14.

A15. Assumption. Static specialization. In Part 10 there is a hypersurface-orthogonal timelike Killing field. Work in its timelike region, with clocks at rest along its flow. Reference: the definition of staticity in metric GR, Wald, chapter 6.

A16. Assumption. Small-ball experiment. Use an infinitesimal ball of freely falling test particles. At the initial event its relative velocity gradient vanishes in the central particle’s inertial frame. The central velocity may be any future timelike velocity. Reference: Baez and Bunn, The Meaning of Einstein’s Equation.

A17. Assumption. Isolated-system boundary conditions. For energy and momentum at spatial infinity, assume an asymptotically flat spacelike end with the falloff and integrability needed for the ADM surface integrals. Reference: Arnowitt, Deser and Misner, The Dynamics of General Relativity.

A18. Assumption. Time symmetry for a Killing charge. Where a time-translation Killing field is used, assume it exists. For the stationary mass at infinity normalize it to unit timelike length there. For a conserved current integrated over a bounded region, specify its boundary flux. Reference: Komar, Covariant Conservation Laws in General Relativity.

A19. Assumption. First-order waves. In Part 13 expand about Minkowski spacetime, retain terms of first order in the metric perturbation, and use a vacuum propagation region to identify the freely propagating polarizations. Reference: linearized GR, Wald, chapter 4.

A20. Assumption. The density of Newton's law. The density \(\rho\) in Newton's law is the matter's rest-energy density divided by \(c^2\). It enters at step 8b. (Named by the check of this derivation.)

A21. Assumption. The chart of Newton's law. The chart's \(t\) and \(x^i\) are the time and the lengths of Newton's law, for observers at rest in the chart. It enters at step 4c and is used again in steps 8a and 8d. (Named by the check of this derivation.)
