07 / RESEARCH NOTES

The Full Schwarzschild Derivation

We derive the Schwarzschild geometry from the Einstein field equations, starting with spherical symmetry and a general metric—not with the Schwarzschild metric itself.

The purpose is to establish every mathematical step, especially the origin of

\[ \boxed{N(r)B(r)=1} \]

and

\[ \boxed{r_s=\frac{2GM}{c^2}}. \]

We also distinguish the assumptions supplied by GR from the relationships that follow mathematically, so that the derivation can later be compared with the conservation of mass-energy.

Context and Core Idea

This is general relativity's own derivation of the Schwarzschild solution, complete, from the field equations to the horizon, so that every premise this paper attacks can be pointed to by its part number: staticity and the vacuum exterior (part 1), the identification of the mass far away (part 9), the extension through the horizon (parts 15 to 17), and the conserved energy that follows from staticity (part 12). The derivation also states general relativity's own reading of the inside, that nothing moves outward there (parts 16 and 17); the paper's answer to that reading is in Sections 9 and 14.
The derivation ends with the finding that matters most for this paper: the Schwarzschild solution rests on two radial relationships, the Gaussian gravitational flux and the clock-ruler constraint NB = 1, and only the first follows from conservation. The second is imported from the field equations under the static premise; in this paper it comes from f dot dr: the ruler of a frame held at rest (Section 4, statement 4).
For a child

Here is the whole recipe the textbooks use to get the black-hole formula, every step written out. It starts by assuming the pull never changes and that there is nothing outside the black hole, works through a lot of algebra, and ends with the formula and its edge. Two things come out at the end: one rule that says how the pull spreads out (which is just energy adding up), and a second rule about clocks and rulers that the recipe takes from Einstein's equations. The second rule is the one nobody has ever checked near the edge.

For a high school physics teacher

The assumptions. Six things are assumed before anything is calculated: the geometry is the same in every direction; it does not change with time (staticity); there is no matter or energy outside the source; far away space is flat; Einstein's equations hold; and \(r\) is defined so that a sphere has area \(4\pi r^2\).

The general metric. With those assumptions the line element can be written \(ds^2=-N(r)^2c^2dt^2+B(r)^2dr^2+r^2d\Omega^2\), with two unknown functions: \(N\), the rate of a clock held at rest (\(d\tau=N\,dt\)), and \(B\), the stretch of a radial ruler (\(d\ell=B\,dr\)). Nothing about the field has been put in yet.

The field equations. In empty space Einstein's equations reduce to \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\). Writing out the curvature (the Christoffel symbols and the Ricci tensor, parts 4 and 5) gives three equations for \(N\) and \(B\).

Clocks and rulers are reciprocal. Adding the time-time and radial-radial equations makes every second derivative cancel and leaves \(N'/N+B'/B=0\), so \(NB\) is constant; flat space far away makes it 1: \(NB=1\). This is the step that fixes the ruler once the clock is known, and it comes from two field equations, not from conservation.

The form of the clock. The remaining angular equation becomes \(\frac{d}{dr}(rN^2)=1\), so \(N^2=1+C/r\). Far from the mass, Newton's law fixes the constant: \(C=-2GM/c^2\). So \(N^2=1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}\) and \(B=1/N\): the Schwarzschild metric. Part 11 checks it by substitution.

Redshift and the edge. Because nothing changes with time, a photon's energy times the clock rate where it is read, \(N\,E_{\rm local}\), is the same everywhere (part 12): that is the exact gravitational redshift. \(N\) is zero where \(r_s=2GM/c^2\) (part 13). The curvature there is finite (part 14), and in coordinates that stay regular (part 15) the formula says that inside \(r_s\) nothing moves to larger \(r\) (parts 16 and 17). The paper's answer to that is in Sections 9 and 14.

What conservation gives, and what it does not. The pull through any sphere, redshifted, is the same, \(4\pi GM\) (part 18): that is the Gaussian-surface relation this paper started from. But it is one equation for two functions. The second equation, \(NB=1\), comes from the field equations under the static premise (parts 19 to 21); in this paper it comes from f dot dr: the ruler of a frame held at rest (Section 4, statement 4), which Section 9 carries into the derivation.

For a theoretical physicist (the derivation, verbatim)

We derive the Schwarzschild geometry from the Einstein field equations, starting with spherical symmetry and a general metric—not with the Schwarzschild metric itself.

The purpose is to establish every mathematical step, especially the origin of

\[ \boxed{N(r)B(r)=1} \]

and

\[ \boxed{r_s=\frac{2GM}{c^2}}. \]

We also distinguish the assumptions supplied by GR from the relationships that follow mathematically, so that the derivation can later be compared with the conservation of mass-energy.

1. Physical thought experiment

Imagine an isolated, nonrotating, electrically neutral spherical mass \(M\), surrounded by two concentric Gaussian surfaces at radii \(r_1\) and \(r_2\).

The two surfaces are imaginary measurement boundaries, not material shells.

We assume:

  1. Spherical symmetry: The geometry is unchanged under spatial rotations.
  2. Staticity: The exterior geometry is time-independent and invariant under time reversal.
  3. Vacuum exterior: No matter or nongravitational field stress-energy is present outside the source.
  4. Asymptotic flatness: Far from the source, spacetime approaches Minkowski spacetime.
  5. Einstein gravity: The metric satisfies Einstein's field equations, with zero cosmological constant.
  6. Areal radius: The coordinate \(r\) is defined so a sphere has area \(4\pi r^2\).

The derivation applies to the static exterior region. We will subsequently extend the resulting geometry through the horizon using regular coordinates. Label (this paper): that extension, parts 15 to 17, is the step this paper attacks. The regular coordinates carry the same static form inside, where nothing has tested it.

2. Construct the most general static spherical metric

Begin with four coordinates:

\[ x^\mu=(ct,r,\theta,\phi). \]

Spherical symmetry restricts the angular part to

\[ r^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2). \]

Staticity permits a time coordinate in which the metric has no time-space cross terms.

Therefore, in the static region,

\[ \boxed{ ds^2=-N(r)^2c^2dt^2+B(r)^2dr^2 +r^2d\theta^2+r^2\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2 } \tag{1} \]

where \(N(r)>0\) and \(B(r)>0\).

At infinity,

\[ \lim_{r\to\infty}N(r)=1,\qquad \lim_{r\to\infty}B(r)=1. \]

We have not yet specified the gravitational field or inserted any Schwarzschild factors.

Physical interpretation

For a stationary clock, \(dr=d\theta=d\phi=0\), so

\[ ds^2=-c^2d\tau^2=-N^2c^2dt^2. \]

Thus,

\[ \boxed{d\tau=N(r)\,dt.} \tag{2} \]

For a radial distance measured at constant \(t\),

\[ \boxed{d\ell=B(r)\,dr.} \tag{3} \]

These define our clock and radial ruler functions.

3. Introduce convenient metric functions

Write

\[ N(r)=e^{\nu(r)},\qquad B(r)=e^{\lambda(r)}. \]

Then

\[ ds^2=-e^{2\nu}c^2dt^2+e^{2\lambda}dr^2+r^2d\Omega^2. \tag{4} \]

For the curvature calculation, temporarily use \(x^0=ct\).

The metric components are

\[ g_{\mu\nu}= \begin{pmatrix} -e^{2\nu}&0&0&0\\ 0&e^{2\lambda}&0&0\\ 0&0&r^2&0\\ 0&0&0&r^2\sin^2\theta \end{pmatrix}. \tag{5} \]

Its inverse is

\[ g^{\mu\nu}= \begin{pmatrix} -e^{-2\nu}&0&0&0\\ 0&e^{-2\lambda}&0&0\\ 0&0&r^{-2}&0\\ 0&0&0&(r^2\sin^2\theta)^{-1} \end{pmatrix}. \tag{6} \]

The determinant is

\[ g=-e^{2(\nu+\lambda)}r^4\sin^2\theta, \]

so

\[ \sqrt{-g}=e^{\nu+\lambda}r^2\sin\theta. \tag{7} \]

The functions \(\nu\) and \(\lambda\) are still completely unknown.

4. Calculate the Christoffel symbols

The Levi-Civita connection is defined by

\[ \boxed{ \Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\nu} =\frac12g^{\alpha\beta} \left( \partial_\mu g_{\beta\nu} +\partial_\nu g_{\beta\mu} -\partial_\beta g_{\mu\nu} \right). } \tag{8} \]

Because the metric is static, all time derivatives vanish. Label (this paper): assumption 2; outside the horizon it follows from conservation, the count inside the surface being constant (Section 4, statements 5 and 6); what this paper attacks is carrying it inside the horizon (parts 15 to 17).

The relevant radial derivatives are

\[ \begin{aligned} \partial_r g_{00}&=-2\nu'e^{2\nu},\\ \partial_r g_{rr}&=2\lambda'e^{2\lambda},\\ \partial_r g_{\theta\theta}&=2r,\\ \partial_r g_{\phi\phi}&=2r\sin^2\theta. \end{aligned} \]

The angular derivatives include

\[ \partial_\theta g_{\phi\phi} =2r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta. \]

A prime denotes differentiation with respect to \(r\).

Example: calculate \(\Gamma^r_{00}\)

By Equation (8),

\[ \Gamma^r_{00} =-\frac12g^{rr}\partial_rg_{00}. \]

Substitute:

\[ =-\frac12e^{-2\lambda}(-2\nu'e^{2\nu}). \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{\Gamma^r_{00}=\nu'e^{2(\nu-\lambda)}.} \]

Complete list of nonzero independent Christoffel symbols

\[ \begin{aligned} \Gamma^0_{0r}&=\nu',\\ \Gamma^r_{00}&=\nu'e^{2(\nu-\lambda)},\\ \Gamma^r_{rr}&=\lambda',\\ \Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}&=-re^{-2\lambda},\\ \Gamma^r_{\phi\phi}&=-re^{-2\lambda}\sin^2\theta,\\ \Gamma^\theta_{r\theta}&=\frac1r,\\ \Gamma^\phi_{r\phi}&=\frac1r,\\ \Gamma^\theta_{\phi\phi}&=-\sin\theta\cos\theta,\\ \Gamma^\phi_{\theta\phi}&=\cot\theta. \end{aligned} \tag{9} \]

The connection is symmetric in its two lower indices, so entries related by exchanging those indices are also present.

This completes the connection calculation.

5. Calculate the Ricci tensor

We adopt the curvature convention

\[ R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu\Gamma^\rho_{\nu\sigma} -\partial_\nu\Gamma^\rho_{\mu\sigma} +\Gamma^\rho_{\mu\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha_{\nu\sigma} -\Gamma^\rho_{\nu\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\sigma}. \]

Contracting gives

\[ R_{\mu\nu}=R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}. \]

Equivalently,

\[ \boxed{ R_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\alpha\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\nu} -\partial_\nu\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\alpha} +\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\nu}\Gamma^\beta_{\alpha\beta} -\Gamma^\beta_{\mu\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha_{\nu\beta}. } \tag{10} \]

We calculate each independent component.

5.1 Time-time component

The first term is

\[ \partial_r\Gamma^r_{00} =e^{2(\nu-\lambda)} \left[\nu''+2\nu'(\nu'-\lambda')\right]. \]

The second term vanishes because the metric is time-independent.

For the third term, use

\[ \Gamma^\beta_{r\beta} =\nu'+\lambda'+\frac2r. \]

Thus,

\[ \Gamma^r_{00}\Gamma^\beta_{r\beta} =e^{2(\nu-\lambda)}\nu' \left(\nu'+\lambda'+\frac2r\right). \]

The fourth term is

\[ -2e^{2(\nu-\lambda)}\nu'^2. \]

Combining the terms,

\[ \boxed{ R_{00}=e^{2(\nu-\lambda)} \left[ \nu''+\nu'^2-\nu'\lambda'+\frac{2\nu'}r \right]. } \tag{11} \]

5.2 Radial-radial component

The four terms in Equation (10) are

\[ \begin{aligned} \partial_\alpha\Gamma^\alpha_{rr}&=\lambda'',\\ -\partial_r\Gamma^\alpha_{r\alpha} &=-\nu''-\lambda''+\frac2{r^2},\\ \Gamma^\alpha_{rr}\Gamma^\beta_{\alpha\beta} &=\lambda'\left(\nu'+\lambda'+\frac2r\right),\\ -\Gamma^\beta_{r\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha_{r\beta} &=-\nu'^2-\lambda'^2-\frac2{r^2}. \end{aligned} \]

Combining,

\[ \boxed{ R_{rr} =-\nu''-\nu'^2+\nu'\lambda'+\frac{2\lambda'}r. } \tag{12} \]

5.3 Angular components

Substituting the angular Christoffel symbols gives

\[ \boxed{ R_{\theta\theta} =1-e^{-2\lambda} \left(1+r\nu'-r\lambda'\right). } \tag{13} \]

Spherical symmetry requires

\[ \boxed{ R_{\phi\phi}=\sin^2\theta\,R_{\theta\theta}. } \tag{14} \]

All off-diagonal Ricci components vanish.

We now have every independent component of the Ricci tensor.

6. Apply the vacuum Einstein equations

Einstein's field equations, with zero cosmological constant, are

\[ R_{\mu\nu}-\frac12Rg_{\mu\nu} =\frac{8\pi G}{c^4}T_{\mu\nu}. \tag{15} \]

In vacuum,

\[ T_{\mu\nu}=0. \]

Hence,

\[ R_{\mu\nu}-\frac12Rg_{\mu\nu}=0. \]

Contract with \(g^{\mu\nu}\):

\[ R-\frac12(4)R=0, \]

giving

\[ -R=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad R=0. \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{R_{\mu\nu}=0.} \tag{16} \]

This reduction is exact for the stated vacuum equations.

7. Derive the ruler-clock relationship

Set Equations (11) and (12) equal to zero:

\[ \nu''+\nu'^2-\nu'\lambda'+\frac{2\nu'}r=0, \tag{17} \]

\[ -\nu''-\nu'^2+\nu'\lambda'+\frac{2\lambda'}r=0. \tag{18} \]

Add them.

The second derivatives cancel:

\[ \nu''-\nu''=0. \]

The quadratic terms cancel:

\[ \nu'^2-\nu'^2=0. \]

The mixed terms cancel:

\[ -\nu'\lambda'+\nu'\lambda'=0. \]

We are left with

\[ \frac{2\nu'}r+\frac{2\lambda'}r=0. \]

For \(r>0\),

\[ \nu'+\lambda'=0. \]

Integrate:

\[ \nu+\lambda=C. \]

Exponentiate:

\[ e^\nu e^\lambda=e^C. \]

Since \(N=e^\nu\) and \(B=e^\lambda\),

\[ NB=e^C. \]

Asymptotic flatness gives \(N(\infty)=B(\infty)=1\), hence \(e^C=1\).

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{NB=1.} \tag{19} \]

This is the complete derivation of the reciprocal clock-ruler relationship, from the field equations under assumption 2. In this paper the same relation comes from setting the f dot dr in the field equal to the f dot dr needed to generate the motion, with no equation of Einstein's (Section 4, statement 4).

The crucial mathematical operation was adding the two independent vacuum Ricci equations.

Notice that no Schwarzschild radius was assumed.

8. Solve the remaining radial equation

Now apply \(R_{\theta\theta}=0\).

From Equation (13),

\[ 1-e^{-2\lambda} (1+r\nu'-r\lambda')=0. \]

Since \(\lambda=-\nu\),

\[ \lambda'=-\nu'. \]

Thus,

\[ 1-e^{-2\lambda}(1+2r\nu')=0. \tag{20} \]

Define

\[ f(r)=e^{2\nu}=N^2=e^{-2\lambda}=B^{-2}. \]

Its derivative is

\[ f'=2\nu'e^{2\nu}=2\nu'f. \]

Consequently,

\[ 2\nu'=\frac{f'}f. \]

Substitute into Equation (20):

\[ 1-f\left(1+\frac{rf'}f\right)=0. \]

Expand:

\[ 1-f-rf'=0. \]

Rearrange:

\[ rf'+f=1. \]

Recognize the product derivative:

\[ \boxed{\frac{d}{dr}(rf)=1.} \tag{21} \]

Integrate:

\[ rf=r+C_1. \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{f(r)=1+\frac{C_1}{r}.} \tag{22} \]

This is the general asymptotically flat static spherical vacuum solution in the chosen areal-radius coordinates, up to identifying the integration constant.

9. Determine the integration constant from Newtonian gravity

We must identify \(C_1\) using the limit far from the mass. This is where the mass \(M\) enters.

For a slowly moving test particle, the radial geodesic equation is

\[ \frac{d^2r}{d\tau^2} +\Gamma^r_{00}\left(\frac{dx^0}{d\tau}\right)^2 +\cdots=0. \]

Far from the mass, in the slow-motion limit,

\[ \frac{dx^0}{d\tau}\approx c,\qquad \frac{d^2r}{d\tau^2}\approx\frac{d^2r}{dt^2}. \]

The leading radial acceleration is therefore

\[ \frac{d^2r}{dt^2}\approx-c^2\Gamma^r_{00}. \]

Using Equation (9),

\[ \Gamma^r_{00}=\nu'e^{2(\nu-\lambda)}. \]

Far from the mass, \(e^{2(\nu-\lambda)}\approx1\), giving

\[ \frac{d^2r}{dt^2}\approx-c^2\nu'. \tag{23} \]

The Newtonian potential \(\Phi\) satisfies

\[ \frac{d^2r}{dt^2}=-\Phi'. \]

Comparing,

\[ c^2\nu'\approx\Phi'. \]

Integrating with both quantities vanishing at infinity,

\[ \nu\approx\frac{\Phi}{c^2}. \]

Since

\[ N^2=e^{2\nu}\approx1+2\nu, \]

we obtain

\[ \boxed{ f(r)=N^2(r)\approx1+\frac{2\Phi(r)}{c^2}. } \tag{24} \]

For a spherical mass,

\[ \Phi(r)=-\frac{GM}{r}. \]

Thus,

\[ f(r)\approx1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}. \]

But our exact solution was

\[ f(r)=1+\frac{C_1}{r}. \]

Matching the coefficient far from the mass gives

\[ \boxed{C_1=-\frac{2GM}{c^2}.} \tag{25} \]

Label (this paper): the solved equation is exact outside the horizon, where conservation gives the same constant (Section 4, statements 4 and 6); inside the horizon nothing has tested the form.

10. Obtain the complete Schwarzschild metric

Substitute Equation (25) into Equation (22):

\[ f(r)=1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}. \]

Since \(N^2=f\) and \(B^2=1/f\),

\[ \boxed{ N(r)=\sqrt{1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}} } \tag{26} \]

and

\[ \boxed{ B(r)=\frac1{\sqrt{1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}}}. } \tag{27} \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{ ds^2= -\left(1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}\right)c^2dt^2 +\left(1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}\right)^{-1}dr^2 +r^2d\Omega^2. } \tag{28} \]

This is the Schwarzschild metric in standard areal-radius coordinates.

Every function in this metric has now been determined.

11. Verify the solution by substitution

A derivation is not complete until we substitute the solution into the original equations.

Let

\[ a=\frac{2GM}{c^2},\qquad f=1-\frac ar. \]

Then

\[ f'=\frac a{r^2},\qquad f''=-\frac{2a}{r^3}. \]

Our functions satisfy

\[ \nu=\frac12\ln f,\qquad \lambda=-\frac12\ln f. \]

Therefore,

\[ \nu'=\frac{f'}{2f},\qquad \lambda'=-\frac{f'}{2f}. \]

Check \(R_{\theta\theta}=0\)

Equation (13) becomes

\[ R_{\theta\theta}=1-f-rf'. \]

Substitute:

\[ R_{\theta\theta} =1-\left(1-\frac ar\right)-r\frac a{r^2}. \]

Thus,

\[ \boxed{R_{\theta\theta}=0.} \]

The \(\phi\phi\) component also vanishes.

Check \(R_{00}=0\)

Using \(\lambda'=-\nu'\), the bracket in Equation (11) becomes

\[ \nu''+2\nu'^2+\frac{2\nu'}r. \]

Because

\[ \nu''+2\nu'^2=\frac{f''}{2f}, \]

the bracket equals

\[ \frac{f''}{2f}+\frac{f'}{fr}. \]

Substituting the derivatives,

\[ \frac1f\left(-\frac a{r^3}+\frac a{r^3}\right)=0. \]

Hence,

\[ \boxed{R_{00}=0.} \]

Check \(R_{rr}=0\)

Equation (12) reduces to the negative of the same bracket:

\[ R_{rr}=-\frac{f''}{2f}-\frac{f'}{fr}=0. \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{R_{\mu\nu}=0} \]

for every component in the Schwarzschild vacuum region.

The solution satisfies the complete vacuum field equations.

12. Derive gravitational redshift from the metric

The exact redshift follows from the metric. In general relativity it rests on staticity, assumption 2, which supplies the Killing vector; in this paper the same relation is the count, \(e=\gamma f\), from conservation and the clock step (Section 4, statements 1 and 3).

Because the metric is stationary, it has a time-translation Killing vector \(\xi^\mu\). With \(x^0=ct\) and \(\xi=\partial_{ct}\), the conserved quantity below is the photon's energy divided by \(c\); with \(\xi=\partial_t\) it is the energy itself, and every ratio below is the same either way.

For a freely propagating photon with four-momentum \(p^\mu\), the quantity

\[ \mathcal E=-p_\mu\xi^\mu \]

is conserved along its geodesic.

A stationary observer at radius \(r\) has four-velocity proportional to \(\xi^\mu\). Its normalization gives a locally measured photon energy

\[ \boxed{E_{\rm local}(r)=\frac{\mathcal E}{N(r)}.} \tag{29} \]

Therefore, for emission at \(r_1\) and reception at \(r_2\),

\[ \frac{E_2}{E_1} =\frac{N(r_1)}{N(r_2)}. \]

Substituting Equation (26),

\[ \boxed{ \frac{E_2}{E_1} = \sqrt{ \frac{1-2GM/(r_1c^2)} {1-2GM/(r_2c^2)} }. } \tag{30} \]

For a receiver at infinity,

\[ \boxed{ E_\infty =E_{\rm emitted} \sqrt{1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}}. } \tag{31} \]

This is the exact Schwarzschild gravitational-redshift relationship for stationary observers. General relativity allows none inside the horizon. This paper's premises 7 and 8 say what holds across it (Section 3).

Check far from the mass

Let \(x=GM/(rc^2)\). For \(x\ll1\),

\[ \sqrt{1-2x} =1-x-\frac{x^2}{2}-\frac{x^3}{2}+O(x^4). \]

Thus,

\[ N(r)\approx1-\frac{GM}{rc^2} \]

at first order, matching the familiar Newtonian-potential redshift.

13. Derive the Schwarzschild radius

The metric function is

\[ f(r)=1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}. \]

The stationary Killing vector has squared norm

\[ \xi^\mu\xi_\mu=-f(r) \]

when the time coordinate is \(ct\).

Its norm becomes zero when

\[ 1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}=0. \]

Solving,

\[ \boxed{r_s=\frac{2GM}{c^2}.} \tag{32} \]

For positive \(M\), the static exterior region is \(r>r_s\).

But we must be careful: finding \(f=0\) identifies a candidate Killing horizon. To establish that this is a regular black-hole horizon rather than a physical singularity, we need to examine the geometry in coordinates that remain regular there.

14. Check whether the horizon is a curvature singularity

For the Schwarzschild metric, the Ricci scalar vanishes:

\[ R=0. \]

The Ricci tensor also vanishes in vacuum:

\[ R_{\mu\nu}=0. \]

But the full Riemann tensor does not vanish.

The Kretschmann scalar is

\[ K=R_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta} R^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}. \]

Direct contraction gives

\[ \boxed{ K=\frac{48G^2M^2}{c^4r^6}. } \tag{33} \]

At the Schwarzschild radius,

\[ K(r_s)=\frac{12}{r_s^4}, \]

which is finite for \(M>0\).

At \(r=0\),

\[ K\longrightarrow\infty. \]

Therefore, \(r=r_s\) is not a curvature singularity. The singularity in the standard Schwarzschild coordinate components is a coordinate singularity.

15. Extend the solution through the horizon

Define the tortoise coordinate \(r_*\) by

\[ \frac{dr_*}{dr}=\frac1{f(r)}. \]

Integrating in the exterior,

\[ \boxed{ r_*=r+r_s\ln\left|\frac r{r_s}-1\right|. } \tag{34} \]

Introduce the ingoing null coordinate

\[ v=t+\frac{r_*}{c}. \]

Thus,

\[ dt=dv-\frac{dr}{cf}. \]

Substitute into the Schwarzschild metric:

\[ ds^2=-fc^2\left(dv-\frac{dr}{cf}\right)^2 +\frac{dr^2}{f}+r^2d\Omega^2. \]

Expand:

\[ ds^2=-fc^2dv^2+2c\,dv\,dr -\frac{dr^2}{f}+\frac{dr^2}{f}+r^2d\Omega^2. \]

The divergent radial terms cancel.

We obtain

\[ \boxed{ ds^2=-\left(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\right)c^2dv^2 +2c\,dv\,dr+r^2d\Omega^2. } \tag{35} \]

This is the ingoing Eddington–Finkelstein metric.

It remains regular at \(r=r_s\).

We have now extended the solution across the Schwarzschild coordinate singularity. Label (this paper): the extension assumes that the static form of assumption 2 holds inside, and it gives one event horizon for every frame. That is the premise under attack in this paper: the merge of the frames' different values into one event horizon. As general relativity states the step: one metric is chosen for all observers, and the same solution with the same mass is continued across \(r_s\).

16. Determine the behavior of outgoing light

For radial light,

\[ ds^2=0,\qquad d\Omega=0. \]

Equation (35) gives

\[ 0=-fc^2dv^2+2c\,dv\,dr. \]

For the outgoing branch with \(dv\ne0\),

\[ \boxed{ \frac{dr}{dv}=\frac c2 \left(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\right). } \tag{36} \]

Examine three regions.

RegionOutgoing radial null trajectory
\(r>r_s\)\(dr/dv>0\)
\(r=r_s\)\(dr/dv=0\)
\(0<r<r_s\)\(dr/dv<0\)

The second radial null family has \(dv=0\) and is ingoing.

More generally, for a future-directed causal trajectory in the black-hole interior, Equation (35) implies

\[ -fc^2dv^2+2c\,dv\,dr+r^2d\Omega^2\le0. \]

For \(0<r<r_s\), \(f<0\). With the future orientation chosen so \(dv>0\),

\[ 2c\,dv\,dr \le fc^2dv^2-r^2d\Omega^2<0. \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{dr<0} \]

along every nontrivial future-directed causal trajectory in the interior, with the horizon-generator case treated at the boundary.

This is general relativity's reading of the inside: with the static form carried inside and the future orientation chosen there (\(dv>0\)), no causal trajectory moves to larger \(r\). It is a consequence of assumption 2 and of that choice, not a test of either. This paper's premise 8 says the opposite: objects can, and do, move beyond their event horizon (Section 3).

17. Establish the global event horizon

A black-hole event horizon is defined globally as the boundary of the region from which future-directed light signals can reach future null infinity.

The Eddington–Finkelstein calculation establishes the local causal behavior. We can additionally use Kruskal–Szekeres coordinates to examine the global extension.

Define the outgoing null coordinate

\[ u=t-\frac{r_*}{c}. \]

In the exterior region, introduce

\[ U=-e^{-cu/(2r_s)},\qquad V=e^{cv/(2r_s)}. \]

Then

\[ UV=-\left(\frac r{r_s}-1\right)e^{r/r_s}. \tag{37} \]

The metric becomes

\[ \boxed{ ds^2= -\frac{4r_s^3}{r}e^{-r/r_s}\,dU\,dV +r^2d\Omega^2. } \tag{38} \]

The coefficient is finite and nonzero at \(r=r_s\).

These coordinates extend smoothly across the horizon. In the maximally extended Schwarzschild spacetime, the future black-hole region is separated from the exterior by a null horizon, and future-directed causal trajectories inside it cannot reach the exterior's future null infinity.

The precise global interpretation requires specifying the spacetime extension and its time orientation. For a physically formed black hole, the relevant extension is the collapse geometry rather than the entire eternal Schwarzschild solution.

This is general relativity's identification of the horizon, resting on assumption 2 carried inside: one event horizon for every frame. Label: PREMISE of general relativity.

18. Return to our original Gaussian surfaces

Now we can connect the result to the conservation-law investigation.

For the static spherical metric,

\[ ds^2=-N^2c^2dt^2+B^2dr^2+r^2d\Omega^2, \]

the proper acceleration needed to hold a test mass at a fixed radius is

\[ g_{\rm hold}=\frac{c^2N'}{NB}. \tag{39} \]

Its locally measured supporting force is \(F_{\rm local}=mg_{\rm hold}\).

The redshifted acceleration is

\[ Ng_{\rm hold}=\frac{c^2N'}B. \]

Define the redshifted gravitational flux through a sphere:

\[ \mathcal F(r)=4\pi r^2\frac{c^2N'}B. \tag{40} \]

For Schwarzschild,

\[ N=\sqrt{1-\frac{2r_g}{r}}, \qquad B=\frac1N, \]

where \(r_g=GM/c^2\).

Differentiate \(N\):

\[ N'=\frac{r_g}{r^2N}. \]

Therefore,

\[ \frac{N'}B=\frac{r_g}{r^2}. \]

Substituting into Equation (40),

\[ \boxed{\mathcal F(r)=4\pi GM.} \tag{41} \]

This is constant at every enclosing sphere in the static vacuum exterior.

In particular,

\[ \boxed{\mathcal F(r_1)=\mathcal F(r_2).} \tag{42} \]

This is the Gaussian-surface relationship of Section 1: the flux is the same through every sphere outside the matter and the same at every time. In general relativity the flux is the same through every sphere by its vacuum field equation (assumption 5) and the same at every time by assumption 2; in this paper both are conservation of mass-energy itself, premise 1 (Section 3; Section 4, statements 5 and 6).

It is important to distinguish what has been shown:

  • We have demonstrated that Schwarzschild satisfies the equal-flux condition.
  • We have not demonstrated that equal flux alone determines the Schwarzschild geometry.
Derive the corresponding conservation identity

Equation (41) can be rewritten as

\[ \boxed{\frac{r^2N'}B=\frac{GM}{c^2}.} \tag{43} \]

This is one differential equation for the two unknown functions \(N\) and \(B\).

The Schwarzschild derivation supplies a second equation:

\[ \boxed{NB=1.} \tag{44} \]

Combining them,

\[ r^2NN'=r_g. \]

Therefore,

\[ \frac{d(N^2)}{dr}=\frac{2r_g}{r^2}. \]

Integrating with \(N(\infty)=1\),

\[ N^2=1-\frac{2r_g}{r}. \]

So the pair of equations reconstructs Schwarzschild exactly.

19. What conservation does and does not establish

We should distinguish three mathematical statements.

First: conservation of stress-energy.

Einstein's equations imply

\[ \boxed{\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0} \tag{45} \]

through the contracted Bianchi identity,

\[ \nabla_\mu G^{\mu\nu}=0. \]

This is a local conservation relationship. It does not uniquely determine the metric.

Second: conservation of the exterior gravitational charge.

For the static spherical vacuum solution, the appropriately normalized Komar mass is the same on every enclosing sphere. Equation (43) expresses this in our metric variables.

Label (this paper): the Komar mass is the complete count, and a body's entry in it is its reading times its clock rate; in general relativity it is fixed by the static vacuum field equations (assumptions 2 and 5), in this paper by conservation (Section 4, statement 5). Outside the horizon the two agree; inside, general relativity's count is read as an energy by no one (Section 9).

Third: the radial geometric field equation.

The reciprocal relation

\[ NB=1 \]

was obtained from

\[ R_{00}=R_{rr}=0, \]

or equivalently from the appropriate difference of mixed Einstein equations.

It is an independent geometric constraint within GR.

That distinction matters because the stress-energy conservation identity alone does not reproduce every component of Einstein's field equations.

20. The second equation, and where this paper gets it

We can formulate the exact mathematical target.

The Gaussian-flux relation is

\[ \frac{r^2N'}B=r_g. \]

The full Schwarzschild result additionally requires

\[ \frac{d}{dr}\ln(NB)=0. \]

In the Einstein-equation derivation, the corresponding general relation is

\[ \boxed{ \frac{d}{dr}\ln(NB) = \frac{4\pi GrB^2}{c^4}(\epsilon+p_r), } \tag{46} \]

where \(\epsilon\) is the local energy density and \(p_r\) is the radial pressure.

For vacuum,

\[ \epsilon=p_r=0, \]

so

\[ \frac{d}{dr}\ln(NB)=0. \]

This identifies the missing ingredient very precisely: a relationship between the radial geometry and the source's energy-density and stress components.

In this paper the second relation is supplied by the step from stationary observers to free fall. The frame that falls from rest far away passes the held frame at \(\gamma=1/N\), the speed that the same f dot dr would generate. It needs no force and keeps A's rulers, and special relativity between the two gives the held frame's ruler along the force at \(N\) of A's, so \(B=1/N\) (Section 4, statement 4). No equation of Einstein's is used.

21. Final derivation audit

ResultMathematical originStatus
General static spherical metricSymmetry, staticity, areal-radius coordinateDerived form
Christoffel symbolsMetric derivativesCalculated
Ricci tensorLevi-Civita curvatureCalculated
\(R_{\mu\nu}=0\)Einstein vacuum equations, \(\Lambda=0\)GR premise and consequence

\(C=-2GM/c^2\)Newtonian mass identification far from the massDerived

Conclusion

The derivation is mathematically complete for the static, spherically symmetric, asymptotically flat vacuum exterior in Einstein gravity with \(\Lambda=0\). The extension of the static form inside gives general relativity's horizon at \(r_s=2GM/c^2\), one for every frame.

For this paper, the most consequential finding is that the exact Schwarzschild solution depends on two distinct radial relationships:

\[ \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \text{Gaussian gravitational flux:}\quad& \frac{r^2N'}B=\frac{GM}{c^2}\\[6pt] \text{Radial geometric constraint:}\quad& NB=1 \end{aligned} } \]

The first relationship is conservation of mass-energy through a Gaussian surface. The second, in this paper, is the ruler of a frame held at rest, which follows from setting the f dot dr in the field equal to the f dot dr needed to generate the motion (Section 4, statement 4). General relativity gets \(NB=1\) for one frame and all from its field equations under assumption 2, the static field, which is what makes the merge of every frame's values into one event horizon possible. The burden is on that premise.

08 / RESEARCH NOTES

The Schwarzschild Derivation: A Complete Worked Example

Purpose. Starting from the Einstein vacuum equations rather than inserting the Schwarzschild metric, solve one simple spherical spacetime, check every independent field equation, and calculate measurable consequences between two Gaussian surfaces. Then show, in numbers, which results rest on the static and empty-exterior premises.

Calculation convention. Use geometric units \(G=c=1\) and choose the source's mass parameter \(M=1\). Distances, times, and masses are consequently represented in consistent geometrized units. At the end, we translate the example to a black hole of ten solar masses. This toy calculation is for an exterior static vacuum, not the interior of a material star. Its horizon is subsequently studied using coordinates that remain regular there.

Context and Core Idea

The same derivation again, with numbers: one black hole with mass parameter M = 1 in units where G = c = 1, two Gaussian surfaces at r = 4 and r = 8, and every measurable quantity between them calculated and checked. It makes the two radial relationships of Section 7 concrete: the Gaussian flux is the same on both spheres, and a pair of functions that satisfies the flux equation but not NB = 1 is written down explicitly (part 16).
At the end the example is converted to a black hole of ten solar masses, so the clocks, rulers, redshift and lifting energy have sizes in kilometres, milliseconds and fractions of the rest energy.
For a child

The same recipe with real numbers. Put the black hole in the middle, draw one bubble at distance 4 and another at distance 8. A clock on the inner bubble ticks at 0.707 of a far-away clock, on the outer one at 0.866. A flash of light sent from the inner bubble arrives at the outer one with 18% less energy. Lifting a stone from the inner bubble to the outer one costs 16% of the stone's rest energy. The pull spreading out through each bubble is exactly the same number, 4π. And the edge is at distance 2, where the clock would stop.

For a high school physics teacher

Setup. \(G=c=1\), \(M=1\), spheres at \(r_1=4\) and \(r_2=8\). The derivation of Section 7 gives \(f=1-2/r\), \(N=\sqrt f\), \(B=1/\sqrt f\). At \(r=4\): \(N=0.707107\), \(B=1.414214\). At \(r=8\): \(N=0.866025\), \(B=1.154701\). In both places \(NB=1\). Part 7 checks every vacuum equation at \(r=4\) by hand.

Redshift. A photon emitted at \(r=4\) with energy 1 arrives at \(r=8\) with energy \(\sqrt{2/3}=0.816497\): an 18.35% loss of energy, a redshift \(z=22.47\%\). The product \(N\,E_{\rm local}=0.707107\) is the same at both spheres.

Lifting a mass. Lifting a body of rest mass \(m\) from 4 to 8 costs \(W=m(\sqrt3/2-1/\sqrt2)=0.158919\,mc^2\), and the same number comes from integrating the local force over the proper distance and redshifting it (part 10): a conservation check on the solution.

The Gaussian flux. \(r^2N'/B=1\) at both spheres, so the redshifted flux is \(4\pi\) on both, although the local accelerations differ: 0.0884 at 4 and 0.0180 at 8 (part 11).

Distances and times. The coordinate gap is 4; the proper radial distance is 4.9709; the outward light travel time in distant time is \(4+2\ln3=6.1972\); the local light speed is still \(c\) (parts 12 and 13).

The edge. \(r_s=2\). The curvature invariant there is 0.75, finite; it diverges only at \(r=0\). In regular coordinates the outgoing light branch has \(dr/dv=+1/4\) at 4, 0 at 2 and \(-1/6\) at 1.5 (part 14).

Ten solar masses. One unit is 14.767 km; the edge is at 29.53 km, the spheres at 59.07 and 118.13 km; the proper distance is 73.40 km and the light time 0.305 ms (part 15).

What is left undetermined. The flux equation \(r^2N'/B=M\) is one equation for two functions. The pair \(\tilde N=\tilde B=e^{-1/r}\) satisfies it exactly and is not Schwarzschild, because \(\tilde N\tilde B\ne1\) (part 16). The relation \(NB=1\) is what the field equations add under the static premise; in this paper it comes from setting the f dot dr in the field equal to the f dot dr needed to generate the motion (Section 4, statement 4).

For a theoretical physicist (the worked example, verbatim)

Purpose. Starting from the Einstein vacuum equations rather than inserting the Schwarzschild metric, solve one simple spherical spacetime, check every independent field equation, and calculate measurable consequences between two Gaussian surfaces. Then show, in numbers, which results rest on the static and empty-exterior premises.

Calculation convention. Use geometric units \(G=c=1\) and choose the source's mass parameter \(M=1\). Distances, times, and masses are consequently represented in consistent geometrized units. At the end, we translate the example to a black hole of ten solar masses. This toy calculation is for an exterior static vacuum, not the interior of a material star. Its horizon is subsequently studied using coordinates that remain regular there.

1. The thought experiment: two Gaussian surfaces

Imagine a spherical, uncharged, nonrotating gravitating source with a time-independent exterior. Surround it with two imaginary concentric spheres:

  • Inner Gaussian surface: \(r_1=4\).
  • Outer Gaussian surface: \(r_2=8\).
  • Enclosed mass parameter: \(M=1\).
  • The coordinate \(r\) is areal radius: each sphere has area \(A=4\pi r^2\).

We want to answer six concrete questions:

  1. What are the clock and radial ruler functions \(N(r)\) and \(B(r)\)?
  2. Does the solution satisfy all independent vacuum Einstein equations?
  3. What redshift is measured for a photon traveling from \(r=4\) to \(r=8\)?
  4. How much externally supplied energy is required to lift a small test mass between the surfaces?
  5. Is the appropriately redshifted gravitational flux the same on both surfaces?
  6. Where is the horizon, and does it represent a true curvature singularity?

Independent premises, stated up front: spherical symmetry; static exterior; empty exterior (\(T_{\mu\nu}=0\)); general relativity with \(\Lambda=0\); asymptotic flatness; and the identification of \(M\) with the Newtonian gravitational mass. These are the hypotheses of the Schwarzschild derivation. Static exterior: outside the horizon this follows from conservation (Section 4); what this paper attacks is the static form carried inside the horizon, with one horizon for every frame.

2. Begin with an unknown metric, not Schwarzschild

The most general static spherical metric in areal-radius coordinates, within a static region, can be written

\[ \boxed{ds^2=-N(r)^2\,dt^2+B(r)^2\,dr^2+r^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2).} \tag{1} \]

The two positive functions are unknown. Their physical meanings are

\[ \boxed{d\tau_{\rm stationary}=N(r)\,dt,\qquad d\ell_{\rm radial}=B(r)\,dr.} \tag{2} \]

The asymptotic boundary conditions are

\[ N(\infty)=1,\qquad B(\infty)=1. \tag{3} \]

Set

\[ N=e^\nu,\qquad B=e^\lambda. \tag{4} \]

Then

\[ ds^2=-e^{2\nu}dt^2+e^{2\lambda}dr^2+r^2d\Omega^2, \quad d\Omega^2=d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2. \tag{5} \]

Nothing in (1)–(5) assumes either \(NB=1\) or a horizon.

3. Compute the geometric connection

The diagonal metric and its inverse are

\[ (g_{\mu\nu})=\operatorname{diag}(-e^{2\nu},e^{2\lambda},r^2,r^2\sin^2\theta), \tag{6} \]

\[ (g^{\mu\nu})=\operatorname{diag}(-e^{-2\nu},e^{-2\lambda},r^{-2},(r^2\sin^2\theta)^{-1}). \tag{7} \]

The Christoffel symbols follow from

\[ \Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\nu}=\frac12g^{\alpha\beta} (\partial_\mu g_{\beta\nu}+\partial_\nu g_{\beta\mu}-\partial_\beta g_{\mu\nu}). \tag{8} \]

For example, because \(g_{tt}=-e^{2\nu}\),

\[ \Gamma^r_{tt}=-\frac12g^{rr}\partial_r g_{tt} =-\frac12e^{-2\lambda}(-2\nu'e^{2\nu}) =\nu'e^{2(\nu-\lambda)}. \tag{9} \]

All independent nonzero symbols (and their lower-index-symmetric partners) are

\[ \begin{aligned} \Gamma^t_{tr}&=\nu', &\Gamma^r_{tt}&=\nu'e^{2(\nu-\lambda)}, &\Gamma^r_{rr}&=\lambda',\\ \Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}&=-re^{-2\lambda}, &\Gamma^r_{\phi\phi}&=-re^{-2\lambda}\sin^2\theta,\\ \Gamma^\theta_{r\theta}&=1/r, &\Gamma^\phi_{r\phi}&=1/r,\\ \Gamma^\theta_{\phi\phi}&=-\sin\theta\cos\theta, &\Gamma^\phi_{\theta\phi}&=\cot\theta. \end{aligned} \tag{10} \]

Use the curvature sign convention

\[ R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu\Gamma^\rho_{\nu\sigma}-\partial_\nu\Gamma^\rho_{\mu\sigma} +\Gamma^\rho_{\mu\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha_{\nu\sigma} -\Gamma^\rho_{\nu\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\sigma}. \tag{11} \]

4. Calculate the full independent Ricci equations

By contraction, \(R_{\mu\nu}=R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}\), or explicitly

\[ R_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\alpha\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\nu} -\partial_\nu\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\alpha} +\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\nu}\Gamma^\beta_{\alpha\beta} -\Gamma^\beta_{\mu\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha_{\nu\beta}. \tag{12} \]

Substituting (10) yields

\[ \boxed{R_{tt}=e^{2(\nu-\lambda)} \left(\nu''+\nu'^2-\nu'\lambda'+\frac{2\nu'}r\right).} \tag{13} \]

\[ \boxed{R_{rr}=-\nu''-\nu'^2+\nu'\lambda'+\frac{2\lambda'}r.} \tag{14} \]

\[ \boxed{R_{\theta\theta}=1-e^{-2\lambda}(1+r\nu'-r\lambda'),} \tag{15} \]

\[ \boxed{R_{\phi\phi}=\sin^2\theta\,R_{\theta\theta}.} \tag{16} \]

All off-diagonal components vanish. Thus (13)–(15) exhaust the independent Ricci equations for this ansatz.

Check the vacuum reduction: Einstein's equations with \(\Lambda=0\) are

\[ R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12R g_{\mu\nu}=8\pi T_{\mu\nu}. \tag{17} \]

For \(T_{\mu\nu}=0\), taking the trace gives \(R-2R=-R=0\), so

\[ \boxed{R_{\mu\nu}=0.} \tag{18} \]

5. Derive the clock–ruler relationship \(NB=1\)

Set (13) and (14) to zero. Divide (13) by its nonzero prefactor in the static exterior:

\[ \nu''+\nu'^2-\nu'\lambda'+\frac{2\nu'}r=0. \tag{19} \]

\[ -\nu''-\nu'^2+\nu'\lambda'+\frac{2\lambda'}r=0. \tag{20} \]

Add, term by term. All second-derivative and quadratic terms cancel:

\[ \frac{2}{r}(\nu'+\lambda')=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \nu'+\lambda'=0. \tag{21} \]

Integrate:

\[ \nu+\lambda=C_0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad NB=e^{C_0}. \tag{22} \]

The boundary values \(N,B\to1\) at infinity give \(C_0=0\). Therefore,

\[ \boxed{N(r)B(r)=1.} \tag{23} \]

Dependency: (23) came from two Einstein vacuum equations under the static and empty-exterior premises.

6. Solve the remaining equation and identify the mass

Since \(\lambda=-\nu\), define

\[ f=e^{2\nu}=N^2=e^{-2\lambda}=B^{-2}. \tag{24} \]

Equation (15), with \(R_{\theta\theta}=0\), becomes

\[ 1-f(1+2r\nu')=0. \tag{25} \]

But \(f'=2f\nu'\), so

\[ 1-f-rf'=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (rf)'=1. \tag{26} \]

Integrate exactly:

\[ rf=r+C_1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(r)=1+\frac{C_1}{r}. \tag{27} \]

Now identify \(C_1\) far from the mass: a test particle must feel the Newtonian potential \(\Phi=-M/r\). Far from the mass the metric obeys \(g_{tt}\simeq-(1+2\Phi)\). Therefore

\[ f(r)\simeq 1-\frac{2M}{r}, \quad \boxed{C_1=-2M=-2.} \tag{28} \]

Thus the derived exact metric function is

\[ \boxed{f(r)=1-\frac2r,\qquad N(r)=\sqrt{1-\frac2r},\qquad B(r)=\left(1-\frac2r\right)^{-1/2}.} \tag{29} \]

The final metric for \(r>2\) is

\[ \boxed{ds^2=-\left(1-\frac2r\right)dt^2 +\frac{dr^2}{1-2/r}+r^2d\Omega^2.} \tag{30} \]

The initial value \(M=1\) was selected only to make the example's arithmetic easy. The coefficient 2 was not assumed from a horizon formula: it followed from matching the integration constant to the Newtonian limit far from the mass.

7. Independently verify every vacuum equation

For \(f=1-2/r\),

\[ f'=\frac2{r^2},\qquad f''=-\frac4{r^3}, \qquad \nu=\tfrac12\ln f,\quad\lambda=-\nu. \tag{31} \]

Using \(\nu'=f'/(2f)\),

\[ \nu''+2\nu'^2=\frac{f''}{2f}. \tag{32} \]

The bracket in (13) therefore becomes

\[ \nu''+\nu'^2-\nu'\lambda'+\frac{2\nu'}r =\frac{f''}{2f}+\frac{f'}{fr} =\frac1f\left(-\frac2{r^3}+\frac2{r^3}\right)=0. \tag{33} \]

Hence \(R_{tt}=0\). The bracket in (14) is its negative, giving \(R_{rr}=0\). The angular component is

\[ R_{\theta\theta}=1-f-rf' =1-\left(1-\frac2r\right)-\frac2r=0. \tag{34} \]

Thus \(R_{\phi\phi}=0\) as well and all the vacuum Ricci equations are satisfied.

Spot check at the inner Gaussian sphere \(r=4\):

\[ f=\tfrac12,\quad f'=\tfrac18,\quad f''=-\tfrac1{16}, \quad\nu'=\tfrac18,\quad\lambda'=-\tfrac18,\quad\nu''=-\tfrac3{32}. \tag{35} \]

Direct substitution gives

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{Bracket of }R_{tt}&=-\tfrac3{32}+\tfrac1{64}+\tfrac1{64}+\tfrac1{16}=0,\\ R_{rr}&=\tfrac3{32}-\tfrac1{64}-\tfrac1{64}-\tfrac1{16}=0,\\ R_{\theta\theta}&=1-\tfrac12\bigl(1+4/8+4/8\bigr)=0. \end{aligned} \tag{36} \]

These numerical checks agree with the symbolic verification.

8. Evaluate clocks and rulers on both Gaussian surfaces

The sphere areas are

\[ A_1=4\pi(4)^2=64\pi,\qquad A_2=4\pi(8)^2=256\pi. \tag{37} \]

Evaluate the geometry:

QuantityInner sphere \(r_1=4\)Outer sphere \(r_2=8\)
\(f=1-2/r\)\(1/2=0.500000\)\(3/4=0.750000\)
\(N=\sqrt f\)\(1/\sqrt2=0.707107\)\(\sqrt3/2=0.866025\)
\(B=1/\sqrt f\)\(\sqrt2=1.414214\)\(2/\sqrt3=1.154701\)
\(NB\)\(1\)\(1\)

A stationary clock at the inner surface advances \(0.707107\) units of proper time per unit distant coordinate time; the outer clock advances \(0.866025\). A small coordinate radial interval \(dr\) corresponds to proper lengths \(1.414214\,dr\) and \(1.154701\,dr\), respectively.

These different clock and ruler factors do not assert that the two observers agree on the numerical value of every local length or duration. The relation \(NB=1\) is specific to the static metric in areal-radius coordinates.

9. Work a photon redshift problem completely

Trial: A stationary emitter at \(r_1=4\) emits a photon with locally measured energy \(E_1=1\) (arbitrary energy unit). A stationary receiver at \(r_2=8\) measures \(E_2\).

The metric is stationary, so the time-translation Killing energy

\[ \mathcal E=-p_\mu\xi^\mu \tag{38} \]

is constant along the photon's freely propagating null geodesic. For stationary observers,

\[ E_{\rm local}(r)=\frac{\mathcal E}{N(r)} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad N(r)E_{\rm local}(r)=\mathcal E. \tag{39} \]

At emission,

\[ \mathcal E=N_1E_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}\times1=0.70710678. \tag{40} \]

At reception,

\[ E_2=\frac{\mathcal E}{N_2} =\frac{1/\sqrt2}{\sqrt3/2} =\sqrt{\frac23} =\boxed{0.81649658}. \tag{41} \]

So the photon loses \(18.350342\%\) of its emitted local energy; its redshift is \(z=E_1/E_2-1=22.474487\%\):

\[ \frac{E_1-E_2}{E_1}=1-\sqrt{\frac23}=0.18350342. \tag{42} \]

Conservation check:

\[ N_1E_1=0.70710678, \qquad N_2E_2=(0.86602540)(0.81649658)=0.70710678. \tag{43} \]

The same Killing energy arrives at the second surface. Local photon energies differ because the observers are stationary at different gravitational potentials.

For a receiver at infinity, \(N_\infty=1\), so \(E_\infty=0.70710678\).

10. Work the gravitational lifting-energy calculation

Trial: Hold a small test body of rest mass \(m\) stationary at \(r=4\). Lift it quasistatically to \(r=8\), so it starts and ends at rest relative to the stationary observer families. Neglect its self-gravity and the lifting device's backreaction.

The energy of a supported stationary body, referenced to infinity, is

\[ E_\infty(r)=mN(r). \tag{44} \]

Thus

\[ \begin{aligned} E_{\infty,1}&=m/\sqrt2=0.70710678\,m,\\ E_{\infty,2}&=m\sqrt3/2=0.86602540\,m. \end{aligned} \tag{45} \]

The reversible external work measured with the distant energy reference is

\[ \boxed{W_\infty=E_{\infty,2}-E_{\infty,1} =m\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right) =0.15891862\,m.} \tag{46} \]

Because \(c=1\), this is \(15.891862\%\) of the body's rest energy. In SI units, restore the factor \(c^2\): \(W_\infty=0.15891862\,mc^2\).

Verify the same work using local force and proper displacement

From \(E_\infty=mN\),

\[ dE_\infty=mN'(r)dr. \tag{47} \]

The supporting proper acceleration is

\[ a_{\rm hold}=\frac{N'}{NB} =\frac{1}{r^2N}, \tag{48} \]

where the final equality uses the already-derived Schwarzschild functions. The local support force is \(F_{\rm local}=ma_{\rm hold}\), and the local radial displacement is \(d\ell=Bdr\).

Redshift the locally supplied work into the common distant-energy reference:

\[ \begin{aligned} dW_\infty&=N F_{\rm local}\,d\ell\\ &=N\left(m\frac{N'}{NB}\right)Bdr\\ &=mN'dr. \end{aligned} \tag{49} \]

Integrate from 4 to 8:

\[ \boxed{W_\infty=m\int_4^8N'(r)dr=m[N(8)-N(4)] =0.15891862\,m.} \tag{50} \]

The global energy difference and the integrated redshifted local work agree exactly. This is a conservation check on the Schwarzschild solution.

11. Evaluate the Gaussian flux at both spheres

For any static spherical metric of the form (1), the stationary proper acceleration is

\[ a_{\rm hold}(r)=\frac{N'}{NB}. \tag{51} \]

Define the redshifted acceleration-flux quantity

\[ \mathcal F(r)=4\pi r^2\,N(r)a_{\rm hold}(r) =4\pi r^2\frac{N'}B. \tag{52} \]

For Schwarzschild,

\[ N'=\frac{1}{r^2N},\qquad B=\frac1N, \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{N'}B=\frac1{r^2}. \tag{53} \]

Therefore

\[ \boxed{\frac{r^2N'}B=1=M,\qquad \mathcal F(r)=4\pi M=4\pi.} \tag{54} \]

Calculate the two surfaces separately:

At \(r=4\):

\[ N'=\frac{1}{16(1/\sqrt2)}=0.08838835, \quad \frac{N'}B=\frac{0.08838835}{1.41421356}=0.06250000. \tag{55} \]

\[ r_1^2\frac{N_1'}{B_1}=16(0.0625)=\boxed{1}, \quad\mathcal F_1=4\pi. \tag{56} \]

At \(r=8\):

\[ N'=\frac{1}{64(\sqrt3/2)}=0.01804220, \quad\frac{N'}B=\frac{0.01804220}{1.15470054}=0.01562500. \tag{57} \]

\[ r_2^2\frac{N_2'}{B_2}=64(0.015625)=\boxed{1}, \quad\mathcal F_2=4\pi. \tag{58} \]

Result: Both Gaussian surfaces have the same redshifted gravitational flux. Their local support accelerations are different:

\[ a_{\rm hold}(4)=0.08838835, \qquad a_{\rm hold}(8)=0.01804220. \tag{59} \]

In GR this surface integral is connected to the appropriately normalized static Komar mass. Its equality in the vacuum exterior follows from the field equations. It is not equal acceleration at the two spheres.

12. Calculate the actual radial ruler distance

The coordinate difference between the surfaces is simply

\[ \Delta r=8-4=4. \tag{60} \]

But the proper radial distance on a Schwarzschild constant-\(t\) exterior slice is

\[ \Delta\ell=\int_4^8B(r)dr =\int_4^8\frac{dr}{\sqrt{1-2/r}}. \tag{61} \]

An antiderivative (with a dimensionless argument in the logarithm) is

\[ L(r)=\sqrt{r(r-2)} +2\ln\left(\frac{\sqrt r+\sqrt{r-2}}{\sqrt2}\right), \quad L'(r)=\frac1{\sqrt{1-2/r}}. \tag{62} \]

At \(r=8\),

\[ L(8)=4\sqrt3+2\ln(2+\sqrt3). \tag{63} \]

At \(r=4\),

\[ L(4)=2\sqrt2+2\ln(1+\sqrt2). \tag{64} \]

Subtract:

\[ \boxed{\Delta\ell =4\sqrt3-2\sqrt2 +2\ln\left(\frac{2+\sqrt3}{1+\sqrt2}\right) =4.97094473.} \tag{65} \]

The proper radial distance is about \(24.27\%\) larger than the areal-coordinate difference of 4. The result depends on the stated spacelike slice; it is not a universal observer-independent travel distance.

13. Calculate the outward light travel time

For a radial photon in the static exterior, set \(ds^2=d\Omega^2=0\) in (30):

\[ 0=-fdt^2+\frac{dr^2}{f}. \tag{66} \]

For the outgoing branch,

\[ \frac{dr}{dt}=f(r)=1-\frac2r, \qquad dt=\frac{dr}{1-2/r}. \tag{67} \]

Integrate from 4 to 8:

\[ \begin{aligned} \Delta t&=\int_4^8\frac{dr}{1-2/r} =\int_4^8\frac{r}{r-2}dr\\ &=\left[r+2\ln|r-2|\right]_4^8\\ &=4+2\ln3=\boxed{6.19722458}. \end{aligned} \tag{68} \]

The distant-coordinate light travel time is longer than both \(\Delta r=4\) and the radial proper-slice distance \(\Delta\ell=4.97094\). These are different operational quantities.

Local light-speed check: A stationary observer measures \(d\ell=Bdr\) and \(d\tau=Ndt\). Hence

\[ \frac{d\ell}{d\tau}=\frac BN\frac{dr}{dt} =\frac1f\,f=\boxed{1=c}. \tag{69} \]

Local light speed is still \(c\); the variable coordinate speed \(dr/dt\) does not represent locally measured speed.

14. Locate the horizon and check its geometry

The static metric function vanishes at

\[ f=1-2/r=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\boxed{r_s=2M=2}. \tag{70} \]

The \(t,r\) chart becomes singular there, but a curvature invariant remains finite. The Kretschmann scalar is

\[ K=R_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}R^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta} =\frac{48M^2}{r^6}=\frac{48}{r^6}. \tag{71} \]

Thus

\[ K(2)=\frac{48}{64}=\boxed{0.75}, \quad K(4)=\frac{48}{4096}=0.01171875, \quad K(8)=\frac{48}{262144}=0.00018310547. \tag{72} \]

There is no curvature blow-up at \(r=2\), whereas \(K\to\infty\) as \(r\to0\).

To confirm regularity, define the tortoise coordinate

\[ r_*=r+2\ln\left|\frac r2-1\right|, \quad\frac{dr_*}{dr}=\frac1f, \tag{73} \]

and advanced coordinate \(v=t+r_*\). After substituting \(dt=dv-dr/f\), the metric becomes

\[ \boxed{ds^2=-f(r)dv^2+2\,dv\,dr+r^2d\Omega^2.} \tag{74} \]

It has finite metric coefficients at \(r=2\). An outgoing radial null branch obeys

\[ \boxed{\frac{dr}{dv}=\frac{f(r)}2=\frac12\left(1-\frac2r\right).} \tag{75} \]

For comparison:

Radius\(dr/dv\) of outgoing null branch
\(r=4\)\(+1/4\)
\(r=2\)\(0\)
\(r=1.5\)\(-1/6\)

The last row is calculated with the regular extension of the static form inside the horizon. General relativity has no observer at rest there. This paper's premises 7 and 8 say what holds across it (Section 3). Label: PREMISE of general relativity. \(r=2\) as the one horizon for every frame is the premise this paper attacks.

15. Restore ordinary units: a ten-solar-mass source

Use

\[ \begin{aligned} G&=6.67430\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}},\\ c&=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\\ M_\odot&=1.98847\times10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg},\\ M_{\rm physical}&=10M_\odot. \end{aligned} \tag{76} \]

One geometrized length unit is

\[ r_g=\frac{GM_{\rm physical}}{c^2}=\boxed{14.76669691\ \mathrm{km}}. \tag{77} \]

Our dimensionless positions correspond to

\[ \begin{aligned} r_s=2r_g&=29.533394\ \mathrm{km},\\ r_1=4r_g&=59.066788\ \mathrm{km},\\ r_2=8r_g&=118.133575\ \mathrm{km}. \end{aligned} \tag{78} \]

The previous dimensionless results convert to

\[ \Delta\ell=4.97094473r_g=\boxed{73.40443\ \mathrm{km}}, \tag{79} \]

\[ \Delta t=6.19722458\frac{r_g}{c} =\boxed{3.05253\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{s}} =0.305253\ \mathrm{ms}. \tag{80} \]

The dimensionless clock ratios, redshift ratios, and work fractions do not change when the source mass is rescaled while all radii remain fixed multiples of \(r_g\).

16. The flux equation alone does not fix the ruler

Our Gaussian-surface calculation found

\[ \boxed{\frac{r^2N'}B=M=1.} \tag{81} \]

Schwarzschild indeed satisfies (81). But (81) is only one differential equation for two unknown functions. Consider, as a concrete counterexample,

\[ \widetilde N(r)=e^{-1/r},\qquad \widetilde B(r)=e^{-1/r}. \tag{82} \]

Both are positive and approach 1 at infinity. Differentiate:

\[ \widetilde N'=\frac1{r^2}e^{-1/r}. \tag{83} \]

Therefore,

\[ \frac{r^2\widetilde N'}{\widetilde B} =r^2\frac{e^{-1/r}/r^2}{e^{-1/r}}=\boxed{1}, \tag{84} \]

exactly the same Gaussian-flux constraint. Yet

\[ \widetilde N\widetilde B=e^{-2/r}\neq1. \tag{85} \]

The resulting metric is not the Schwarzschild vacuum solution of Einstein's equations. The flux condition alone does not determine the ruler; a second relation is needed.

What completed the standard derivation was the independent radial geometric relationship

\[ \boxed{NB=1,} \tag{86} \]

which followed from \(R_{tt}=R_{rr}=0\). In this paper the second relation is supplied by the step from stationary observers to free fall. The frame that falls from rest far away passes the held frame at \(\gamma=1/N\), the speed that the same f dot dr would generate. It needs no force and keeps A's rulers, and special relativity between the two gives the held frame's ruler along the force at \(N\) of A's, so \(B=1/N\) (Section 4, statement 4). General relativity's \(NB=1\) for one frame and all rests on its field equations under the static premise.

09 / RESEARCH NOTES

The Schwarzschild Derivation, Reconciled with Conservation of Mass-Energy

Section 7 derived the Schwarzschild solution the way general relativity does. Section 4 derived the clocks and the rulers around one point mass from the conservation laws, on the f dot dr idea. This section lays the two side by side the way a code review shows a change: the lines taken away in red, the lines that replace them or are added beside them in green, the lines that stay in grey.

Each box below holds the Schwarzschild derivation first, as it stands in Section 7, and then the same derivation line by line with the changes marked. The child's box carries the recipe, the teacher's box the simplified derivation, and the physicist's box the full derivation.

1. What stays.

Around one body at rest, outside \(L\), the two derivations give the same clocks, the same rulers and the same count of a free body:

\[ f^2=1-\frac Lr,\qquad d\ell=\frac{dr}{f},\qquad e=\gamma f,\qquad L=\frac{2G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}}{c^2}. \]

So the redshift and the curvature are the same there, to every figure, and so is the fall of a body along the radius (Section 4, statement 6). The orbits and the paths of light are not yet derived from Section 4 (Section 6, A6). For several bodies, and when the count moves, the two derivations part outside \(L\) as well (Section 6, statement 3).

2. What the Schwarzschild derivation assumes and the conservation derivation derives.

The Schwarzschild derivation assumesThe conservation derivation derives it from
That nothing changes with time (assumption 2)the count does not change while nothing crosses the surface (premise 1), which keeps the clocks and rulers outside a round body at rest the same; when bodies move, the same sum holds at every moment (premise 6)
Einstein's equations in empty space (assumption 5)not used: the three steps of f dot dr give the clock, and the pull is set by the count
\(NB=1\), from two of the field equationsthe f dot dr in the field set equal to the f dot dr needed to generate the motion (Section 4, statement 4)
The mass \(M\), a constant fixed by Newton's law far awaythe complete count inside the surface, \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}=E_{\mathrm{enc}}/c^2\), every kind of energy once; the counted pull is Newton's law at every distance, exactly
A conserved energy, from the sameness in timethe count of a free body, \(e=\gamma f\): the gain of its motion canceled by the clock rate where it is (premise 3)
One mass for every framea frame held at rest reads the body at \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}/f\), by count and by weighing (Section 4, statement 2)

The last row is already inside the solution. A frame held at rest feels the pull \(G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}/(r^2f)\): Newton's law with the mass that it reads itself. Put the far mass into each held frame's own law instead, and the clock rate comes out as \(1-L/2r\) and every redshift comes out lower (Section 17).

3. Where the two part.

At \(L\). General relativity continues its solution across \(L\) (Section 7, parts 15 to 17): one metric for all observers, with the same solution and the same mass continued across \(L\). Nothing outside \(L\) requires that step. It is the step by which general relativity merges the frames' different values into one event horizon, and it is the error that this paper names (Section 18). From it, with the direction of time that the continuation chooses inside \(L\), follow one event horizon for every frame of reference, crossed one way only, and the fall of everything inside to the centre.

The same step leaves no frame at rest inside \(L\), and no one there to keep the count. In the continued form \(t\) points along space inside \(L\), so a frame held at rest would need a four-velocity along space. The conserved \(e\) becomes a momentum along that direction: there \(\xi=\partial_t\) has \(g(\xi,\xi)=c^2(L/r-1)\gt0\), and along the unit vector \(s=\xi/(ck)\), with \(k=\sqrt{L/r-1}\), a body's momentum is \(p\cdot s=-m_0c\,e/k\), which no observer at rest exists to read as an energy, and the only observers left are moving ones. The energy of a body inside is then measured against a moving observer, for example the one that falls with \(e=0\): \(E_{\mathrm{local}}=mc^2\sqrt{1+e^2/k^2}\), with \(k=\sqrt{L/r-1}\). The frame held at rest is replaced by a falling one. The form was fixed first, by the premise that nothing changes with time carried inside, and the observers were removed to fit it. Conservation of mass-energy is a count kept by an observer (Section 2). So inside \(L\) the continued solution conserves a momentum, and keeps no count of mass-energy in this paper's sense, although general relativity's own rule is that all energy gravitates, and its masses defined far away (Komar, ADM) say nothing about the count inside.

The bridge, and the loophole it closes. Going from one frame of reference to another takes the energy that f dot dr gives, whatever makes the change (Section 4, statements 1 and 4): between two frames held at rest in a pull, the net f dot dr between them, \(\int\mathbf g\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell/c^2\); between two frames with no pull, in relative motion or acceleration, the f dot dr that the motion takes, \(\int\mathbf F\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell/(mc^2)\). The two are equal, \(\ln\gamma=\ln(1/f)\) for a body let go from rest far away, and every frame's clock, its ruler along the pull and its scale change by that same f dot dr (premise 5). That is what keeps the count: whatever a free body gains in reading on the way, the scale of the frame that reads it loses, \(d(\gamma f)=0\), and an energy \(E\), unchanged in its own frame, taken from one frame of reference to another is charged \(E\,df=E\,f\,d\ln f\) in A's units. Keep one frame's scale \(f_*\) for every frame, and that charge is left out: the entry of a free body read at that scale changes by \(f_*(\gamma_2-\gamma_1)\,m_0c^2\) in A's units between two frames, with nothing to pay for it, which is uncompensated kinetic energy; and a scale changed with no f dot dr behind it is the same loophole the other way round. The machine of Section 1 is this loophole in one cycle: the store \(U\) taken up without its charge \(U(f_2-f_1)\). Inside \(L\) the continuation keeps one metric and the far mass for every frame and leaves no frame held at rest: a frame held at rest would move along \(\xi=\partial_t\), with the four-velocity \(u=\alpha\,\xi\) and \(g(u,u)=-c^2\), so \(\alpha^2F=1\), and where \(F\lt0\) no real \(\alpha\) exists, whatever the coordinates. So inside \(L\) the continued solution has no frame whose scale the f dot dr updates, and no frame held at rest to take up the f dot dr of a body or an energy that goes from one frame to another: the update that closes the loophole has nowhere to act, so the loophole is left open there, and the count of Section 2 cannot be kept. [DERIVED: the bridge on premises 1 to 5 (Section 4, statements 1 and 4); that no frame is held at rest inside \(L\), from the continued form itself, on the comparison side (Section 7, part 15), with the paragraph before (the conserved \(e\) a momentum, the only observers moving ones)]

The conservation derivation does not take that step. Premises 7 and 8 stand in its place:

\[ s_{PQ}=\pm\,i\,\sqrt{\frac{L/r_Q-1}{1-L/r_P}}\ \ \text{across } L,\qquad \Big(\frac{dr}{d\tau}\Big)^2=c^2\Big(e^2-\Big|1-\frac Lr\Big|\Big),\qquad \Big|\frac{dr}{d\tau}\Big|_{L}=c\,e . \]

What two frames read is real for each from its own frame of reference. An inferred measurement across \(L\) has two solutions, and they are complex. Objects move beyond their event horizon: a body in free motion has the speed \(c\,e\) on its own clock at \(L\), and it gets there in a finite time of its own, by the same law in both directions. Inside \(L\) the pull points outward: a body that falls in turns back at \(L/(1+e^2)\) and comes out, where the continued solution still has it moving inward, with \((dr/d\tau)^2=2c^2e^2\) (Section 14, Part 7). An observer at rest far away cannot and does not observe the passage. \(L\) is the causal boundary, which is also the event horizon, of that observer, and the causal boundary depends on the frame of reference.

The observation that decides: anything, light or matter, arriving outside from inside an event horizon (Section 18).

4. How the Schwarzschild derivation is reconciled with the conservation laws.

By three changes. Its assumption that nothing changes with time becomes a result, and its field equations are not needed. Its solution outside \(L\) is kept, because the count gives the same. And its continuation across \(L\), one account for every frame of reference, is replaced by premises 7 and 8.

For a child

The recipe, as it stands in Section 7

Here is the whole recipe the textbooks use to get the black-hole formula, every step written out.

It starts by assuming the pull never changes and that there is nothing outside the black hole, works through a lot of algebra, and ends with the formula and its edge.

Two things come out at the end: one rule that says how the pull spreads out (which is just energy adding up), and a second rule about clocks and rulers that the recipe takes from Einstein's equations.

The second rule is the one nobody has ever checked near the edge.

The recipe, redone, line by line

− red: taken away  ·  + green: replaces it, or is added beside it  ·  grey: unchanged

 

Here is the whole recipe the textbooks use to get the black-hole formula, every step written out.

−

It starts by assuming the pull never changes and that there is nothing outside the black hole, works through a lot of algebra, and ends with the formula and its edge.

+

It starts from everything inside the bubble, whose total never changes because the lid stays on. It follows a falling ball one small step at a time: the pull does work on the ball, the ball gets heavier by that much, and the clock where the ball is runs slower by the same share. It ends with the same formula outside, and the same edge.

−

Two things come out at the end: one rule that says how the pull spreads out (which is just energy adding up), and a second rule about clocks and rulers that the recipe takes from Einstein's equations.

+

Two things come out at the end: one rule that says how the pull spreads out (which is just energy adding up), and a second rule about clocks and rulers. The second rule comes from two people at the same place, one held there and one falling past. The one who falls keeps the ruler they started with, and the two are simply moving past each other.

−

The second rule is the one nobody has ever checked near the edge.

+

At the edge the textbook goes on with one story for everybody, and says that nothing ever comes back out. Our rules do not do that. They say that each person's numbers are real for that person, and that things can, and do, move past their edge. Nobody has ever checked what the textbook says happens there.

For a high school physics teacher

The simplified derivation, as it stands in Section 7

The assumptions. Six things are assumed before anything is calculated: the geometry is the same in every direction; it does not change with time (staticity); there is no matter or energy outside the source; far away space is flat; Einstein's equations hold; and \(r\) is defined so that a sphere has area \(4\pi r^2\).

The general metric. With those assumptions the line element can be written \(ds^2=-N(r)^2c^2dt^2+B(r)^2dr^2+r^2d\Omega^2\), with two unknown functions: \(N\), the rate of a clock held at rest (\(d\tau=N\,dt\)), and \(B\), the stretch of a radial ruler (\(d\ell=B\,dr\)). Nothing about the field has been put in yet.

The field equations. In empty space Einstein's equations reduce to \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\). Writing out the curvature (the Christoffel symbols and the Ricci tensor, parts 4 and 5) gives three equations for \(N\) and \(B\).

Clocks and rulers are reciprocal. Adding the time-time and radial-radial equations makes every second derivative cancel and leaves \(N'/N+B'/B=0\), so \(NB\) is constant; flat space far away makes it 1: \(NB=1\). This is the step that fixes the ruler once the clock is known, and it comes from two field equations, not from conservation.

The form of the clock. The remaining angular equation becomes \(\frac{d}{dr}(rN^2)=1\), so \(N^2=1+C/r\). Far from the mass, Newton's law fixes the constant: \(C=-2GM/c^2\). So \(N^2=1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}\) and \(B=1/N\): the Schwarzschild metric. Part 11 checks it by substitution.

Redshift and the edge. Because nothing changes with time, a photon's energy times the clock rate where it is read, \(N\,E_{\rm local}\), is the same everywhere (part 12): that is the exact gravitational redshift. \(N\) is zero where \(r_s=2GM/c^2\) (part 13). The curvature there is finite (part 14), and in coordinates that stay regular (part 15) the formula says that inside \(r_s\) nothing moves to larger \(r\) (parts 16 and 17).

What conservation gives, and what it does not. The pull through any sphere, redshifted, is the same, \(4\pi GM\) (part 18): that is the Gaussian-surface relation this paper started from. But it is one equation for two functions. The second equation, \(NB=1\), comes from the field equations under the static premise (parts 19 to 21).

The simplified derivation, redone with conservation, line by line

− red: taken away  ·  + green: replaces it, or is added beside it  ·  grey: unchanged
