Six things are assumed before anything is calculated: the geometry is the same in every direction; it does not change with time (staticity); there is no matter or energy outside the source; far away space is flat; Einstein's equations hold; and \(r\) is defined so that a sphere has area \(4\pi r^2\).

+

In the conservation derivation two of the six are not assumed. That the pull is the same at every time follows from the count: it does not change while nothing crosses the surface (premise 1). And Einstein's equations are not used: the three steps of f dot dr give the clock, and the step from stationary observers to free fall gives the ruler (Section 4, statements 1 and 4).

 

The general metric. With those assumptions the line element can be written \(ds^2=-N(r)^2c^2dt^2+B(r)^2dr^2+r^2d\Omega^2\), with two unknown functions: \(N\), the rate of a clock held at rest (\(d\tau=N\,dt\)), and \(B\), the stretch of a radial ruler (\(d\ell=B\,dr\)). Nothing about the field has been put in yet.

 

The field equations. In empty space Einstein's equations reduce to \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\). Writing out the curvature (the Christoffel symbols and the Ricci tensor, parts 4 and 5) gives three equations for \(N\) and \(B\).

−

Clocks and rulers are reciprocal. Adding the time-time and radial-radial equations makes every second derivative cancel and leaves \(N'/N+B'/B=0\), so \(NB\) is constant; flat space far away makes it 1: \(NB=1\). This is the step that fixes the ruler once the clock is known, and it comes from two field equations, not from conservation.

+

Clocks and rulers are reciprocal, from f dot dr. A frame that falls from rest far away passes the frame held at rest at the speed that the same f dot dr would generate, \(\gamma=1/N\). The falling frame needs no force and keeps A's clock and rulers (premise 4). Special relativity between the two then gives the held frame's ruler along the force at \(N\) of A's, so \(B=1/N\) and \(NB=1\) (Section 4, statement 4). No equation of Einstein's is used.

 

The form of the clock. The remaining angular equation becomes \(\frac{d}{dr}(rN^2)=1\), so \(N^2=1+C/r\). Far from the mass, Newton's law fixes the constant: \(C=-2GM/c^2\). So \(N^2=1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}\) and \(B=1/N\): the Schwarzschild metric. Part 11 checks it by substitution.

+

The same form, from the pull counted through every sphere, \(4\pi r^2N\,g_{\rm hold}=4\pi G\mathcal M_{\rm enc}\), and the clock step: \(N^2=1-L/r\) (Section 4, statement 6). \(M\) is the complete count inside the surface, \(\mathcal M_{\rm enc}\): every kind of energy once, with the mass equivalent of potential energy (Section 4, statement 5). In the frame of the calculation the counted pull is Newton's law, exactly, at every distance.

−

Redshift and the edge. Because nothing changes with time, a photon's energy times the clock rate where it is read, \(N\,E_{\rm local}\), is the same everywhere (part 12): that is the exact gravitational redshift. \(N\) is zero where \(r_s=2GM/c^2\) (part 13). The curvature there is finite (part 14), and in coordinates that stay regular (part 15) the formula says that inside \(r_s\) nothing moves to larger \(r\) (parts 16 and 17).

+

Redshift and the event horizon. The energy that a frame at rest reads for a free body, times that frame's clock rate, is the same at every step, \(\gamma N=e\) (premise 3; Section 4, statements 1 and 3): the same redshift, from the count, with no assumption that nothing changes with time. \(N\) is zero at \(r=L\), where the escape velocity is \(c\): the causal boundary, which is also the event horizon, of a frame at rest far away. A zero of the clock rate is not a singularity. The conservation derivation does not carry one account across \(L\) for every frame. Premises 7 and 8 stand there instead (Section 3). What two frames read is real for each from its own frame of reference. An inferred measurement across \(L\) has two solutions, and they are complex. And objects move beyond their event horizon: at \(L\) a body in free motion has the speed \(c\,e\) on its own clock, and it gets there in a finite time of its own, by the same law in both directions.

−

What conservation gives, and what it does not. The pull through any sphere, redshifted, is the same, \(4\pi GM\) (part 18): that is the Gaussian-surface relation this paper started from. But it is one equation for two functions. The second equation, \(NB=1\), comes from the field equations under the static premise (parts 19 to 21).

+

What conservation gives. The pull through any sphere outside the matter is \(4\pi G\mathcal M_{\rm enc}\): the same on every sphere and the same at every time, because the count does not change (premise 1). The second equation, \(NB=1\), comes from f dot dr (Section 4, statement 4). So both equations come from the conservation laws and the premises, the second with special relativity at one place. Nothing is taken from a field equation or from a static premise, and nothing is carried across \(L\).

For a theoretical physicist

The full derivation, as it stands in Section 7

We derive the Schwarzschild geometry from the Einstein field equations, starting with spherical symmetry and a general metric—not with the Schwarzschild metric itself.

The purpose is to establish every mathematical step, especially the origin of

\[ \boxed{N(r)B(r)=1} \]

and

\[ \boxed{r_s=\frac{2GM}{c^2}}. \]

We also distinguish the assumptions supplied by GR from the relationships that follow mathematically, so that the derivation can later be compared with the conservation of mass-energy.

1. Physical thought experiment

Imagine an isolated, nonrotating, electrically neutral spherical mass \(M\), surrounded by two concentric Gaussian surfaces at radii \(r_1\) and \(r_2\).

The two surfaces are imaginary measurement boundaries, not material shells.

We assume:

  1. Spherical symmetry: The geometry is unchanged under spatial rotations.
  2. Staticity: The exterior geometry is time-independent and invariant under time reversal.
  3. Vacuum exterior: No matter or nongravitational field stress-energy is present outside the source.
  4. Asymptotic flatness: Far from the source, spacetime approaches Minkowski spacetime.
  5. Einstein gravity: The metric satisfies Einstein's field equations, with zero cosmological constant.
  6. Areal radius: The coordinate \(r\) is defined so a sphere has area \(4\pi r^2\).

The derivation applies to the static exterior region. We will subsequently extend the resulting geometry through the horizon using regular coordinates. Label (this paper): that extension, parts 15 to 17, is the step this paper attacks. The regular coordinates carry the same static form inside, where nothing has tested it.

2. Construct the most general static spherical metric

Begin with four coordinates:

\[ x^\mu=(ct,r,\theta,\phi). \]

Spherical symmetry restricts the angular part to

\[ r^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2). \]

Staticity permits a time coordinate in which the metric has no time-space cross terms.

Therefore, in the static region,

\[ \boxed{ ds^2=-N(r)^2c^2dt^2+B(r)^2dr^2 +r^2d\theta^2+r^2\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2 } \tag{1} \]

where \(N(r)>0\) and \(B(r)>0\).

At infinity,

\[ \lim_{r\to\infty}N(r)=1,\qquad \lim_{r\to\infty}B(r)=1. \]

We have not yet specified the gravitational field or inserted any Schwarzschild factors.

Physical interpretation

For a stationary clock, \(dr=d\theta=d\phi=0\), so

\[ ds^2=-c^2d\tau^2=-N^2c^2dt^2. \]

Thus,

\[ \boxed{d\tau=N(r)\,dt.} \tag{2} \]

For a radial distance measured at constant \(t\),

\[ \boxed{d\ell=B(r)\,dr.} \tag{3} \]

These define our clock and radial ruler functions.

3. Introduce convenient metric functions

Write

\[ N(r)=e^{\nu(r)},\qquad B(r)=e^{\lambda(r)}. \]

Then

\[ ds^2=-e^{2\nu}c^2dt^2+e^{2\lambda}dr^2+r^2d\Omega^2. \tag{4} \]

For the curvature calculation, temporarily use \(x^0=ct\).

The metric components are

\[ g_{\mu\nu}= \begin{pmatrix} -e^{2\nu}&0&0&0\\ 0&e^{2\lambda}&0&0\\ 0&0&r^2&0\\ 0&0&0&r^2\sin^2\theta \end{pmatrix}. \tag{5} \]

Its inverse is

\[ g^{\mu\nu}= \begin{pmatrix} -e^{-2\nu}&0&0&0\\ 0&e^{-2\lambda}&0&0\\ 0&0&r^{-2}&0\\ 0&0&0&(r^2\sin^2\theta)^{-1} \end{pmatrix}. \tag{6} \]

The determinant is

\[ g=-e^{2(\nu+\lambda)}r^4\sin^2\theta, \]

so

\[ \sqrt{-g}=e^{\nu+\lambda}r^2\sin\theta. \tag{7} \]

The functions \(\nu\) and \(\lambda\) are still completely unknown.

4. Calculate the Christoffel symbols

The Levi-Civita connection is defined by

\[ \boxed{ \Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\nu} =\frac12g^{\alpha\beta} \left( \partial_\mu g_{\beta\nu} +\partial_\nu g_{\beta\mu} -\partial_\beta g_{\mu\nu} \right). } \tag{8} \]

Because the metric is static, all time derivatives vanish. Label (this paper): assumption 2; outside the horizon it follows from conservation, the count inside the surface being constant (Section 4, statements 5 and 6); what this paper attacks is carrying it inside the horizon (parts 15 to 17).

The relevant radial derivatives are

\[ \begin{aligned} \partial_r g_{00}&=-2\nu'e^{2\nu},\\ \partial_r g_{rr}&=2\lambda'e^{2\lambda},\\ \partial_r g_{\theta\theta}&=2r,\\ \partial_r g_{\phi\phi}&=2r\sin^2\theta. \end{aligned} \]

The angular derivatives include

\[ \partial_\theta g_{\phi\phi} =2r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta. \]

A prime denotes differentiation with respect to \(r\).

Example: calculate \(\Gamma^r_{00}\)

By Equation (8),

\[ \Gamma^r_{00} =-\frac12g^{rr}\partial_rg_{00}. \]

Substitute:

\[ =-\frac12e^{-2\lambda}(-2\nu'e^{2\nu}). \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{\Gamma^r_{00}=\nu'e^{2(\nu-\lambda)}.} \]

Complete list of nonzero independent Christoffel symbols

\[ \begin{aligned} \Gamma^0_{0r}&=\nu',\\ \Gamma^r_{00}&=\nu'e^{2(\nu-\lambda)},\\ \Gamma^r_{rr}&=\lambda',\\ \Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}&=-re^{-2\lambda},\\ \Gamma^r_{\phi\phi}&=-re^{-2\lambda}\sin^2\theta,\\ \Gamma^\theta_{r\theta}&=\frac1r,\\ \Gamma^\phi_{r\phi}&=\frac1r,\\ \Gamma^\theta_{\phi\phi}&=-\sin\theta\cos\theta,\\ \Gamma^\phi_{\theta\phi}&=\cot\theta. \end{aligned} \tag{9} \]

The connection is symmetric in its two lower indices, so entries related by exchanging those indices are also present.

This completes the connection calculation.

5. Calculate the Ricci tensor

We adopt the curvature convention

\[ R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu\Gamma^\rho_{\nu\sigma} -\partial_\nu\Gamma^\rho_{\mu\sigma} +\Gamma^\rho_{\mu\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha_{\nu\sigma} -\Gamma^\rho_{\nu\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\sigma}. \]

Contracting gives

\[ R_{\mu\nu}=R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}. \]

Equivalently,

\[ \boxed{ R_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\alpha\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\nu} -\partial_\nu\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\alpha} +\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\nu}\Gamma^\beta_{\alpha\beta} -\Gamma^\beta_{\mu\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha_{\nu\beta}. } \tag{10} \]

We calculate each independent component.

5.1 Time-time component

The first term is

\[ \partial_r\Gamma^r_{00} =e^{2(\nu-\lambda)} \left[\nu''+2\nu'(\nu'-\lambda')\right]. \]

The second term vanishes because the metric is time-independent.

For the third term, use

\[ \Gamma^\beta_{r\beta} =\nu'+\lambda'+\frac2r. \]

Thus,

\[ \Gamma^r_{00}\Gamma^\beta_{r\beta} =e^{2(\nu-\lambda)}\nu' \left(\nu'+\lambda'+\frac2r\right). \]

The fourth term is

\[ -2e^{2(\nu-\lambda)}\nu'^2. \]

Combining the terms,

\[ \boxed{ R_{00}=e^{2(\nu-\lambda)} \left[ \nu''+\nu'^2-\nu'\lambda'+\frac{2\nu'}r \right]. } \tag{11} \]

5.2 Radial-radial component

The four terms in Equation (10) are

\[ \begin{aligned} \partial_\alpha\Gamma^\alpha_{rr}&=\lambda'',\\ -\partial_r\Gamma^\alpha_{r\alpha} &=-\nu''-\lambda''+\frac2{r^2},\\ \Gamma^\alpha_{rr}\Gamma^\beta_{\alpha\beta} &=\lambda'\left(\nu'+\lambda'+\frac2r\right),\\ -\Gamma^\beta_{r\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha_{r\beta} &=-\nu'^2-\lambda'^2-\frac2{r^2}. \end{aligned} \]

Combining,

\[ \boxed{ R_{rr} =-\nu''-\nu'^2+\nu'\lambda'+\frac{2\lambda'}r. } \tag{12} \]

5.3 Angular components

Substituting the angular Christoffel symbols gives

\[ \boxed{ R_{\theta\theta} =1-e^{-2\lambda} \left(1+r\nu'-r\lambda'\right). } \tag{13} \]

Spherical symmetry requires

\[ \boxed{ R_{\phi\phi}=\sin^2\theta\,R_{\theta\theta}. } \tag{14} \]

All off-diagonal Ricci components vanish.

We now have every independent component of the Ricci tensor.

6. Apply the vacuum Einstein equations

Einstein's field equations, with zero cosmological constant, are

\[ R_{\mu\nu}-\frac12Rg_{\mu\nu} =\frac{8\pi G}{c^4}T_{\mu\nu}. \tag{15} \]

In vacuum,

\[ T_{\mu\nu}=0. \]

Hence,

\[ R_{\mu\nu}-\frac12Rg_{\mu\nu}=0. \]

Contract with \(g^{\mu\nu}\):

\[ R-\frac12(4)R=0, \]

giving

\[ -R=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad R=0. \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{R_{\mu\nu}=0.} \tag{16} \]

This reduction is exact for the stated vacuum equations.

7. Derive the ruler-clock relationship

Set Equations (11) and (12) equal to zero:

\[ \nu''+\nu'^2-\nu'\lambda'+\frac{2\nu'}r=0, \tag{17} \]

\[ -\nu''-\nu'^2+\nu'\lambda'+\frac{2\lambda'}r=0. \tag{18} \]

Add them.

The second derivatives cancel:

\[ \nu''-\nu''=0. \]

The quadratic terms cancel:

\[ \nu'^2-\nu'^2=0. \]

The mixed terms cancel:

\[ -\nu'\lambda'+\nu'\lambda'=0. \]

We are left with

\[ \frac{2\nu'}r+\frac{2\lambda'}r=0. \]

For \(r>0\),

\[ \nu'+\lambda'=0. \]

Integrate:

\[ \nu+\lambda=C. \]

Exponentiate:

\[ e^\nu e^\lambda=e^C. \]

Since \(N=e^\nu\) and \(B=e^\lambda\),

\[ NB=e^C. \]

Asymptotic flatness gives \(N(\infty)=B(\infty)=1\), hence \(e^C=1\).

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{NB=1.} \tag{19} \]

This is the complete derivation of the reciprocal clock-ruler relationship, from the field equations under assumption 2. In this paper the same relation comes from setting the f dot dr in the field equal to the f dot dr needed to generate the motion, with no equation of Einstein's (Section 4, statement 4).

The crucial mathematical operation was adding the two independent vacuum Ricci equations.

Notice that no Schwarzschild radius was assumed.

8. Solve the remaining radial equation

Now apply \(R_{\theta\theta}=0\).

From Equation (13),

\[ 1-e^{-2\lambda} (1+r\nu'-r\lambda')=0. \]

Since \(\lambda=-\nu\),

\[ \lambda'=-\nu'. \]

Thus,

\[ 1-e^{-2\lambda}(1+2r\nu')=0. \tag{20} \]

Define

\[ f(r)=e^{2\nu}=N^2=e^{-2\lambda}=B^{-2}. \]

Its derivative is

\[ f'=2\nu'e^{2\nu}=2\nu'f. \]

Consequently,

\[ 2\nu'=\frac{f'}f. \]

Substitute into Equation (20):

\[ 1-f\left(1+\frac{rf'}f\right)=0. \]

Expand:

\[ 1-f-rf'=0. \]

Rearrange:

\[ rf'+f=1. \]

Recognize the product derivative:

\[ \boxed{\frac{d}{dr}(rf)=1.} \tag{21} \]

Integrate:

\[ rf=r+C_1. \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{f(r)=1+\frac{C_1}{r}.} \tag{22} \]

This is the general asymptotically flat static spherical vacuum solution in the chosen areal-radius coordinates, up to identifying the integration constant.

9. Determine the integration constant from Newtonian gravity

We must identify \(C_1\) using the limit far from the mass. This is where the mass \(M\) enters.

For a slowly moving test particle, the radial geodesic equation is

\[ \frac{d^2r}{d\tau^2} +\Gamma^r_{00}\left(\frac{dx^0}{d\tau}\right)^2 +\cdots=0. \]

Far from the mass, in the slow-motion limit,

\[ \frac{dx^0}{d\tau}\approx c,\qquad \frac{d^2r}{d\tau^2}\approx\frac{d^2r}{dt^2}. \]

The leading radial acceleration is therefore

\[ \frac{d^2r}{dt^2}\approx-c^2\Gamma^r_{00}. \]

Using Equation (9),

\[ \Gamma^r_{00}=\nu'e^{2(\nu-\lambda)}. \]

Far from the mass, \(e^{2(\nu-\lambda)}\approx1\), giving

\[ \frac{d^2r}{dt^2}\approx-c^2\nu'. \tag{23} \]

The Newtonian potential \(\Phi\) satisfies

\[ \frac{d^2r}{dt^2}=-\Phi'. \]

Comparing,

\[ c^2\nu'\approx\Phi'. \]

Integrating with both quantities vanishing at infinity,

\[ \nu\approx\frac{\Phi}{c^2}. \]

Since

\[ N^2=e^{2\nu}\approx1+2\nu, \]

we obtain

\[ \boxed{ f(r)=N^2(r)\approx1+\frac{2\Phi(r)}{c^2}. } \tag{24} \]

For a spherical mass,

\[ \Phi(r)=-\frac{GM}{r}. \]

Thus,

\[ f(r)\approx1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}. \]

But our exact solution was

\[ f(r)=1+\frac{C_1}{r}. \]

Matching the coefficient far from the mass gives

\[ \boxed{C_1=-\frac{2GM}{c^2}.} \tag{25} \]

Label (this paper): the solved equation is exact outside the horizon, where conservation gives the same constant (Section 4, statement 6); inside the horizon nothing has tested the form.

10. Obtain the complete Schwarzschild metric

Substitute Equation (25) into Equation (22):

\[ f(r)=1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}. \]

Since \(N^2=f\) and \(B^2=1/f\),

\[ \boxed{ N(r)=\sqrt{1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}} } \tag{26} \]

and

\[ \boxed{ B(r)=\frac1{\sqrt{1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}}}. } \tag{27} \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{ ds^2= -\left(1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}\right)c^2dt^2 +\left(1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}\right)^{-1}dr^2 +r^2d\Omega^2. } \tag{28} \]

This is the Schwarzschild metric in standard areal-radius coordinates.

Every function in this metric has now been determined.

11. Verify the solution by substitution

A derivation is not complete until we substitute the solution into the original equations.

Let

\[ a=\frac{2GM}{c^2},\qquad f=1-\frac ar. \]

Then

\[ f'=\frac a{r^2},\qquad f''=-\frac{2a}{r^3}. \]

Our functions satisfy

\[ \nu=\frac12\ln f,\qquad \lambda=-\frac12\ln f. \]

Therefore,

\[ \nu'=\frac{f'}{2f},\qquad \lambda'=-\frac{f'}{2f}. \]

Check \(R_{\theta\theta}=0\)

Equation (13) becomes

\[ R_{\theta\theta}=1-f-rf'. \]

Substitute:

\[ R_{\theta\theta} =1-\left(1-\frac ar\right)-r\frac a{r^2}. \]

Thus,

\[ \boxed{R_{\theta\theta}=0.} \]

The \(\phi\phi\) component also vanishes.

Check \(R_{00}=0\)

Using \(\lambda'=-\nu'\), the bracket in Equation (11) becomes

\[ \nu''+2\nu'^2+\frac{2\nu'}r. \]

Because

\[ \nu''+2\nu'^2=\frac{f''}{2f}, \]

the bracket equals

\[ \frac{f''}{2f}+\frac{f'}{fr}. \]

Substituting the derivatives,

\[ \frac1f\left(-\frac a{r^3}+\frac a{r^3}\right)=0. \]

Hence,

\[ \boxed{R_{00}=0.} \]

Check \(R_{rr}=0\)

Equation (12) reduces to the negative of the same bracket:

\[ R_{rr}=-\frac{f''}{2f}-\frac{f'}{fr}=0. \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{R_{\mu\nu}=0} \]

for every component in the Schwarzschild vacuum region.

The solution satisfies the complete vacuum field equations.

12. Derive gravitational redshift from the metric

The exact redshift follows from the metric. In general relativity it rests on staticity, assumption 2, which supplies the Killing vector; in this paper the same relation is the count, \(e=\gamma f\), from conservation and the clock step (Section 4, statements 1 and 3).

Because the metric is stationary, it has a time-translation Killing vector \(\xi^\mu\). With \(x^0=ct\) and \(\xi=\partial_{ct}\), the conserved quantity below is the photon's energy divided by \(c\); with \(\xi=\partial_t\) it is the energy itself, and every ratio below is the same either way.

For a freely propagating photon with four-momentum \(p^\mu\), the quantity

\[ \mathcal E=-p_\mu\xi^\mu \]

is conserved along its geodesic.

A stationary observer at radius \(r\) has four-velocity proportional to \(\xi^\mu\). Its normalization gives a locally measured photon energy

\[ \boxed{E_{\rm local}(r)=\frac{\mathcal E}{N(r)}.} \tag{29} \]

Therefore, for emission at \(r_1\) and reception at \(r_2\),

\[ \frac{E_2}{E_1} =\frac{N(r_1)}{N(r_2)}. \]

Substituting Equation (26),

\[ \boxed{ \frac{E_2}{E_1} = \sqrt{ \frac{1-2GM/(r_1c^2)} {1-2GM/(r_2c^2)} }. } \tag{30} \]

For a receiver at infinity,

\[ \boxed{ E_\infty =E_{\rm emitted} \sqrt{1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}}. } \tag{31} \]

This is the exact Schwarzschild gravitational-redshift relationship for stationary observers. General relativity allows none inside the horizon. This paper's premises 7 and 8 say what holds across it (Section 3).

Check far from the mass

Let \(x=GM/(rc^2)\). For \(x\ll1\),

\[ \sqrt{1-2x} =1-x-\frac{x^2}{2}-\frac{x^3}{2}+O(x^4). \]

Thus,

\[ N(r)\approx1-\frac{GM}{rc^2} \]

at first order, matching the familiar Newtonian-potential redshift.

13. Derive the Schwarzschild radius

The metric function is

\[ f(r)=1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}. \]

The stationary Killing vector has squared norm

\[ \xi^\mu\xi_\mu=-f(r) \]

when the time coordinate is \(ct\).

Its norm becomes zero when

\[ 1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}=0. \]

Solving,

\[ \boxed{r_s=\frac{2GM}{c^2}.} \tag{32} \]

For positive \(M\), the static exterior region is \(r>r_s\).

But we must be careful: finding \(f=0\) identifies a candidate Killing horizon. To establish that this is a regular black-hole horizon rather than a physical singularity, we need to examine the geometry in coordinates that remain regular there.

14. Check whether the horizon is a curvature singularity

For the Schwarzschild metric, the Ricci scalar vanishes:

\[ R=0. \]

The Ricci tensor also vanishes in vacuum:

\[ R_{\mu\nu}=0. \]

But the full Riemann tensor does not vanish.

The Kretschmann scalar is

\[ K=R_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta} R^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}. \]

Direct contraction gives

\[ \boxed{ K=\frac{48G^2M^2}{c^4r^6}. } \tag{33} \]

At the Schwarzschild radius,

\[ K(r_s)=\frac{12}{r_s^4}, \]

which is finite for \(M>0\).

At \(r=0\),

\[ K\longrightarrow\infty. \]

Therefore, \(r=r_s\) is not a curvature singularity. The singularity in the standard Schwarzschild coordinate components is a coordinate singularity.

15. Extend the solution through the horizon

Define the tortoise coordinate \(r_*\) by

\[ \frac{dr_*}{dr}=\frac1{f(r)}. \]

Integrating in the exterior,

\[ \boxed{ r_*=r+r_s\ln\left|\frac r{r_s}-1\right|. } \tag{34} \]

Introduce the ingoing null coordinate

\[ v=t+\frac{r_*}{c}. \]

Thus,

\[ dt=dv-\frac{dr}{cf}. \]

Substitute into the Schwarzschild metric:

\[ ds^2=-fc^2\left(dv-\frac{dr}{cf}\right)^2 +\frac{dr^2}{f}+r^2d\Omega^2. \]

Expand:

\[ ds^2=-fc^2dv^2+2c\,dv\,dr -\frac{dr^2}{f}+\frac{dr^2}{f}+r^2d\Omega^2. \]

The divergent radial terms cancel.

We obtain

\[ \boxed{ ds^2=-\left(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\right)c^2dv^2 +2c\,dv\,dr+r^2d\Omega^2. } \tag{35} \]

This is the ingoing Eddington–Finkelstein metric.

It remains regular at \(r=r_s\).

We have now extended the solution across the Schwarzschild coordinate singularity. Label (this paper): the extension assumes that the static form of assumption 2 holds inside, and it gives one event horizon for every frame. That is the premise under attack in this paper: the merge of the frames' different values into one event horizon. As general relativity states the step: one metric is chosen for all observers, and the same solution with the same mass is continued across \(r_s\).

16. Determine the behavior of outgoing light

For radial light,

\[ ds^2=0,\qquad d\Omega=0. \]

Equation (35) gives

\[ 0=-fc^2dv^2+2c\,dv\,dr. \]

For the outgoing branch with \(dv\ne0\),

\[ \boxed{ \frac{dr}{dv}=\frac c2 \left(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\right). } \tag{36} \]

Examine three regions.

RegionOutgoing radial null trajectory
\(r>r_s\)\(dr/dv>0\)
\(r=r_s\)\(dr/dv=0\)
\(0<r<r_s\)\(dr/dv<0\)

The second radial null family has \(dv=0\) and is ingoing.

More generally, for a future-directed causal trajectory in the black-hole interior, Equation (35) implies

\[ -fc^2dv^2+2c\,dv\,dr+r^2d\Omega^2\le0. \]

For \(0<r<r_s\), \(f<0\). With the future orientation chosen so \(dv>0\),

\[ 2c\,dv\,dr \le fc^2dv^2-r^2d\Omega^2<0. \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{dr<0} \]

along every nontrivial future-directed causal trajectory in the interior, with the horizon-generator case treated at the boundary.

This is general relativity's reading of the inside: with the static form carried inside and the future orientation chosen there (\(dv>0\)), no causal trajectory moves to larger \(r\). It is a consequence of assumption 2 and of that choice, not a test of either. This paper's premise 8 says the opposite: objects can, and do, move beyond their event horizon (Section 3).

17. Establish the global event horizon

A black-hole event horizon is defined globally as the boundary of the region from which future-directed light signals can reach future null infinity.

The Eddington–Finkelstein calculation establishes the local causal behavior. We can additionally use Kruskal–Szekeres coordinates to examine the global extension.

Define the outgoing null coordinate

\[ u=t-\frac{r_*}{c}. \]

In the exterior region, introduce

\[ U=-e^{-cu/(2r_s)},\qquad V=e^{cv/(2r_s)}. \]

Then

\[ UV=-\left(\frac r{r_s}-1\right)e^{r/r_s}. \tag{37} \]

The metric becomes

\[ \boxed{ ds^2= -\frac{4r_s^3}{r}e^{-r/r_s}\,dU\,dV +r^2d\Omega^2. } \tag{38} \]

The coefficient is finite and nonzero at \(r=r_s\).

These coordinates extend smoothly across the horizon. In the maximally extended Schwarzschild spacetime, the future black-hole region is separated from the exterior by a null horizon, and future-directed causal trajectories inside it cannot reach the exterior's future null infinity.

The precise global interpretation requires specifying the spacetime extension and its time orientation. For a physically formed black hole, the relevant extension is the collapse geometry rather than the entire eternal Schwarzschild solution.

This is general relativity's identification of the horizon, resting on assumption 2 carried inside: one event horizon for every frame. Label: PREMISE of general relativity.

18. Return to our original Gaussian surfaces

Now we can connect the result to the conservation-law investigation.

For the static spherical metric,

\[ ds^2=-N^2c^2dt^2+B^2dr^2+r^2d\Omega^2, \]

the proper acceleration needed to hold a test mass at a fixed radius is

\[ g_{\rm hold}=\frac{c^2N'}{NB}. \tag{39} \]

Its locally measured supporting force is \(F_{\rm local}=mg_{\rm hold}\).

The redshifted acceleration is

\[ Ng_{\rm hold}=\frac{c^2N'}B. \]

Define the redshifted gravitational flux through a sphere:

\[ \mathcal F(r)=4\pi r^2\frac{c^2N'}B. \tag{40} \]

For Schwarzschild,

\[ N=\sqrt{1-\frac{2r_g}{r}}, \qquad B=\frac1N, \]

where \(r_g=GM/c^2\).

Differentiate \(N\):

\[ N'=\frac{r_g}{r^2N}. \]

Therefore,

\[ \frac{N'}B=\frac{r_g}{r^2}. \]

Substituting into Equation (40),

\[ \boxed{\mathcal F(r)=4\pi GM.} \tag{41} \]

This is constant at every enclosing sphere in the static vacuum exterior.

In particular,

\[ \boxed{\mathcal F(r_1)=\mathcal F(r_2).} \tag{42} \]

This is the Gaussian-surface relationship of Section 1: the flux is the same through every sphere outside the matter and the same at every time. In general relativity the flux is the same through every sphere by its vacuum field equation (assumption 5) and the same at every time by assumption 2; in this paper both are conservation of mass-energy itself, premise 1 (Section 3; Section 4, statements 5 and 6).

It is important to distinguish what has been shown:

  • We have demonstrated that Schwarzschild satisfies the equal-flux condition.
  • We have not demonstrated that equal flux alone determines the Schwarzschild geometry.
Derive the corresponding conservation identity

Equation (41) can be rewritten as

\[ \boxed{\frac{r^2N'}B=\frac{GM}{c^2}.} \tag{43} \]

This is one differential equation for the two unknown functions \(N\) and \(B\).

The Schwarzschild derivation supplies a second equation:

\[ \boxed{NB=1.} \tag{44} \]

Combining them,

\[ r^2NN'=r_g. \]

Therefore,

\[ \frac{d(N^2)}{dr}=\frac{2r_g}{r^2}. \]

Integrating with \(N(\infty)=1\),

\[ N^2=1-\frac{2r_g}{r}. \]

So the pair of equations reconstructs Schwarzschild exactly.

19. What conservation does and does not establish

We should distinguish three mathematical statements.

First: conservation of stress-energy.

Einstein's equations imply

\[ \boxed{\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0} \tag{45} \]

through the contracted Bianchi identity,

\[ \nabla_\mu G^{\mu\nu}=0. \]

This is a local conservation relationship. It does not uniquely determine the metric.

Second: conservation of the exterior gravitational charge.

For the static spherical vacuum solution, the appropriately normalized Komar mass is the same on every enclosing sphere. Equation (43) expresses this in our metric variables.

Label (this paper): the Komar mass is the complete count, and a body's entry in it is its reading times its clock rate; in general relativity it is fixed by the static vacuum field equations (assumptions 2 and 5), in this paper by conservation (Section 4, statement 5). Outside the horizon the two agree; inside, general relativity's count is read as an energy by no one (Section 9).

Third: the radial geometric field equation.

The reciprocal relation

\[ NB=1 \]

was obtained from

\[ R_{00}=R_{rr}=0, \]

or equivalently from the appropriate difference of mixed Einstein equations.

It is an independent geometric constraint within GR.

That distinction matters because the stress-energy conservation identity alone does not reproduce every component of Einstein's field equations.

20. The second equation, and where this paper gets it

We can formulate the exact mathematical target.

The Gaussian-flux relation is

\[ \frac{r^2N'}B=r_g. \]

The full Schwarzschild result additionally requires

\[ \frac{d}{dr}\ln(NB)=0. \]

In the Einstein-equation derivation, the corresponding general relation is

\[ \boxed{ \frac{d}{dr}\ln(NB) = \frac{4\pi GrB^2}{c^4}(\epsilon+p_r), } \tag{46} \]

where \(\epsilon\) is the local energy density and \(p_r\) is the radial pressure.

For vacuum,

\[ \epsilon=p_r=0, \]

so

\[ \frac{d}{dr}\ln(NB)=0. \]

This identifies the missing ingredient very precisely: a relationship between the radial geometry and the source's energy-density and stress components.

In this paper the second relation is supplied by the step from stationary observers to free fall. The frame that falls from rest far away passes the held frame at \(\gamma=1/N\), the speed that the same f dot dr would generate. It needs no force and keeps A's rulers, and special relativity between the two gives the held frame's ruler along the force at \(N\) of A's, so \(B=1/N\) (Section 4, statement 4). No equation of Einstein's is used.

Conclusion

The derivation is mathematically complete for the static, spherically symmetric, asymptotically flat vacuum exterior in Einstein gravity with \(\Lambda=0\). The extension of the static form inside gives general relativity's horizon at \(r_s=2GM/c^2\), one for every frame.

For this paper, the most consequential finding is that the exact Schwarzschild solution depends on two distinct radial relationships:

\[ \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \text{Gaussian gravitational flux:}\quad& \frac{r^2N'}B=\frac{GM}{c^2}\\[6pt] \text{Radial geometric constraint:}\quad& NB=1 \end{aligned} } \]

The first relationship is conservation of mass-energy through a Gaussian surface. The second, in this paper, is the ruler of a frame held at rest, which follows from setting the f dot dr in the field equal to the f dot dr needed to generate the motion (Section 4, statement 4). General relativity gets \(NB=1\) for one frame and all from its field equations under assumption 2, the static field, which is what makes the merge of every frame's values into one event horizon possible. The burden is on that premise.

The full derivation, redone with conservation, line by line

− red: taken away  ·  + green: replaces it, or is added beside it  ·  grey: unchanged

 

We derive the Schwarzschild geometry from the Einstein field equations, starting with spherical symmetry and a general metric—not with the Schwarzschild metric itself.

 

The purpose is to establish every mathematical step, especially the origin of

 

\[ \boxed{N(r)B(r)=1} \]

+

In the conservation derivation \(NB=1\) is the ruler of a frame held at rest. The f dot dr in the field is set equal to the f dot dr needed to generate the motion, the frame that falls keeps A's rulers, and special relativity between the two gives the held frame's ruler along the force (Section 4, statement 4). No equation of Einstein's is used.

 

and

 

\[ \boxed{r_s=\frac{2GM}{c^2}}. \]

+

The same radius in the conservation derivation, \(L=2G\mathcal M_{\rm enc}/c^2\): the place where the escape velocity is \(c\). It is the causal boundary, which is also the event horizon, of a frame at rest far away (premise 8).

 

We also distinguish the assumptions supplied by GR from the relationships that follow mathematically, so that the derivation can later be compared with the conservation of mass-energy.

 

1. Physical thought experiment

 

Imagine an isolated, nonrotating, electrically neutral spherical mass \(M\), surrounded by two concentric Gaussian surfaces at radii \(r_1\) and \(r_2\).

 

The two surfaces are imaginary measurement boundaries, not material shells.

 

We assume:

 
  1. Spherical symmetry: The geometry is unchanged under spatial rotations.
 
  1. Staticity: The exterior geometry is time-independent and invariant under time reversal.
+

In the conservation derivation this is not assumed. The count inside the surface does not change while nothing crosses it, so the pull through every sphere is the same at every time (premise 1; Section 4, statement 5). When the bodies inside move, the same sum holds at every moment (premise 6; Section 4, statement 8).

 
  1. Vacuum exterior: No matter or nongravitational field stress-energy is present outside the source.
 
  1. Asymptotic flatness: Far from the source, spacetime approaches Minkowski spacetime.
 
  1. Einstein gravity: The metric satisfies Einstein's field equations, with zero cosmological constant.
+

Not used in the conservation derivation. The clock comes from the three steps of f dot dr, the ruler from the step from stationary observers to free fall, and the pull from the count (Section 4, statements 1, 4 and 6).

 
  1. Areal radius: The coordinate \(r\) is defined so a sphere has area \(4\pi r^2\).
−

The derivation applies to the static exterior region. We will subsequently extend the resulting geometry through the horizon using regular coordinates. Label (this paper): that extension, parts 15 to 17, is the step this paper attacks. The regular coordinates carry the same static form inside, where nothing has tested it.

+

The derivation applies outside \(L\). The conservation derivation does not extend one account across \(L\) for every frame of reference. Premises 7 and 8 say what holds there (Section 3).

 

2. Construct the most general static spherical metric

 

Begin with four coordinates:

 

\[ x^\mu=(ct,r,\theta,\phi). \]

 

Spherical symmetry restricts the angular part to

 

\[ r^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2). \]

 

Staticity permits a time coordinate in which the metric has no time-space cross terms.

 

Therefore, in the static region,

 

\[ \boxed{ ds^2=-N(r)^2c^2dt^2+B(r)^2dr^2 +r^2d\theta^2+r^2\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2 } \tag{1} \]

 

where \(N(r)>0\) and \(B(r)>0\).

 

At infinity,

 

\[ \lim_{r\to\infty}N(r)=1,\qquad \lim_{r\to\infty}B(r)=1. \]

 

We have not yet specified the gravitational field or inserted any Schwarzschild factors.

 
Physical interpretation
 

For a stationary clock, \(dr=d\theta=d\phi=0\), so

 

\[ ds^2=-c^2d\tau^2=-N^2c^2dt^2. \]

 

Thus,

 

\[ \boxed{d\tau=N(r)\,dt.} \tag{2} \]

 

For a radial distance measured at constant \(t\),

 

\[ \boxed{d\ell=B(r)\,dr.} \tag{3} \]

 

These define our clock and radial ruler functions.

 

3. Introduce convenient metric functions

 

Write

 

\[ N(r)=e^{\nu(r)},\qquad B(r)=e^{\lambda(r)}. \]

 

Then

 

\[ ds^2=-e^{2\nu}c^2dt^2+e^{2\lambda}dr^2+r^2d\Omega^2. \tag{4} \]

 

For the curvature calculation, temporarily use \(x^0=ct\).

 

The metric components are

 

\[ g_{\mu\nu}= \begin{pmatrix} -e^{2\nu}&0&0&0\\ 0&e^{2\lambda}&0&0\\ 0&0&r^2&0\\ 0&0&0&r^2\sin^2\theta \end{pmatrix}. \tag{5} \]

 

Its inverse is

 

\[ g^{\mu\nu}= \begin{pmatrix} -e^{-2\nu}&0&0&0\\ 0&e^{-2\lambda}&0&0\\ 0&0&r^{-2}&0\\ 0&0&0&(r^2\sin^2\theta)^{-1} \end{pmatrix}. \tag{6} \]

 

The determinant is

 

\[ g=-e^{2(\nu+\lambda)}r^4\sin^2\theta, \]

 

so

 

\[ \sqrt{-g}=e^{\nu+\lambda}r^2\sin\theta. \tag{7} \]

 

The functions \(\nu\) and \(\lambda\) are still completely unknown.

 

4. Calculate the Christoffel symbols

 

The Levi-Civita connection is defined by

 

\[ \boxed{ \Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\nu} =\frac12g^{\alpha\beta} \left( \partial_\mu g_{\beta\nu} +\partial_\nu g_{\beta\mu} -\partial_\beta g_{\mu\nu} \right). } \tag{8} \]

 

Because the metric is static, all time derivatives vanish. Label (this paper): assumption 2; outside the horizon it follows from conservation, the count inside the surface being constant (Section 4, statements 5 and 6); what this paper attacks is carrying it inside the horizon (parts 15 to 17).

+

In the conservation derivation the time derivatives vanish around a round body at rest because its count is constant (premise 1), not by assumption.

 

The relevant radial derivatives are

 

\[ \begin{aligned} \partial_r g_{00}&=-2\nu'e^{2\nu},\\ \partial_r g_{rr}&=2\lambda'e^{2\lambda},\\ \partial_r g_{\theta\theta}&=2r,\\ \partial_r g_{\phi\phi}&=2r\sin^2\theta. \end{aligned} \]

 

The angular derivatives include

 

\[ \partial_\theta g_{\phi\phi} =2r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta. \]

 

A prime denotes differentiation with respect to \(r\).

 
Example: calculate \(\Gamma^r_{00}\)
 

By Equation (8),

 

\[ \Gamma^r_{00} =-\frac12g^{rr}\partial_rg_{00}. \]

 

Substitute:

 

\[ =-\frac12e^{-2\lambda}(-2\nu'e^{2\nu}). \]

 

Therefore,

 

\[ \boxed{\Gamma^r_{00}=\nu'e^{2(\nu-\lambda)}.} \]

 
Complete list of nonzero independent Christoffel symbols
 

\[ \begin{aligned} \Gamma^0_{0r}&=\nu',\\ \Gamma^r_{00}&=\nu'e^{2(\nu-\lambda)},\\ \Gamma^r_{rr}&=\lambda',\\ \Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}&=-re^{-2\lambda},\\ \Gamma^r_{\phi\phi}&=-re^{-2\lambda}\sin^2\theta,\\ \Gamma^\theta_{r\theta}&=\frac1r,\\ \Gamma^\phi_{r\phi}&=\frac1r,\\ \Gamma^\theta_{\phi\phi}&=-\sin\theta\cos\theta,\\ \Gamma^\phi_{\theta\phi}&=\cot\theta. \end{aligned} \tag{9} \]

 

The connection is symmetric in its two lower indices, so entries related by exchanging those indices are also present.

 

This completes the connection calculation.

 

5. Calculate the Ricci tensor

 

We adopt the curvature convention

 

\[ R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu\Gamma^\rho_{\nu\sigma} -\partial_\nu\Gamma^\rho_{\mu\sigma} +\Gamma^\rho_{\mu\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha_{\nu\sigma} -\Gamma^\rho_{\nu\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\sigma}. \]

 

Contracting gives

 

\[ R_{\mu\nu}=R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}. \]

 

Equivalently,

 

\[ \boxed{ R_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\alpha\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\nu} -\partial_\nu\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\alpha} +\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\nu}\Gamma^\beta_{\alpha\beta} -\Gamma^\beta_{\mu\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha_{\nu\beta}. } \tag{10} \]

 

We calculate each independent component.

 
5.1 Time-time component
 

The first term is

 

\[ \partial_r\Gamma^r_{00} =e^{2(\nu-\lambda)} \left[\nu''+2\nu'(\nu'-\lambda')\right]. \]

 

The second term vanishes because the metric is time-independent.

 

For the third term, use

 

\[ \Gamma^\beta_{r\beta} =\nu'+\lambda'+\frac2r. \]

 

Thus,

 

\[ \Gamma^r_{00}\Gamma^\beta_{r\beta} =e^{2(\nu-\lambda)}\nu' \left(\nu'+\lambda'+\frac2r\right). \]

 

The fourth term is

 

\[ -2e^{2(\nu-\lambda)}\nu'^2. \]

 

Combining the terms,

 

\[ \boxed{ R_{00}=e^{2(\nu-\lambda)} \left[ \nu''+\nu'^2-\nu'\lambda'+\frac{2\nu'}r \right]. } \tag{11} \]

 
5.2 Radial-radial component
 

The four terms in Equation (10) are

 

\[ \begin{aligned} \partial_\alpha\Gamma^\alpha_{rr}&=\lambda'',\\ -\partial_r\Gamma^\alpha_{r\alpha} &=-\nu''-\lambda''+\frac2{r^2},\\ \Gamma^\alpha_{rr}\Gamma^\beta_{\alpha\beta} &=\lambda'\left(\nu'+\lambda'+\frac2r\right),\\ -\Gamma^\beta_{r\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha_{r\beta} &=-\nu'^2-\lambda'^2-\frac2{r^2}. \end{aligned} \]

 

Combining,

 

\[ \boxed{ R_{rr} =-\nu''-\nu'^2+\nu'\lambda'+\frac{2\lambda'}r. } \tag{12} \]

 
5.3 Angular components
 

Substituting the angular Christoffel symbols gives

 

\[ \boxed{ R_{\theta\theta} =1-e^{-2\lambda} \left(1+r\nu'-r\lambda'\right). } \tag{13} \]

 

Spherical symmetry requires

 

\[ \boxed{ R_{\phi\phi}=\sin^2\theta\,R_{\theta\theta}. } \tag{14} \]

 

All off-diagonal Ricci components vanish.

 

We now have every independent component of the Ricci tensor.

 

6. Apply the vacuum Einstein equations

 

Einstein's field equations, with zero cosmological constant, are

 

\[ R_{\mu\nu}-\frac12Rg_{\mu\nu} =\frac{8\pi G}{c^4}T_{\mu\nu}. \tag{15} \]

 

In vacuum,

 

\[ T_{\mu\nu}=0. \]

 

Hence,

 

\[ R_{\mu\nu}-\frac12Rg_{\mu\nu}=0. \]

 

Contract with \(g^{\mu\nu}\):

 

\[ R-\frac12(4)R=0, \]

 

giving

 

\[ -R=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad R=0. \]

 

Therefore,

 

\[ \boxed{R_{\mu\nu}=0.} \tag{16} \]

 

This reduction is exact for the stated vacuum equations.

 

7. Derive the ruler-clock relationship

 

Set Equations (11) and (12) equal to zero:

 

\[ \nu''+\nu'^2-\nu'\lambda'+\frac{2\nu'}r=0, \tag{17} \]

 

\[ -\nu''-\nu'^2+\nu'\lambda'+\frac{2\lambda'}r=0. \tag{18} \]

 

Add them.

 

The second derivatives cancel:

 

\[ \nu''-\nu''=0. \]

 

The quadratic terms cancel:

 

\[ \nu'^2-\nu'^2=0. \]

 

The mixed terms cancel:

 

\[ -\nu'\lambda'+\nu'\lambda'=0. \]

 

We are left with

 

\[ \frac{2\nu'}r+\frac{2\lambda'}r=0. \]

 

For \(r>0\),

 

\[ \nu'+\lambda'=0. \]

 

Integrate:

 

\[ \nu+\lambda=C. \]

 

Exponentiate:

 

\[ e^\nu e^\lambda=e^C. \]

 

Since \(N=e^\nu\) and \(B=e^\lambda\),

 

\[ NB=e^C. \]

 

Asymptotic flatness gives \(N(\infty)=B(\infty)=1\), hence \(e^C=1\).

 

Therefore,

 

\[ \boxed{NB=1.} \tag{19} \]

 

This is the complete derivation of the reciprocal clock-ruler relationship, from the field equations under assumption 2. In this paper the same relation comes from setting the f dot dr in the field equal to the f dot dr needed to generate the motion, with no equation of Einstein's (Section 4, statement 4).

+

In the conservation derivation: the frame that falls from rest far away passes the held frame at \(\gamma=1/N\), the speed that the same f dot dr would generate. It needs no force, so it keeps A's clock and rulers (premise 4). Special relativity between the two then gives the held frame's ruler along the force at \(N\) of A's and leaves its sideways rulers alone. So \(B=1/N\) (Section 4, statement 4).

−

The crucial mathematical operation was adding the two independent vacuum Ricci equations.

+

In the conservation derivation the crucial step is setting the f dot dr in the field equal to the f dot dr needed to generate the motion. No two field equations are added.

 

Notice that no Schwarzschild radius was assumed.

 

8. Solve the remaining radial equation

 

Now apply \(R_{\theta\theta}=0\).

 

From Equation (13),

 

\[ 1-e^{-2\lambda} (1+r\nu'-r\lambda')=0. \]

 

Since \(\lambda=-\nu\),

 

\[ \lambda'=-\nu'. \]

 

Thus,

 

\[ 1-e^{-2\lambda}(1+2r\nu')=0. \tag{20} \]

 

Define

 

\[ f(r)=e^{2\nu}=N^2=e^{-2\lambda}=B^{-2}. \]

 

Its derivative is

 

\[ f'=2\nu'e^{2\nu}=2\nu'f. \]

 

Consequently,

 

\[ 2\nu'=\frac{f'}f. \]

 

Substitute into Equation (20):

 

\[ 1-f\left(1+\frac{rf'}f\right)=0. \]

 

Expand:

 

\[ 1-f-rf'=0. \]

 

Rearrange:

 

\[ rf'+f=1. \]

 

Recognize the product derivative:

 

\[ \boxed{\frac{d}{dr}(rf)=1.} \tag{21} \]

 

Integrate:

 

\[ rf=r+C_1. \]

 

Therefore,

 

\[ \boxed{f(r)=1+\frac{C_1}{r}.} \tag{22} \]

 

This is the general asymptotically flat static spherical vacuum solution in the chosen areal-radius coordinates, up to identifying the integration constant.

 

9. Determine the integration constant from Newtonian gravity

 

We must identify \(C_1\) using the limit far from the mass. This is where the mass \(M\) enters.

+

\(M\) is \(\mathcal M_{\rm enc}\), the complete count inside the surface: every kind of energy once, with the mass equivalent of potential energy (Section 2; Section 4, statement 5). It does not change, by conservation. Newton's law far away fixes \(G\) in both derivations. In the conservation derivation the counted pull is Newton's law at every distance, exactly: \(N\,g_{\rm hold}=G\mathcal M_{\rm enc}/r^2\) (Section 4, statement 6).

 

For a slowly moving test particle, the radial geodesic equation is

 

\[ \frac{d^2r}{d\tau^2} +\Gamma^r_{00}\left(\frac{dx^0}{d\tau}\right)^2 +\cdots=0. \]

 

Far from the mass, in the slow-motion limit,

 

\[ \frac{dx^0}{d\tau}\approx c,\qquad \frac{d^2r}{d\tau^2}\approx\frac{d^2r}{dt^2}. \]

 

The leading radial acceleration is therefore

 

\[ \frac{d^2r}{dt^2}\approx-c^2\Gamma^r_{00}. \]

 

Using Equation (9),

 

\[ \Gamma^r_{00}=\nu'e^{2(\nu-\lambda)}. \]

 

Far from the mass, \(e^{2(\nu-\lambda)}\approx1\), giving

 

\[ \frac{d^2r}{dt^2}\approx-c^2\nu'. \tag{23} \]

 

The Newtonian potential \(\Phi\) satisfies

 

\[ \frac{d^2r}{dt^2}=-\Phi'. \]

 

Comparing,

 

\[ c^2\nu'\approx\Phi'. \]

 

Integrating with both quantities vanishing at infinity,

 

\[ \nu\approx\frac{\Phi}{c^2}. \]

 

Since

 

\[ N^2=e^{2\nu}\approx1+2\nu, \]

 

we obtain

 

\[ \boxed{ f(r)=N^2(r)\approx1+\frac{2\Phi(r)}{c^2}. } \tag{24} \]

 

For a spherical mass,

 

\[ \Phi(r)=-\frac{GM}{r}. \]

 

Thus,

 

\[ f(r)\approx1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}. \]

 

But our exact solution was

 

\[ f(r)=1+\frac{C_1}{r}. \]

 

Matching the coefficient far from the mass gives

 

\[ \boxed{C_1=-\frac{2GM}{c^2}.} \tag{25} \]

 

Label (this paper): the solved equation is exact outside the horizon, where conservation gives the same constant (Section 4, statement 6); inside the horizon nothing has tested the form.

 

10. Obtain the complete Schwarzschild metric

 

Substitute Equation (25) into Equation (22):

 

\[ f(r)=1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}. \]

 

Since \(N^2=f\) and \(B^2=1/f\),

 

\[ \boxed{ N(r)=\sqrt{1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}} } \tag{26} \]

 

and

 

\[ \boxed{ B(r)=\frac1{\sqrt{1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}}}. } \tag{27} \]

 

Therefore,

 

\[ \boxed{ ds^2= -\left(1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}\right)c^2dt^2 +\left(1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}\right)^{-1}dr^2 +r^2d\Omega^2. } \tag{28} \]

 

This is the Schwarzschild metric in standard areal-radius coordinates.

+

The same clocks and rulers outside \(L\) in the conservation derivation (Section 4, statement 6). In the terms of the frames that fall from rest far away they read \(ds^2=-c^2dT^2+(dr+v\,dT)^2+r^2d\Omega^2\) with \(v=c\sqrt{L/r}\): flat space and A's time for the frames that need no force. A frame held at rest reads the body at \(\mathcal M_{\rm enc}/N\), heavier than the frame far away does, by count and by weighing (Section 4, statement 2).

 

Every function in this metric has now been determined.

 

11. Verify the solution by substitution

 

A derivation is not complete until we substitute the solution into the original equations.

 

Let

 

\[ a=\frac{2GM}{c^2},\qquad f=1-\frac ar. \]

 

Then

 

\[ f'=\frac a{r^2},\qquad f''=-\frac{2a}{r^3}. \]

 

Our functions satisfy

 

\[ \nu=\frac12\ln f,\qquad \lambda=-\frac12\ln f. \]

 

Therefore,

 

\[ \nu'=\frac{f'}{2f},\qquad \lambda'=-\frac{f'}{2f}. \]

 
Check \(R_{\theta\theta}=0\)
 

Equation (13) becomes

 

\[ R_{\theta\theta}=1-f-rf'. \]

 

Substitute:

 

\[ R_{\theta\theta} =1-\left(1-\frac ar\right)-r\frac a{r^2}. \]

 

Thus,

 

\[ \boxed{R_{\theta\theta}=0.} \]

 

The \(\phi\phi\) component also vanishes.

 
Check \(R_{00}=0\)
 

Using \(\lambda'=-\nu'\), the bracket in Equation (11) becomes

 

\[ \nu''+2\nu'^2+\frac{2\nu'}r. \]

 

Because

 

\[ \nu''+2\nu'^2=\frac{f''}{2f}, \]

 

the bracket equals

 

\[ \frac{f''}{2f}+\frac{f'}{fr}. \]

 

Substituting the derivatives,

 

\[ \frac1f\left(-\frac a{r^3}+\frac a{r^3}\right)=0. \]

 

Hence,

 

\[ \boxed{R_{00}=0.} \]

 
Check \(R_{rr}=0\)
 

Equation (12) reduces to the negative of the same bracket:

 

\[ R_{rr}=-\frac{f''}{2f}-\frac{f'}{fr}=0. \]

 

Therefore,

 

\[ \boxed{R_{\mu\nu}=0} \]

 

for every component in the Schwarzschild vacuum region.

 

The solution satisfies the complete vacuum field equations.

 

12. Derive gravitational redshift from the metric

 

The exact redshift follows from the metric. In general relativity it rests on staticity, assumption 2, which supplies the Killing vector; in this paper the same relation is the count, \(e=\gamma f\), from conservation and the clock step (Section 4, statements 1 and 3).

 

Because the metric is stationary, it has a time-translation Killing vector \(\xi^\mu\). With \(x^0=ct\) and \(\xi=\partial_{ct}\), the conserved quantity below is the photon's energy divided by \(c\); with \(\xi=\partial_t\) it is the energy itself, and every ratio below is the same either way.

+

In the conservation derivation the same conserved quantity is the count: the energy that a frame at rest reads, times that frame's clock rate, \(N\,E_{\rm local}\) for light and \(\gamma N\,m_0c^2\) for a body (premise 3; Section 4, statements 1 and 3). For a body it comes from the work of the pull on its mass as it is at that moment, \(dm/m=\mathbf g\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell/c^2\), which the clock rate cancels. No Killing vector is used.

 

For a freely propagating photon with four-momentum \(p^\mu\), the quantity

 

\[ \mathcal E=-p_\mu\xi^\mu \]

 

is conserved along its geodesic.

 

A stationary observer at radius \(r\) has four-velocity proportional to \(\xi^\mu\). Its normalization gives a locally measured photon energy

 

\[ \boxed{E_{\rm local}(r)=\frac{\mathcal E}{N(r)}.} \tag{29} \]

 

Therefore, for emission at \(r_1\) and reception at \(r_2\),

 

\[ \frac{E_2}{E_1} =\frac{N(r_1)}{N(r_2)}. \]

 

Substituting Equation (26),

 

\[ \boxed{ \frac{E_2}{E_1} = \sqrt{ \frac{1-2GM/(r_1c^2)} {1-2GM/(r_2c^2)} }. } \tag{30} \]

 

For a receiver at infinity,

 

\[ \boxed{ E_\infty =E_{\rm emitted} \sqrt{1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}}. } \tag{31} \]

 

This is the exact Schwarzschild gravitational-redshift relationship for stationary observers. General relativity allows none inside the horizon. This paper's premises 7 and 8 say what holds across it (Section 3).

+

The same redshift in the conservation derivation, \(1+z=1/N\), from the unit of energy of the held frame and Planck's relation (Section 4, statement 1).

 
Check far from the mass
 

Let \(x=GM/(rc^2)\). For \(x\ll1\),

 

\[ \sqrt{1-2x} =1-x-\frac{x^2}{2}-\frac{x^3}{2}+O(x^4). \]

 

Thus,

 

\[ N(r)\approx1-\frac{GM}{rc^2} \]

 

at first order, matching the familiar Newtonian-potential redshift.

 

13. Derive the Schwarzschild radius

 

The metric function is

 

\[ f(r)=1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}. \]

 

The stationary Killing vector has squared norm

 

\[ \xi^\mu\xi_\mu=-f(r) \]

 

when the time coordinate is \(ct\).

 

Its norm becomes zero when

 

\[ 1-\frac{2GM}{rc^2}=0. \]

 

Solving,

 

\[ \boxed{r_s=\frac{2GM}{c^2}.} \tag{32} \]

−

For positive \(M\), the static exterior region is \(r>r_s\).

+

At \(r=L\) the clock rate of a frame held at rest, as a frame far away reads it, is zero, and the escape velocity is \(c\): the causal boundary, which is also the event horizon, of the frame far away (premise 8). A zero is not a singularity.

−

But we must be careful: finding \(f=0\) identifies a candidate Killing horizon. To establish that this is a regular black-hole horizon rather than a physical singularity, we need to examine the geometry in coordinates that remain regular there.

+

What \(f=0\) marks is the causal boundary of a frame at rest far away. The causal boundary depends on the frame of reference. At \(L\) a frame at rest and a frame that falls in would need the speed \(c\) to escape, and a frame on its way out with the count \(e\le1\) needs \(c\,(1-e^2)/(1+e^2)\) (premise 8). The conservation derivation does not go on to one geometry for every frame.

 

14. Check whether the horizon is a curvature singularity

 

For the Schwarzschild metric, the Ricci scalar vanishes:

 

\[ R=0. \]

 

The Ricci tensor also vanishes in vacuum:

 

\[ R_{\mu\nu}=0. \]

 

But the full Riemann tensor does not vanish.

 

The Kretschmann scalar is

 

\[ K=R_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta} R^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}. \]

 

Direct contraction gives

 

\[ \boxed{ K=\frac{48G^2M^2}{c^4r^6}. } \tag{33} \]

 

At the Schwarzschild radius,

 

\[ K(r_s)=\frac{12}{r_s^4}, \]

 

which is finite for \(M>0\).

 

At \(r=0\),

 

\[ K\longrightarrow\infty. \]

 

Therefore, \(r=r_s\) is not a curvature singularity. The singularity in the standard Schwarzschild coordinate components is a coordinate singularity.

−

15. Extend the solution through the horizon

−

Define the tortoise coordinate \(r_*\) by

−

\[ \frac{dr_*}{dr}=\frac1{f(r)}. \]

−

Integrating in the exterior,

−

\[ \boxed{ r_*=r+r_s\ln\left|\frac r{r_s}-1\right|. } \tag{34} \]

−

Introduce the ingoing null coordinate

−

\[ v=t+\frac{r_*}{c}. \]

−

Thus,

−

\[ dt=dv-\frac{dr}{cf}. \]

−

Substitute into the Schwarzschild metric:

−

\[ ds^2=-fc^2\left(dv-\frac{dr}{cf}\right)^2 +\frac{dr^2}{f}+r^2d\Omega^2. \]

−

Expand:

−

\[ ds^2=-fc^2dv^2+2c\,dv\,dr -\frac{dr^2}{f}+\frac{dr^2}{f}+r^2d\Omega^2. \]

−

The divergent radial terms cancel.

−

We obtain

−

\[ \boxed{ ds^2=-\left(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\right)c^2dv^2 +2c\,dv\,dr+r^2d\Omega^2. } \tag{35} \]

−

This is the ingoing Eddington–Finkelstein metric.

−

It remains regular at \(r=r_s\).

−

We have now extended the solution across the Schwarzschild coordinate singularity. Label (this paper): the extension assumes that the static form of assumption 2 holds inside, and it gives one event horizon for every frame. That is the premise under attack in this paper: the merge of the frames' different values into one event horizon. As general relativity states the step: one metric is chosen for all observers, and the same solution with the same mass is continued across \(r_s\).

+

15. At \(L\): two frames, two real readings

The conservation derivation does not extend one account across \(L\). General relativity's step here is to take one metric for all observers and to continue the same solution, with the same mass, across \(L\). Nothing outside \(L\) requires that step. It is the step that merges the frames' different values into one event horizon, and it is the error that this paper names (Section 18). In its place stands premise 7: when two frames of reference observe different values, both are real from the frame of reference that they are observed from. A reading of a frame Q is converted into a frame P with the factor between their clock rates, \(s_{PQ}^{\,2}=(1-L/r_Q)/(1-L/r_P)\). When P and Q lie on opposite sides of \(L\) the square is negative, and the inferred measurement has two solutions, \(s_{PQ}=\pm\,i\sqrt{(L/r_Q-1)/(1-L/r_P)}\) (Section 3, premise 7).

−

16. Determine the behavior of outgoing light

−

For radial light,

−

\[ ds^2=0,\qquad d\Omega=0. \]

−

Equation (35) gives

−

\[ 0=-fc^2dv^2+2c\,dv\,dr. \]

−

For the outgoing branch with \(dv\ne0\),

−

\[ \boxed{ \frac{dr}{dv}=\frac c2 \left(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\right). } \tag{36} \]

−

Examine three regions.

−
RegionOutgoing radial null trajectory
−
\(r>r_s\)\(dr/dv>0\)
−
\(r=r_s\)\(dr/dv=0\)
−
\(0<r<r_s\)\(dr/dv<0\)
−

The second radial null family has \(dv=0\) and is ingoing.

−

More generally, for a future-directed causal trajectory in the black-hole interior, Equation (35) implies

−

\[ -fc^2dv^2+2c\,dv\,dr+r^2d\Omega^2\le0. \]

−

For \(0<r<r_s\), \(f<0\). With the future orientation chosen so \(dv>0\),

−

\[ 2c\,dv\,dr \le fc^2dv^2-r^2d\Omega^2<0. \]

−

Therefore,

−

\[ \boxed{dr<0} \]

−

along every nontrivial future-directed causal trajectory in the interior, with the horizon-generator case treated at the boundary.

−

This is general relativity's reading of the inside: with the static form carried inside and the future orientation chosen there (\(dv>0\)), no causal trajectory moves to larger \(r\). It is a consequence of assumption 2 and of that choice, not a test of either. This paper's premise 8 says the opposite: objects can, and do, move beyond their event horizon (Section 3).

+

16. Objects move beyond their event horizon

A body in free motion keeps its count, \(e=\gamma f\). On its own clock, with \(r\) the radius of the circles around the source, \((dr/d\tau)^2=c^2(e^2-|1-L/r|)\), one law on both sides of \(L\). At \(L\) its speed on its own clock is \(c\,e\), which is not zero, and the time on its own clock to reach \(L\) is finite. So it moves beyond \(L\), and the same law holds in both directions (Section 3, premise 8). Inside \(L\) the pull points outward: a body that falls in turns back at \(L/(1+e^2)\) and comes out (Section 14, Part 7). An observer at rest far away cannot and does not observe the passage: on that observer's clock its time has no finite value. Light sent outward at \(L\), read as \(E\) by its source, reaches an observer far away with the count \(2e\,E\) when the source is on its way out, and with zero when the source is at rest or falls in.

−

17. Establish the global event horizon

−

A black-hole event horizon is defined globally as the boundary of the region from which future-directed light signals can reach future null infinity.

−

The Eddington–Finkelstein calculation establishes the local causal behavior. We can additionally use Kruskal–Szekeres coordinates to examine the global extension.

−

Define the outgoing null coordinate

−

\[ u=t-\frac{r_*}{c}. \]

−

In the exterior region, introduce

−

\[ U=-e^{-cu/(2r_s)},\qquad V=e^{cv/(2r_s)}. \]

−

Then

−

\[ UV=-\left(\frac r{r_s}-1\right)e^{r/r_s}. \tag{37} \]

−

The metric becomes

−

\[ \boxed{ ds^2= -\frac{4r_s^3}{r}e^{-r/r_s}\,dU\,dV +r^2d\Omega^2. } \tag{38} \]

−

The coefficient is finite and nonzero at \(r=r_s\).

−

These coordinates extend smoothly across the horizon. In the maximally extended Schwarzschild spacetime, the future black-hole region is separated from the exterior by a null horizon, and future-directed causal trajectories inside it cannot reach the exterior's future null infinity.

−

The precise global interpretation requires specifying the spacetime extension and its time orientation. For a physically formed black hole, the relevant extension is the collapse geometry rather than the entire eternal Schwarzschild solution.

−

This is general relativity's identification of the horizon, resting on assumption 2 carried inside: one event horizon for every frame. Label: PREMISE of general relativity.

+

17. The causal boundary is read by a frame of reference

A frame's event horizon is where that frame would need the speed of light to escape, and it depends on how the frame moves. The frame of reference changes during motion. So things can exist, or no longer exist, in the frame of reference of an observer because a particle has moved and now has a new frame of reference, and not because anything passed through the causal boundary of a frame (Section 3, premise 8). One event horizon for every frame, crossed one way only, is the premise of general relativity that the conservation derivation does not take. Nothing has tested it. The observation that decides: anything, light or matter, arriving outside from inside an event horizon (Section 18).

 

18. Return to our original Gaussian surfaces

 

Now we can connect the result to the conservation-law investigation.

 

For the static spherical metric,

 

\[ ds^2=-N^2c^2dt^2+B^2dr^2+r^2d\Omega^2, \]

 

the proper acceleration needed to hold a test mass at a fixed radius is

 

\[ g_{\rm hold}=\frac{c^2N'}{NB}. \tag{39} \]

 

Its locally measured supporting force is \(F_{\rm local}=mg_{\rm hold}\).

 

The redshifted acceleration is

 

\[ Ng_{\rm hold}=\frac{c^2N'}B. \]

 

Define the redshifted gravitational flux through a sphere:

 

\[ \mathcal F(r)=4\pi r^2\frac{c^2N'}B. \tag{40} \]

 

For Schwarzschild,

 

\[ N=\sqrt{1-\frac{2r_g}{r}}, \qquad B=\frac1N, \]

 

where \(r_g=GM/c^2\).

 

Differentiate \(N\):

 

\[ N'=\frac{r_g}{r^2N}. \]

 

Therefore,

 

\[ \frac{N'}B=\frac{r_g}{r^2}. \]

 

Substituting into Equation (40),

 

\[ \boxed{\mathcal F(r)=4\pi GM.} \tag{41} \]

+

Premise 1: the pull counted through every sphere outside the matter is \(4\pi G\mathcal M_{\rm enc}\), the same on every sphere and the same at every time (Section 4, statements 5 and 6).

−

This is constant at every enclosing sphere in the static vacuum exterior.

+

This is constant on every enclosing sphere outside the matter, and constant in time, by conservation: it is premise 1, not a consequence of a static premise.

 

In particular,

 

\[ \boxed{\mathcal F(r_1)=\mathcal F(r_2).} \tag{42} \]

 

This is the Gaussian-surface relationship of Section 1: the flux is the same through every sphere outside the matter and the same at every time. In general relativity the flux is the same through every sphere by its vacuum field equation (assumption 5) and the same at every time by assumption 2; in this paper both are conservation of mass-energy itself, premise 1 (Section 3; Section 4, statements 5 and 6).

 

It is important to distinguish what has been shown:

 
  • We have demonstrated that Schwarzschild satisfies the equal-flux condition.
 
  • We have not demonstrated that equal flux alone determines the Schwarzschild geometry.
+
  • The second relation comes from f dot dr: the ruler of the frame held at rest (Section 4, statement 4). With the clock step it closes the conservation derivation without an equation of Einstein's.
 
Derive the corresponding conservation identity
 

Equation (41) can be rewritten as

 

\[ \boxed{\frac{r^2N'}B=\frac{GM}{c^2}.} \tag{43} \]

 

This is one differential equation for the two unknown functions \(N\) and \(B\).

−

The Schwarzschild derivation supplies a second equation:

+

The step from stationary observers to free fall supplies the second equation:

 

\[ \boxed{NB=1.} \tag{44} \]

 

Combining them,

 

\[ r^2NN'=r_g. \]

 

Therefore,

 

\[ \frac{d(N^2)}{dr}=\frac{2r_g}{r^2}. \]

 

Integrating with \(N(\infty)=1\),

 

\[ N^2=1-\frac{2r_g}{r}. \]

 

So the pair of equations reconstructs Schwarzschild exactly.

 

19. What conservation does and does not establish

 

We should distinguish three mathematical statements.

 

First: conservation of stress-energy.

 

Einstein's equations imply

 

\[ \boxed{\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0} \tag{45} \]

 

through the contracted Bianchi identity,

 

\[ \nabla_\mu G^{\mu\nu}=0. \]

 

This is a local conservation relationship. It does not uniquely determine the metric.

 

Second: conservation of the exterior gravitational charge.

 

For the static spherical vacuum solution, the appropriately normalized Komar mass is the same on every enclosing sphere. Equation (43) expresses this in our metric variables.

 

Label (this paper): the Komar mass is the complete count, and a body's entry in it is its reading times its clock rate; in general relativity it is fixed by the static vacuum field equations (assumptions 2 and 5), in this paper by conservation (Section 4, statement 5). Outside the horizon the two agree; inside, general relativity's count is read as an energy by no one (Section 9).

 

Third: the radial geometric field equation.

 

The reciprocal relation

 

\[ NB=1 \]

 

was obtained from

 

\[ R_{00}=R_{rr}=0, \]

 

or equivalently from the appropriate difference of mixed Einstein equations.

−

It is an independent geometric constraint within GR.

+

In the conservation derivation it is the ruler of the frame held at rest, from f dot dr (Section 4, statement 4).

 

That distinction matters because the stress-energy conservation identity alone does not reproduce every component of Einstein's field equations.

 

20. The second equation, and where this paper gets it

 

We can formulate the exact mathematical target.

 

The Gaussian-flux relation is

 

\[ \frac{r^2N'}B=r_g. \]

 

The full Schwarzschild result additionally requires

 

\[ \frac{d}{dr}\ln(NB)=0. \]

 

In the Einstein-equation derivation, the corresponding general relation is

 

\[ \boxed{ \frac{d}{dr}\ln(NB) = \frac{4\pi GrB^2}{c^4}(\epsilon+p_r), } \tag{46} \]

 

where \(\epsilon\) is the local energy density and \(p_r\) is the radial pressure.

 

For vacuum,

 

\[ \epsilon=p_r=0, \]

 

so

 

\[ \frac{d}{dr}\ln(NB)=0. \]

 

This identifies the missing ingredient very precisely: a relationship between the radial geometry and the source's energy-density and stress components.

 

In this paper the second relation is supplied by the step from stationary observers to free fall. The frame that falls from rest far away passes the held frame at \(\gamma=1/N\), the speed that the same f dot dr would generate. It needs no force and keeps A's rulers, and special relativity between the two gives the held frame's ruler along the force at \(N\) of A's, so \(B=1/N\) (Section 4, statement 4). No equation of Einstein's is used.

Conclusion

−

The derivation is mathematically complete for the static, spherically symmetric, asymptotically flat vacuum exterior in Einstein gravity with \(\Lambda=0\). The extension of the static form inside gives general relativity's horizon at \(r_s=2GM/c^2\), one for every frame.

+

The derivation is complete outside \(L\), where the conservation laws and the premises give the same clocks and rulers without an equation of Einstein's. At \(L\) and beyond it the conservation derivation does not continue one account for every frame: premises 7 and 8 hold there.

 

For this paper, the most consequential finding is that the exact Schwarzschild solution depends on two distinct radial relationships:

−

\[ \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \text{Gaussian gravitational flux:}\quad& \frac{r^2N'}B=\frac{GM}{c^2}\\[6pt] \text{Radial geometric constraint:}\quad& NB=1 \end{aligned} } \]

+

\[ \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \text{The pull through a sphere:}\quad& \frac{r^2N'}B=\frac{G\mathcal M_{\rm enc}}{c^2}\\[6pt] \text{The ruler of the held frame:}\quad& NB=1\quad\text{(from f dot dr, Section 4, statement 4)} \end{aligned} } \]

 

The first relationship is conservation of mass-energy through a Gaussian surface. The second, in this paper, is the ruler of a frame held at rest, which follows from setting the f dot dr in the field equal to the f dot dr needed to generate the motion (Section 4, statement 4). General relativity gets \(NB=1\) for one frame and all from its field equations under assumption 2, the static field, which is what makes the merge of every frame's values into one event horizon possible. The burden is on that premise.

The Curvature of Space Is the Curvature of the Wave Function's Rate of Oscillation

Instead of treating spacetime curvature as an external rule handed down by standard field equations or the Schwarzschild solution, this section reconstructs gravitational pull, clock rates, redshifts, and curvature from standing matter waves, local rulers, and basic conservation and flux principles outside a still, round body—and shows that spreading a particle's rest energy as a wave avoids a central point-mass pull blow-up.
For a child

Imagine a particle isn't a tiny hard dot—it's more like a steady wave spread out across space, ticking at a certain rhythm. Where gravity is stronger, that ticking rhythm changes from place to place, and how much that rhythm curves tells you how space and time are curved. If you spread the wave out instead of squeezing everything into one single dot, the pull right at the center drops to zero instead of shooting up to infinity, and you can figure out how clocks, light, and falling things behave without using the standard black-hole formulas.

For a high school physics teacher

This section derives gravitational pull, clock rates, redshift, overlap energies, and spacetime curvature outside a still, round body without assuming general relativity's field equations, action, or Schwarzschild metric as inputs:

  • Wave hypothesis and spatial energy density: A particle is modeled as a standing wave in spacetime, with its rest energy distributed according to the quantum probability density \(dP=\vert\psi\vert^2\,dV\) over local ruler volume elements (totaling 1), while external gravitational pull responds to the complete enclosed energy count.
  • Chain from pull to curvature and integration: From flux and work/energy rules outside a round body, you get the inward pull in both far and local units, the clock rate, and gravitational redshift; taking derivatives of the clock rate (and standing-wave oscillation rate/wavelength) yields the curvature components without borrowing from Schwarzschild, and integrating along a radius rebuilds clock comparisons, light travel times, and radial free fall.
  • Two-particle overlap and no central singularity: For a probe or two spread-out waves, pair-wise overlap energy and flux rules give time-involving curvature parts, while spreading a wave avoids the \(1/d^2\) point-mass divergence at the center because outer shells cancel symmetrically and the enclosed pull shrinks to zero as \(d\to0\).
For a theoretical physicist
The curvature of space is the curvature, from place to place, of the wave function's rate of oscillation. We can calculate the curvature of space, and do GR calculations, by just integrating the curvature of M3,1 between two points. (M3,1 is space and time together: three directions of space and one of time.)
This section shows both for the outside of a still, round body, outside its event horizon. The rate of oscillation is compared across identical standing waves held at rest at different places, counted on one far clock, against the distance along the radius on the local rulers. Its second derivative, divided by the rate, is the curvature in the plane of time and the radius, and outside a round body it fixes the other three parts of the curvature as well.
The pull, the clock rate and the redshift follow in one chain from the premises of this paper and one hypothesis about matter. The curvature then follows from the clock rate by two derivatives: it no longer has to be supplied, and nothing is taken from the Schwarzschild solution. Integrated from A to B along a radius, with the clock rate, the radius and their slopes at A, the curvature gives the clock rate and the radii at B, with no approximation. The clock rates at the two ends give the comparison of clocks. The profile rebuilt along the way gives the travel time of light along the radius, light moving at c on each frame's own clock and ruler, and the fall of a body along the radius, with H2, H3 for a free body and the body's start. For two given particles held in their shapes, giving each pair of pieces the energy the two would have alone, to first order, and counting it once gives the energy of their overlap and their pulls, and the flux rule used through both waves gives every part of the curvature between them that involves time, to first order (Parts 12 to 16).

Context and Core Idea

The hypothesis about matter. A particle is a standing wave, and its wave function is in M3,1. It is hypothesized that what a particle is lies in its standing wave. For the purpose of this paper the internal dimensions do not matter; we hypothesize that this model is correct. One more statement is used: a particle's rest energy counts in space as the square of its wave, dP = |ψ|² dV, the shares adding up to 1 (the square rule of quantum mechanics). Here dV is the volume measured by the local rulers of the frames at rest, and dP is the share of the particle's rest energy in that volume. What pulls from outside is the complete count inside, binding included (Section 4, the physicist's box). [the hypothesis: the standing wave, and its rest energy spread as its squared wave; the square rule is taken from quantum mechanics]
What else goes in, and what does not. H1, H2 and H3 of Section 3 and the ruler rule of Section 4 go in as they stand (inside one wave, Part 16 takes the ruler of each sphere in that sphere's frame); for light, that it moves at c on each frame's own clock and ruler. What does not go in, by name: the field equations of general relativity; an action of general relativity; any solution of them, taken as data; and a law of free motion taken from general relativity.
The word curvature. The second derivative of a curve measures how fast its slope changes. Put identical standing waves at rest at different places along a radius, and count from far away how many cycles each completes in a second. Plot that counted rate of oscillation against the distance along the radius, measured with the local rulers. The second derivative of that curve, divided by the rate, is the part of the curvature of space and time in the plane of time and the radius, in the exact sense the word has in geometry (Part 11).

The Chain

Part 1. What goes in. The hypothesis about matter, with \(dP=|\psi|^2\,dV\) the share of a particle's rest energy in the volume \(dV\), the shares adding up to 1; H1 with its flux of the far-counted pull, H2, H3 and the ruler rule. [the hypotheses: the standing wave, and its rest energy spread as its squared wave; the square rule, taken from quantum mechanics; H1 with its flux of the far-counted pull; H2; H3; the ruler rule]

Part 2. Both pulls from one step of work. Lift a small body of rest energy \(mc^2\), held at rest, by \(d\ell\) on its own ruler. By H3 the far observer counts the work \(dE=mc^2\,df=m\,f\,g\,d\ell\), and by H1 \(4\pi r^2 f g=4\pi G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}\) (Section 4, statements 1 and 6). So the sizes of the two inward pulls, the one that the far observer counts and the one in the frame's own units, are \[F_{\mathrm{far}}=\frac{G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}\,m}{r^2},\qquad F_{\mathrm{own}}=\frac{G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}\,m}{f\,r^2}.\] [DERIVED from H3 and H1's flux of the far-counted pull, for a round body, with Newton's law far away fixing \(G\)]

Part 3. The clock rate. Outside the body, \(f=\sqrt{1-L/r}\) with \(L=2G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}/c^2\) and \(f\to1\) far away, and the ruler is \(d\ell=dr/f\) (Section 4, statements 4 and 6). A body at rest counts, from far away, as \(f\) times its rest energy: per unit of rest energy the shift is \(f-1\). [DERIVED from Part 2, H3 and the ruler rule, outside the body, with \(f\to1\) far away]

Part 4. The redshift. A particle at rest at \(r\) completes the same cycles on its own clock and on the far clock, \(dn=\nu_{\mathrm{own}}\,d\tau=\nu_{\mathrm{far}}\,dt\). So the far observer counts \(f\) times its frequency and \(f\) times its rest energy: \[\nu_{\mathrm{far}}=f\,\nu_{\mathrm{own}},\qquad E_{\mathrm{far}}=f\,mc^2.\] [DERIVED from the clock rate and H3]

Part 5. The overlap. Put a particle B in the clock rates that a round body A sets. B's rest energy, as counted from far away, shifts by its rest energy times the sum, over space, of B's squared wave times A's clock shift there: \[U_{A\to B}=m_Bc^2\int\big[f_A(x)-1\big]\,dP_B(x).\] [DERIVED from Parts 1 and 4, for B's rest energy in the clock rates set by A]

Part 6. The first step beyond Newton. With all of B's wave outside A, and \(\langle q\rangle_B=\int q\,dP_B\): \[U_{A\to B}=m_Bc^2\Big\langle\sqrt{1-L_A/r}-1\Big\rangle_B=-G\mathcal M_A m_B\,\langle r^{-1}\rangle_B-\frac{G^2\mathcal M_A^2\,m_B}{2c^2}\,\langle r^{-2}\rangle_B-\dots\] The average of the square root is exact; the two terms shown are the first two of its series in \(L_A/r\). The first is Newton's energy. The second is the first term that the clock rate adds. Keeping only these two terms gives the energy through second order when \(L_A/r\ll1\) everywhere in B's wave. [DERIVED from Parts 3 and 5, with B's wave outside A and the same shares of B's rest energy in every term]

Part 7. The wave's law with the clock in it. For a slow particle B in A's clock rates, count the energy of motion of quantum mechanics' wave law at \(f\) times its local value, as H3 counts the rest energy, and take out the steady phase of the far rest energy. With \(\Phi=c^2(f-1)\): \[i\hbar\,\partial_t\psi=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\,\nabla_i\big(f\,\nabla^i\psi\big)+m\,\Phi\,\psi.\] For a small, well-localized particle at rest for an instant, with its internal pushes negligible, this gives back both pulls of Part 2. [a hypothesis for the motion: the energy of motion is taken from the wave law of quantum mechanics and counted at \(f\) times its local value; the shift of the rest energy is DERIVED from H3 and Part 1]

Parts 1 to 6 hold for a particle B in the clock rates of a still, round body A. Two spread-out particles that both set clock rates are in Parts 12 to 16.

The Curvature, and Integrating It Between Two Points

Part 8. The curvature follows from the clock rate. Write \(N\) for the clock rate along the way, \(N=f\), and a prime for the change per unit of distance on the local ruler, so that \(r'=f\) by the ruler rule. The definition of curvature then gives, for the plane of time and the radius and for the plane of the sphere and the radius, \[C_t=\frac{N''}{N}=-\frac{L}{r^3},\qquad C_s=-\frac{r''}{r}=-\frac{L}{2r^3}.\] Since \(r'=N\), the second is \(-N'/r\) and the first \(N''/N\): one and two derivatives of the clock rate of Section 4, statements 4 and 6. The curvature no longer has to be supplied, and nothing is taken from the Schwarzschild solution. [DERIVED from Section 4, statements 4, 5 and 6, and the definition of curvature]

Part 9. Integrating the curvature from A to B. Put A at the distance 0 and B at the distance \(D\) along the radius, counted on the local rulers. Integrating twice, \[N_B=N_A+D\,N'_A+\int_0^D(D-s)\,C_t\,N\,ds,\qquad r_B=r_A+D\,r'_A-\int_0^D(D-s)\,C_s\,r\,ds.\] This is proved, with no approximation. The curvature integrated from A to B gives the clock rate and the radii at B. In words: the clock rate at B is the clock rate at A, plus the length of the way times its slope at A, plus the sum along the way of the distance still to go, times the curvature in time, times the clock rate there. The radius of the sphere at B is the radius at A, plus the length times its slope at A, minus the sum along the way of the distance still to go, times the curvature in space, times the radius there. What has to be known at A is the clock rate and the radius there, with their slopes; outside a round body the count and the radius at A fix all four: going outward, \(N_A=f_A\), \(N'_A=L/(2r_A^2)\), \(r_A\) and \(r'_A=f_A\). The curvature is taken at the radius reached at each step. Here the second integral alone already returns the clock rate, because \(N=r'\). And between two known radii one number is enough: the sum of \(K\) (Part 11), \(\int_{r_A}^{r_B}K\,dr=(12L^2/5)\,(r_A^{-5}-r_B^{-5})\), fixes \(L\) and with it the whole geometry outside the body. [DERIVED from Part 8 by integrating twice along the radius, with the four values at A]

Part 10. Clocks, light and falling bodies. From the clock rate and the radii rebuilt along the radius follow: the comparison of clocks held at rest, over the same stretch of far time, \(d\tau_B/d\tau_A=N_B/N_A\); the travel time of light going outward along the radius, light moving at \(c\) on each frame's own clock and ruler, \[c\,\Delta t=\int_0^D\frac{d\ell}{N}=r_B-r_A+L\ln\frac{r_B-L}{r_A-L};\] the frequency of a photon sent from A and read at B, \(\nu_B/\nu_A=N_A/N_B\), because two crests take the same time for the same still path; and the fall of a body along the radius: by H2 and H3 for a free body \(\gamma f=\varepsilon\) stays the same, with \(\varepsilon=\gamma_0f(r_0)\) from its start, so on the body's own clock \((dr/d\tau)^2=c^2(\varepsilon^2-f^2)\). [DERIVED from the profile rebuilt in Part 9; the light uses its speed \(c\) on each frame's own clock and ruler and the same path for successive crests; the fall uses H2, H3 for a free body and the body's start] For motion that is not along the radius, H2 and H3 fix the speed at each radius reached; these premises give no rule for its direction.
