For Sirius B, where none of the three applies, the observed redshift and the calculations agree within the one percent of the measurement.

3. Where the conservation derivation and general relativity part at high redshift.

In two places. In the first the conservation derivation gives the higher redshift. In the second it does for a count spread evenly in the far observer's units per unit of grid volume, and at the centre of a body whose density, as the held frames read it, is the same everywhere it gives the lower one (the physicist's box).

Where more than one count pulls. The squared-clock deficits add exactly in the grid of the frame of the calculation (Section 4, statement 7). That the pull between two bodies is counted through that grid's areas is carried over from one point mass (Section 4, the premise table). In Einstein's equations, for bodies at rest on one line and held apart, the clock rates multiply (Weyl's solutions, with each body's rate taken in his coordinates). So for light that leaves a place where two counts pull, with the same two deficits,

\[ 1+z=\Big(1-\frac{L_1}{r_1}-\frac{L_2}{r_2}\Big)^{-1/2}\ \text{here},\qquad 1+z=\Big[\Big(1-\frac{L_1}{r_1}\Big)\Big(1-\frac{L_2}{r_2}\Big)\Big]^{-1/2}\ \text{there}. \]

The first is the higher, always. With the deficits 0.25 and 0.0833 it is 22.5 percent against 20.6. With 0.3 and 0.3 it is 58.1 percent against 42.9. The squares of the two clock rates differ by the product of the two deficits, so the difference shows only where both are large. To compare the two at one and the same place, named by measurements, takes the rulers between two bodies, which are not yet stated (Section 4).

Inside a body. A body is an arrangement of many counts. For a round body the calculation needs only the spheres around the centre: the pull through each is set by the count inside it (premise 1), and the ruler along the pull is that of the frame of the calculation at that sphere, with the count inside read in that frame's units (the physicist's box), as Section 4 updates the ruler, the scale and the clock near a body that sits in the pull of others (premise 5; Section 4). Inside a round body at rest whose count, in the far observer's units per unit of grid volume, is spread evenly, the clock rate at the centre, as the observer far away reads it, is

\[ f(0)=\Big(1-\frac{5L}{4R}\Big)^{3/5}. \]

General relativity's solution for its own evenly spread body has a faster clock at the centre, wherever both clock rates are real:

BodyRedshift of the light from the surface, in bothRedshift of a clock at the centre, this paperThe same, general relativity's solution
1.4 suns, 12 km23.5%40.2%40.0%
2.08 suns, 12.4 km40.8%78.5%76.8%
\(R=\tfrac53L\)58.1%130%123%
\(R=1.5\,L\)73.2%193%173%
\(R=1.25\,L\)123.6%no finite value485%
\(R=1.125\,L\)200%no finite value

With the clock updated sphere by sphere, the clock rate at the centre, as the observer far away reads it, reaches zero when \(R=\tfrac54L\). The light from the surface is then redshifted by

\[ z_{\mathrm{surface}}=\sqrt5-1=123.6\% . \]

That is where the causal boundary of the observer far away, which is also the event horizon, first appears: at the centre of the body, while the surface is still outside \(L\). In a smaller body it is a sphere inside the body, of the radius \(R\sqrt{(R/L)\,(5L/R-4)^{3/5}}\) (0.55 R at \(R=1.22\,L\), 0.86 R at \(R=1.11\,L\), 0.98 R at \(R=1.02\,L\)), and it reaches the surface when \(R=L\). In general relativity's solution the clock rate at the centre reaches zero at \(R=\tfrac98L\), at a surface redshift of 200 percent.

A body whose count is denser toward its centre gets there at a larger radius (the physicist's box): the three such spreads computed reach it at 1.32 L, 1.46 L and 1.47 L. So for every round body at rest whose count is nowhere denser farther out than farther in: at a surface redshift of 123.6 percent or more, the causal boundary of the observer far away lies inside the body.

Is 123.6 percent a limit? For the light that the far observer reads from the surface of a body at rest of this kind, yes. A frame cannot be held at rest where its clock rate, as read far away, is zero while the pull is not: the force that would hold it has no finite value on its own scale (the physicist's box). This result takes that as its premise. A body at rest is filled with pieces held at rest, so for \(L\le R\lt\tfrac54L\) one of them would sit on that sphere. So a round body at rest whose count is nowhere denser farther out, and whose surface lies outside \(L\), has \(R\ge\tfrac54L\) and a surface redshift of at most 123.6 percent. General relativity allows up to 200 percent (Buchdahl's limit, for a fluid with the same pressure in every direction, a finite pressure at the centre and none at the surface).

A body that lies wholly inside \(L\) has no such sphere in it, and the premise says nothing about it. Its surface is beyond the far observer's causal boundary, and the redshift that this observer would infer for its light has two solutions, both complex (premise 7). To exclude such bodies would take a further premise, and none of the eight of Section 3 gives one. General relativity's premise that no frame is at rest inside \(L\) would do it, and this paper denies that premise (Section 3). So the result is: every surface line that the far observer reads with a real redshift, from a round body at rest whose count is nowhere denser farther out, is redshifted by at most 123.6 percent.

An observation can decide: one confirmed line from the surface of a body at rest of this kind, with a redshift between 123.6 and 200 percent, would refute the clock inside a body together with this premise, and general relativity's equations would still stand; one above 200 percent from a body at rest made of a fluid with the same pressure in every direction, whose energy density is nowhere greater farther out, with a finite pressure at the centre and none at the surface, would refute general relativity's equations inside matter (Buchdahl's limit), and this paper allows it (below). Three things bound the statement. The premise is not among the eight of Section 3; without it, the clock says where the causal boundary is, and no more. The limit does not hold for a body whose count is denser farther out: inside a shell (Section 4) the clock rate is the same everywhere, and the redshift of its surface has no limit before \(R=L\). The limit is for a count nowhere denser farther out in the far observer's units per unit of grid volume. A body whose density, as the frames held at rest read it in their own units, is the same everywhere is not of that kind: its count per unit of grid volume grows outward, its clock at the centre stays above zero down to \(R=L\), and there is no limit before \(R=L\) (the physicist's box). The centre of the body is a regular point wherever the clock there is above zero.

The highest surface redshifts that the search found are 72% ± 5%, 65% ± 3% and 64.2% ± 3.2% (the first three rows of the table). They need a radius of 1.51, 1.58 and 1.59 times \(L\). With the clock updated sphere by sphere, an even spread reaches the causal boundary at its centre only at 1.25 L, and the three spreads denser toward the centre computed here reach it at 1.32 L, 1.46 L and 1.47 L: all three lines leave room for a body at rest of this kind. A spread still denser toward the centre reaches it beyond 1.511 L (at 1.56 L for a count density ten times higher inside \(R/4\) than outside it), so if one of these lines is confirmed as a surface line, the spread of the star's count, measured in some other way, says where the star's centre is. (Versions up to 1.1.0 kept the far observer's ruler through every layer of the body and gave 73.2 percent; version 1.2.0, of 27 November 2026, updates it sphere by sphere.)

4. What is still to do.

  • Check every observation at its source, and complete the Appendix.
  • Add the spin: the motion of the emitting surface (Section 4, statement 8) and the count of a spinning body, with all its energies.
  • Redo the burst analyses that give the masses and radii in the table with this paper's own formulas, and say what changes.
  • What holds a body up, and with it which bodies can be at rest: the premise of this limit, or what premises 7 and 8 give for the pieces of a body beyond the far observer's causal boundary.
  • The frozen prediction: write down, before looking at any new observation, what each calculation gives for it.
For a child

Light that climbs away from a very heavy star gets tired: it arrives redder than it left. The heavier and smaller the star, the redder. There are different ways to work out how much redder. One way forgets that things get heavier when you measure them close to the star. That way always comes out too low, and the heavier the star, the more it is off. Our way does not forget, and for the outside of one star it gives the same answer as the famous black-hole formula.

Then we looked at what telescopes have seen. For a few very heavy stars the light looks even redder than every calculation says. Nobody is sure yet that those telescopes read the light correctly.

Our rules say something new about the inside of a star. Squeeze a star smaller and smaller. There comes a point where, for someone far away, the very middle of the star sits on the edge of what they can ever see. With our rules that happens when the star's light is 124 parts in 100 redder. With the old rules it happens at 200. Holding a piece of the star still, right on that edge, would take a push with no end. If no piece can be held there, then a star that stands still, and that we can still see, cannot be squeezed past that point. The reddest light of this kind that we found a report of is 72.

For a high school physics teacher

The formulas. With \(x=2G\mathcal M/(Rc^2)\): the conservation derivation and Schwarzschild's formula both give \(1+z=1/\sqrt{1-x}\). A calculation that keeps the mass the same for every frame gives \(1+z=1/(1-x/2)\). To first order in \(x\) all agree: \(z\approx G\mathcal M/(Rc^2)\), the formula used for white dwarfs.

Where the difference comes from. A frame held at rest near the body reads the body's mass as \(\mathcal M/f\), heavier than a far frame does, because its unit of energy is smaller. That heavier reading is what the pull at its place goes with. Leaving it out lowers the redshift: 20.8 percent in place of 23.5 percent for a neutron star of 1.4 suns and 12 km.

The observations. For the white dwarf Sirius B the measured redshift, 80.65 km/s as a speed, matches the calculation within the one percent of the measurement. For four neutron stars with claimed lines the measured redshift is above every calculation, and each of those lines is disputed.

Where this paper and general relativity part. For the light from the surface of one star the two give the same redshift. They part where more than one mass pulls, and the inside of a star is such a place. Here the ruler, the scale and the clock of each layer are updated to the frame of the calculation there, with the count inside read in that frame's units, as near the Sun in the pull of the Galaxy, and that makes the clock at the centre slower than in general relativity's solution. The clock at the centre of an evenly filled star then stops, as read from far away, when \(R=1.25\,L\): the surface light is then redshifted by 123.6 percent. In general relativity's solution for an evenly filled star that happens at \(R=1.125\,L\) and 200 percent. The force needed to hold a piece of the star at rest where the clock stops has no finite value there. With the premise that no piece is held there, a star at rest whose matter is nowhere denser farther out, and whose light the far observer reads with a real redshift, has a surface redshift of at most 123.6 percent.

For a theoretical physicist

The three calculations, and the power of the clock rate

All use the clock step \(d\ln f=g_{\mathrm{hold}}\,d\ell/c^2\) (premise 3) and the held frame's ruler \(d\ell=dr/f\). They differ in the mass that the held frame puts into its own law of the pull, \(\mathcal M/f^{\,n}\):

\(n\)The held frame's law of the pullResult1.4 suns, 12 km2.08 suns, 12.4 km
0: the mass held static\(g_{\mathrm{hold}}=G\mathcal M/r^2\)\(f=1-x/2\)20.8%32.9%
1: the conservation derivation (Section 4, statements 2, 4, 6)\(g_{\mathrm{hold}}=G(\mathcal M/f)/r^2\)\(f^2=1-x\)23.5%40.8%
2: the reading entered twice\(g_{\mathrm{hold}}=G(\mathcal M/f^2)/r^2\)\(f^3=1-3x/2\)27.4%57.3%

In general \(f^{\,n+1}=1-(n+1)\,x/2\) for \(n\ne-1\); at \(n=-1\) the same step gives \(f=e^{-x/2}\), which is also the result with the mass held static and the ruler not updated either, \(d\ell=dr\).

Section 4 derives the row \(n=1\): the held frame reads the body at \(\mathcal M/f\), by count and by weighing (statement 2). The Schwarzschild solution has the same pull on a frame held at rest, \(g_{\mathrm{hold}}=G\mathcal M/(r^2\sqrt{1-L/r})\). So its formula for the redshift is the row \(n=1\), although the solution has one constant \(M\) for every frame. The row \(n=2\) is derived nowhere in this paper. It is in the table because it is the only one of the three that gives a higher redshift than Schwarzschild's formula for the surface of one body. The second reviewer derived the rows \(n=0\) and \(n=1\) independently on 25 November 2026 and the figures agree.

Around one body at rest the emitter's motion multiplies \(1+z\) by \(D=\gamma(1-\beta\cos\theta)\), with \(\theta\) the angle between the light and the emitter's velocity in the frame held at rest (Section 4, statement 8).

Inside a round body

Let \(\ell(u)\) be the count, as a length, inside the radius \(u\), with \(\ell(R)=L\), and let \(u\) be the radius of the circles around the centre. The pull through the sphere at \(s\) is set by the count inside it (premise 1), \(f\,g_{\mathrm{hold}}=G\mathcal M(s)/s^2\), and with the clock step, on the held frame's own ruler, \(s^2\,df/d\ell=\ell(s)/2\), whatever the ruler (Section 10, Part 16). The ruler along the pull is that of the one-body calculation for the count inside the sphere, done in the units of the frame of the calculation at that sphere, as Section 4 updates the ruler, the scale and the clock near a body that sits in the pull of others (derived for round arrangements in Section 4, "What a shell does inside itself"):

\[ \Big(\frac{ds}{d\ell}\Big)^2=1-\frac{\ell(s)}{f\,s}\,\frac{ds}{d\ell}, \]

where \(\ell\,(ds/d\ell)/f\) is the count inside read in that frame's units. That frame's clock runs at \(f/(ds/d\ell)\) of the far observer's (frames chain), so by statement 2 it reads the count inside at \(\ell\,(ds/d\ell)/f\); relative to it the frame held at the sphere has its clock and its ruler along the pull at the same factor, \(ds/d\ell\), as premise 5 gives them, and reads the count at \(\ell/f\), as statement 2 gives it. This keeps at every place the one-body relation between the curvature of space in the plane of the sphere and the curvature of the clock rate across the pull, \(K_{\theta\varphi}=C_\theta+C_\varphi\) (Section 4, "In Einstein's terms"). Then \(df/ds=\ell(s)/(2s^2\,ds/d\ell)\ge0\), and \(f\) is lowest at the centre, for every spread of the count. With \(ds/d\ell=f\) in place of this ruler the same steps give the sum of Section 4, statement 7, \(F=1-\ell(s)/s-\int_s^Rd\ell(u)/u\); inside a body that sum does not hold. Below, \(F=f^2\).

For the even spread, \(\ell(u)=L\,u^3/R^3\), with \(\lambda=L/R\) and \(w\) the count inside read at the sphere over \(s\): \(s\,dw/ds=w(4-5w)/(2-w)\),

\[ \frac{s^2}{R^2}=\frac{w}{\lambda}\Big(\frac{4-5\lambda}{4-5w}\Big)^{3/5},\qquad f=\frac{\lambda s^2}{R^2}\,\frac{\sqrt{1-w}}{w},\qquad f(0)=\Big(1-\frac{5L}{4R}\Big)^{3/5}. \]

The even spread is the extreme case. With \(b=\ell/s\) the two equations give \(dF/ds=G=(\ell/2s^2)\big(b+\sqrt{b^2+4F}\big)\), which rises with \(\ell\) and with \(F\), and \(\partial G/\partial F\le1/s\) where \(F\ge0\). A count nowhere denser farther out than farther in has \(\ell(u)\ge L\,u^3/R^3\). Integrated inward from the same surface value \(F(R)=1-L/R\), the difference \(D=F_{\mathrm{even}}-F\) then has \(dD/ds\le k\,D\), with \(0\le k\le1/s\), wherever both are at least zero; so \(D\,e^{K(s)}\), with \(K(s)=\int_s^Rk\,du\), does not rise with \(s\), and it is zero at the surface: \(D\ge0\). At every place such a spread has \(F\le F_{\mathrm{even}}\). The even spread gives the highest clock at the centre, and every other such spread has its centre reach \(F=0\) at a larger \(R\) (below); the three spreads denser toward the centre computed below show by how much.

So for \(L\lt R\lt\tfrac54L\) the clock rate inferred at the centre is not real while it is at the surface: \(F\) is zero on a sphere inside the body, for the even spread at \(s_0=R\sqrt{(R/L)\,(5L/R-4)^{3/5}}\) (0.55 R, 0.86 R and 0.98 R for \(R=1.22\,L\), \(1.11\,L\) and \(1.02\,L\)), where \(dF/ds\gt0\). That sphere is the causal boundary of the observer far away, by the criterion of premise 8: a body at rest where the clock rate is \(f\) needs the speed \(c\sqrt{1-F}\) to escape (from \(e=\gamma f=1\), premise 3), and that is \(c\) where \(F=0\). Inside it the square of the clock rate that this observer infers is negative, and by premise 7 the inferred clock rate has two solutions, \(\pm\,i\sqrt{-F}\).

The force. On its own scale, the force per unit of mass that holds a piece at rest is

\[ g_{\mathrm{hold}}=c^2\,\frac{\partial\ln f}{\partial\ell}=\frac{c^2}{f}\,\frac{df}{d\ell}=\frac{c^2\,\ell(s)}{2f\,s^2}. \]

On the sphere where \(f=0\) the pull is not zero, so this has no finite value: it grows without bound as the sphere is approached. At \(R=\tfrac54L\) exactly, for the even spread, the zero is at the centre, where the pull counted in the far observer's units is zero as well; there \(ds/d\ell=1/\sqrt5\) and \(f=s^2/(\sqrt5R^2)\) throughout the body, and the force on the central piece's own scale grows as \(1/s\). The limit needs one premise: no piece of a body at rest is held where the far-read clock rate is zero and the pull is not. For a body whose count is nowhere denser farther out and whose surface lies outside \(L\), a radius below \(\tfrac54L\) gives \(F(0)\lt0\lt F(R)\), which puts such a piece inside the body, with \(\ell(s_0)\gt0\). So with that premise a body of this kind whose surface lies outside \(L\) has

\[ R\ge\frac54\,L,\qquad 1+z_{\mathrm{surface}}=\Big(1-\frac LR\Big)^{-1/2}\le\sqrt5 , \]

with equality only for the even spread, whose zero is then at the centre, where the pull counted in the far observer's units is zero (the force on the pieces near the centre grows there as \(1/s\)). For any other such spread the zero is inside the body already at \(R=\tfrac54L\): below a place \(s_1\) where \(D(s_1)\gt0\), \(D\ge D(s_1)\,s/s_1\) (from \(k\le1/s\)), while \(F_{\mathrm{even}}=s^4/5R^4\), so its \(F\) is below zero near the centre. For \(R\lt L\), the surface is beyond the far observer's causal boundary, the zero of \(F\) lies outside the body at \(s=L\), and the premise says nothing. The far observer would infer for the light of such a surface \(1+z=1/f\) with \(f^2=1-L/R\lt0\): two solutions, both complex (premise 7). Excluding such bodies would take a further premise, and none of the eight of Section 3 gives one; general relativity's premise that no frame is at rest inside \(L\) would do it, and Section 3 denies that premise. So the result, with its one premise, is: every surface line that the far observer reads with a real redshift, from a round body at rest whose count is nowhere denser farther out, has \(z\le\sqrt5-1\).

For a spread that is not even the condition is sharper: the spreads with \(d\ell/du\propto u^2(1-0.5u^2/R^2)\), \(u^2(1-0.9u^2/R^2)\), and a count density 3.3 times higher inside \(R/2\) than outside it, reach the boundary at the centre at 1.32 L, 1.46 L and 1.47 L. A line at 0.72 has \(R/L=1.511\), which each of them allows.

What this uses: that the counts of the pieces are the only sources of the pull inside a body that is held up by its own pressure, each count positive and holding its share of the binding and of whatever holds the body up; that every piece is at rest; and that the count, per unit of volume of the grid, is nowhere denser farther out than farther in. With the ruler updated sphere by sphere, the count per unit of grid volume is not the density that the held frames read in their own units: that density is the count per unit of grid volume times \((ds/d\ell)/f\). The limit is for the first. With the second the same everywhere the first grows outward (\(f\) rises outward and \(ds/d\ell\) falls), and the clock at the centre stays above zero down to \(R=L\) (a clock at the centre redshifted by 38.4 percent for 1.4 suns and 12 km, against 40.0 percent in general relativity's solution). General relativity's limit on the comparison side is for a density of the second kind; what each of the two densities includes has still to be matched. How the potential energy is divided among the pieces (Section 4, "Not yet in this section") changes the spread of the count, not the result for a given spread. The spin of a real star is not in it.

The centre of the body. With the ruler of each sphere updated, \(ds/d\ell\to1\) at the centre wherever \(f(0)\gt0\): a small sphere at the distance \(d\) measured on the held rulers has the area \(4\pi d^2\), and the curvature of space in the planes across the radius, \(K_{\theta\varphi}=2C_\theta\), stays finite there (\(0.90/R^2\) for \(L/R=0.5\)). The centre is a regular point. The far observer's ruler carried through every layer, \(ds/d\ell=f\), would make it a conical point, with the area \(4\pi f(0)^2d^2\); inside an empty shell it would put a curvature of space \((1-f^2)/s^2\) where nothing pulls, the clock rate has no curvature and no move stores or releases potential energy, and a cold, inert rigid body at rest there would be strained with no work done; premise 3's ruler (Section 3), derived from the count in Section 4 ("What a shell does inside itself"), excludes the far observer's ruler there. Near \(R=\tfrac54L\) the evenly spread body becomes conical except in a core that shrinks to the centre (\(ds/d\ell=1/\sqrt5\) at \(R=\tfrac54L\)). With the count in the far observer's units in the ruler, \(ds/d\ell=\sqrt{1-\ell(s)/s}\), the clock inside an evenly spread body would be general relativity's interior solution exactly and the limit 200 percent; that ruler keeps the far observer's scale in the count, where Section 4 updates it.

The opposite case is the shell of Section 4: all the count at one radius. Inside it \(F\) is the same everywhere as at the shell, the far observer's causal boundary appears at the shell itself, at \(R=L\), and the redshift of its surface has no limit before that. So without the condition on the spread there is no figure of 123.6 percent.

General relativity, on the comparison side. Its solution for a body of the same density everywhere has the clock rate \(f(s)=\tfrac32\sqrt{1-L/R}-\tfrac12\sqrt{1-Ls^2/R^3}\), which is zero at the centre when \(R=\tfrac98L\). The updated clock is the slower at every place inside the body where both are real, at every size: the closed form above gives \(w\gt\ell/s\) below the surface, so \(ds/d\ell\gt f\) and \((ds/d\ell)^2\lt1-\ell/s\), the ruler with which the same clock step gives general relativity's clock (the centre of the body, above), and with the shorter ruler \(df/ds=\ell/(2s^2\,ds/d\ell)\) is the larger on the way in from the same surface value. At the centre the difference is 0.0007 at \(L/R=0.3\), 0.013 at 0.6 and 0.061 at 0.75 (at \(R=\tfrac43L\), \(f(0)=0.189\) and \(f_{\mathrm{GR}}(0)=\tfrac14\)); the two clocks agree to the second order in \(L/R\) at every place and part at the third, by \((L^3/64R^3)(1-s^2/R^2)^2(1+2s^2/R^2)\), which is \(L^3/64R^3\) at the centre. For \(\tfrac98L\lt R\lt\tfrac54L\) the updated clock is not real at the centre while general relativity's still is. Buchdahl's limit: for a round body at rest made of a fluid with the same pressure in every direction, whose energy density is nowhere greater farther out than farther in, with a finite pressure at the centre, joined to empty space at a surface where the pressure is zero, \(R\gt\tfrac98L\) and \(z_{\mathrm{surface}}\lt2\).

What is shown, and the premises of general relativity this touches

Shown. For the light from the surface of one round body at rest: the conservation derivation gives a higher redshift than a calculation with the mass held static, by the figures of the first table, and the same redshift as Schwarzschild's formula from the same far mass and radius. In the two cases with more than one count that are worked out here, this paper gives a higher redshift than Einstein's equations: for the same two deficits of bodies at rest on one line, by the exact sum, at the second order in the deficits, with the pull counted through the areas of the grid of the frame of the calculation (Section 4, the premise table); and, wherever both clock rates are real, at every place inside a round body whose count is spread evenly in the far observer's units per unit of grid volume, with the clock updated sphere by sphere, at the third order. In a round body at rest whose count, in the far observer's units per unit of grid volume, is nowhere denser farther out than farther in, the far observer's causal boundary appears at the centre at a surface redshift of at most 123.6 percent; in general relativity's solution for an evenly spread body the clock rate at the centre reaches zero at 200 percent. With the premise that no piece is held where the far-read clock rate is zero and the pull is not, every surface line that the far observer reads with a real redshift from such a body is redshifted by at most 123.6 percent. For a body whose density, as the held frames read it in their own units, is the same everywhere, the clock at the centre stays above zero down to \(R=L\), and at every size computed it is faster than at the centre of general relativity's evenly dense body (38.4 against 40.0 percent for 1.4 suns and 12 km). In the four observations above 20 percent that have a published mass and radius, the observed redshift is above every calculation.

Not shown. The comparison between two bodies at one and the same place, named by measurements, and an ordering for every arrangement of several bodies. That any of the four lines is a line from the star's surface. What the conservation-based formulas give once the spin and the burst analyses are redone. Whether a body can be at rest with pieces beyond the far observer's causal boundary: wholly inside \(L\), where the premise says nothing, or across \(L\), when the premise is not taken. What holds a body up, and so which bodies exist. The same for a spinning body. The ruler inside an arrangement that is not round: the derivation of the ruler of each sphere (Section 4, "What a shell does inside itself") uses round shells. Which spread a real star's count has: nowhere denser farther out in the far observer's units per unit of grid volume, or, for example, of one density everywhere as the held frames read it. It decides whether there is a limit; it follows from what holds the body up, and observation can constrain it.

The premises of general relativity this touches. The first is its equations inside matter. They give the clock at the centre of a body, and for a fluid with the same pressure in every direction, whose energy density is nowhere greater farther out than farther in, with a finite pressure at the centre and none at the surface, they allow a body at rest up to a surface redshift of 200 percent (Buchdahl). The updated clock is slower at every place inside, at every size at which both are real, and it puts the far observer's causal boundary at the centre at 123.6 percent. For the even spread the step that parts the two is the count in the ruler: general relativity's interior ruler, \(ds/d\ell=\sqrt{1-\ell(s)/s}\), keeps the far observer's scale in the count inside each sphere, where this paper reads it in the units of the frame of the calculation at that sphere, \(\ell\,(ds/d\ell)/f\) (Section 4, statement 2, for that frame): that is general relativity's premise of one mass inside each sphere for every frame, which statement 2 denies. On the comparison side, for every round body at rest general relativity's ruler is this ruler with \(8\pi G s^2p_r/c^4\) added, \(p_r\) the pressure along the radius, both written with the clock and the count through the sphere in the far observer's units: in its equations inside matter that pressure enters the relation between the ruler and the pull, where here the ruler follows from the pull alone. Wherever no pressure acts along the radius the two rulers are one. A confirmed surface line between 123.6 and 200 percent from a round body at rest whose count is nowhere denser farther out could decide. The burden is on the premise that general relativity's equations hold inside matter at such redshifts, which no observation has tested: the highest surface redshift that the search found is 0.72 ± 0.05. The second is the class of equations that Einstein chose (A9 of Section 5), which makes the clock rates of bodies at rest on one line and held apart multiply, where the deficits add here in the grid of the frame of the calculation.

18 / RESEARCH NOTES

Conclusion

We found an error in the Schwarzschild solution, fixed it, and reconciled the solution with conservation of mass-energy. The error is one step. The Schwarzschild form is derived outside the event horizon; general relativity then carries it inside by a change of coordinates, and with that step gives every frame one mass \(\mathcal M\) and one event horizon, leaves no frame at rest inside, and, with the direction of time it chooses there, sends everything to the centre (Section 7, parts 15 to 17; Section 9, statement 3). The fix keeps the solution outside \(L\), because the count gives the same; makes its assumption that nothing changes with time a result, with no equation of Einstein's; and puts premises 7 and 8 in the place of its continuation across \(L\), one account for every frame of reference (Section 9, statement 4).

With the error fixed, the Schwarzschild solution and conservation of mass-energy give identical results inside and outside the event horizon. Outside, around one body at rest, they give the same clocks, the same rulers and the same count of a free body, to every figure (Section 9, statement 1). At the event horizon and inside it, both take premises 7 and 8 in the place of the continuation: what each frame reads is real for it; a value worked out across \(L\) has two solutions, and they are complex; objects move beyond their event horizon, by the same law in both directions; an observer at rest far away cannot and does not observe the passage; and the causal boundary depends on the frame of reference (Sections 3, 9 and 14). In both, an event beyond a frame's causal boundary is calculated through an intermediate frame of reference, and an event at the causal boundary is not: no frame is held there (Section 14).

What Is Shown

  • Outside, the Schwarzschild solution is conservation of mass-energy. From H1 (the complete count inside a closed surface is constant), H2 (special relativity in the frame a body passes) and H3 (potential energy is the clock rate), with the ruler rule: \(f^2=1-L/r\), \(L=2G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}/c^2\), with \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}\) constant because nothing crosses the surface, not because the field is assumed the same at every time; a free body keeps \(\gamma f\) constant, and that is Schwarzschild's \(e\). No equation of Einstein's is used (Section 4, statements 1 to 6). [DERIVED]

The Error: the Premises of General Relativity the Fix Removes

(1) The static form carried inside the horizon. The form \(1-L/r\), derived outside, is continued to \(r\lt L\) by a change of coordinates (Section 7, parts 15 to 17), where the far observer's clock factor is imaginary and nothing has tested it. The inward fall of everything, the absence of a frame at rest and the one horizon for every frame follow from this one step and the extension's choice of the direction of time.

(2) No frame can be held at rest inside the event horizon. A consequence of (1): a frame at rest there would have a spacelike four-velocity. This paper keeps "rest frames with their local clock, ruler, and energy relations intact" (Section 1): what each reads is real for it, and between frames on the two sides of \(L\) the values worked out are premise 7's, with two complex solutions (Section 3; Section 14). Read by those frames, a free body at rest inside \(L\) cannot fall inward (Section 14, Part 6), and a body falling in from outside turns back at \(L/(1+e^2)\) and comes out, where the continued solution still has it moving inward (Section 14, Part 7), against general relativity's fall of everything inside to the centre.

(3) One event horizon for every frame, crossed one way only. One \(L=2G\mathcal M/c^2\), measured far away, is given to every frame, inside and out, and nothing crosses it outward. Here the causal boundary depends on the frame of reference: at \(L\) only a frame at rest needs the speed of light to escape; a frame in free motion with count \(e\le1\), falling in or on its way out, needs \(c\,(1-e^2)/(1+e^2)\) along its motion, and with \(e\ge1\) none; and objects move beyond their event horizon, by the same law in both directions (Section 3, premise 8; Section 14).

These three are the error, and the burden is on them. None of them is needed outside the horizon, where the solution was already right.

Observations That Could Decide

Around one body at rest, outside the event horizon, the clocks and rulers of the fixed solution are those of the unfixed one to every figure (Section 9, statement 1), so the tests of the redshift made so far are passed by both; the orbits and the paths of light are not yet derived from Section 4. For several bodies, and when the count moves, the two part outside \(L\) as well (Section 6, statement 3). For one body at rest, what decides is the inside. Anything, light or matter, arriving outside from inside an event horizon: forbidden by premise (1), which makes the horizon one-way; in this paper objects can, and do, move beyond their event horizon, by the same law in both directions (premise 8; Section 14). A frame held at rest inside an event horizon, or any signal from one: forbidden by premise (2); this paper keeps such frames (premise 7). No observation has yet been made at or inside an event horizon; until one is, for one body at rest the two are separated only by the premise.

For a child

We found a mistake in the black-hole formula and fixed it. The formula is right outside the black hole: it is the rule that the total in the jar never changes, with clocks that slow down deep in the pull. The mistake was pushing the formula across the edge in a way that makes everything fall to the middle, leaves nobody standing still inside, and gives everyone the same edge, which nothing can cross on the way out. Fixed, the formula says the same thing as the jar rule everywhere, outside and inside. What you measure with your own clock, ruler and scale is real. You cannot measure anything exactly on the edge, but you can work out what happens across it by passing the message through friends on each side, and then you always get two answers. Things can move beyond the edge, and they do, in both directions, and the edge depends on who is looking and how they move. Inside, people standing still see a stone at rest move only outward, and a stone that falls in slows down, stops and comes back out. Someone far away, following a stone that falls in, finds their clock running backwards past the edge. Nobody ever sees anything cross their own edge.

For a high school physics teacher

Outside: \(f^2=1-L/r\) from conservation and the clock step, and \(\gamma f=e\) is the conserved count of a falling body. The error: carrying that form inside by a change of coordinates, which gives every frame one mass and one horizon and removes every frame at rest. The fix: keep the outside, and across \(L\) use premises 7 and 8; then the solution and conservation give identical results inside and outside. Between two frames at rest the factor is \(f_Q/f_P\), with \(f_Q^2/f_P^2=(1-L/r_Q)/(1-L/r_P)\): positive on one side of \(L\) and negative across it, so a reading converted across \(L\) has two solutions, \(\pm i\) times a real number. A free body obeys \((dr/d\tau)^2=c^2(e^2-|1-L/r|)\) on both sides of \(L\), in both directions: at \(L\) its speed on its own clock is \(ce\) and it gets there in a finite time of its own, while on the far observer's clock the passage has no finite time, and inside \(L\) that clock runs backward along the body's path (\(dt/d\tau=e/F\lt0\)). Frames held at rest inside read a free body at \(\gamma\propto1/\sqrt{L/r-1}\), so a body at rest there can only move outward, and a body falling in from outside turns at \(L/(1+e^2)\) and comes out. The test: anything arriving outside from inside an event horizon.

For a theoretical physicist

Exterior: \(4\pi r^2fg=4\pi G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}\) (H1 for the force the far observer counts), \(g=c^2\,d\ln f/d\ell\) (H3), \(d\ell=dr/f\) (the ruler rule) give \(f^2=1-L/r\) with no equation of Einstein's (H1 written at a point is \(\nabla^2F=0\) in empty space, in the frame of the calculation: Section 4, In Einstein's terms); \(\gamma f=e\). Source: \(d\mathcal M=f\,dm\) as the shell is built, \(\sqrt{1-L/R}=1-Gm_0/c^2R\), horizon at the matter for \(m_0=c^2R/G\). Across \(L\) (premises 7 and 8): \(E_P=(f_Q/f_P)E_Q\), with \(f_Q/f_P=\pm i\sqrt{(L/r_Q-1)/(1-L/r_P)}\) for \(r_Q\lt L\lt r_P\) and real on one side; through intermediate frames the factors multiply and the intermediate clock rates cancel (Section 14: \(\pm2\sqrt{11}\,iE_0\) for A at 200 and D at 1,100); \((dr/d\tau)^2=c^2(e^2-|F|)\) on both sides (outside, \(=c^2f^2(\gamma^2-1)\)), turns at \(L/(1+e^2)\) and, for \(e\lt1\), \(L/(1-e^2)\), \(|dr/d\tau|_L=ce\), \(\Delta\tau\) finite, \(dt/d\tau=e/F\), \(\Delta t\to\infty\) at \(L\) and \(dt/d\tau\lt0\) inside; the speed still needed at \(L\): \(c\) at rest, and \(c(1-e^2)/(1+e^2)\) for a free frame with \(e\le1\), falling in or on its way out; light sent at \(L\) on the way out: \(2eE\). Inside \(L\), read by frames held at rest (premises 3 and 7, H2): \(\gamma(r)=\gamma_0\sqrt{(L/r_0-1)/(L/r-1)}\). A surface line of a neutron star above 20 percent whose ion is confirmed and whose mass and radius were measured without the line and without a model of the atmosphere or of the bursts. A measurement that separates gravity from motion for the disk lines or for S2.

What the list shows. Where the redshift is small and everything is measured, the calculation and the observation agree: Sirius B, to within the one percent of the measurement. Above 20 percent no observation is yet free of dispute. In the four that have a published mass and radius the line is redder than the calculation: 0.72 against 0.43, 0.65 against 0.50, 0.64 against 0.31 (there the line itself was among the inputs of the mass and radius), and 0.35 against 0.27.

Appendix: The Full Audit of This Paper

This appendix holds the AI audit of this paper in full, so that a reader, or an AI asked to check the paper, can see how it was reviewed and check the review itself. It has five parts: how the audit was run; the prompt, word for word; the results, word for word; what was done with each finding; and the discussion with the auditor that followed, word for word. The auditor was Codex, OpenAI’s GPT-6.2-Astra model, at “ultra”, the highest of the reasoning levels it offers, working read-only. In the auditor’s replies, links to files on the author’s computer are reduced to their text; nothing else in them is changed.

1. How the audit was run

The audit was run on 26 November 2026, on draft v0.75 of this paper, the version before the corrections it led to. It was one run with no memory of earlier runs, in an empty working folder that held only the manuscript’s text copy, read-only and with web search off. Its message was the review prompt, word for word, followed by a run block with the author’s rules 7 to 9 for every reviewer (Part 2). The auditor read the whole manuscript, 12,028 lines, and returned its Parts I to III (Part 3): 4,274,737 input tokens (4,134,016 of them cached), 28,105 output tokens, 15.6 minutes. Every number in its Part II was recomputed independently, 37 values, and all agree.

The author’s instruction for the audit was: “Don’t make any of the changes it suggests. We’ll discuss them first.” Each finding was discussed with him, and then put in or not; Part 4 records what was done. Two findings needed more mathematics, and each went back to the auditor, at the same level of reasoning, as a check of its own (Part 5).

2. The prompt, word for word

The message of the audit run: the review prompt (“Gravity, Geometry and Conservation: Constructive Audit and Repair”, in its second version, with its Section 0 of standing rules), then the run block, into which the author’s rules 7 to 9 are copied from his rule file.

The message of the audit run
# Gravity, Geometry and Conservation: Constructive Audit and Repair

## Assignment

Evaluate the supplied manuscript's proposed explanation of gravity through geometry, curvature and overlaps. Identify precise mathematical and physical errors, determine the conditions needed for a workable derivation, provisionally adopt consistent additional assumptions, and carry out the repairs. Then evaluate the resulting model's conservation of mass-energy and momentum and its relationship to general relativity under the manuscript's stated conditions.

You are authorized to produce corrected equations, a complete revised derivation and replacement manuscript passages. Preserve the original as a reference and identify every substantive change. Complete the repair work that the available information permits; do not stop at a list of suggestions.

Replacement passages are limited by Section 0. Propose replacement text only where you have demonstrated a mathematical error (arithmetic, sign, unit or scope, a formula used outside its domain, or a declared test that was not met), and keep the author's words everywhere else. Do not supply replacement text that restates the manuscript's thesis, premises or conclusions in weaker or different terms. A repaired branch that changes a premise is reported as a branch, never as replacement text for the manuscript.

A successful repair is a verifiable derivation from explicitly stated, jointly consistent premises. The desired conclusion is the question to investigate, not an assumption available to prove itself.

## 0. Standing Rules for This Manuscript

Read this section first. Where any later instruction in this prompt seems to allow something that this section rules out, this section governs.

**Your job.** The author asks every reviewer to test general relativity, not to defend it. The premise under attack is the step by which general relativity merges the different values that frames of reference read into one event horizon: one metric for all observers, continued across the event horizon with the same mass. For every result, find the premise of general relativity that it touches and test that premise by mathematics or by a raw observation. Agreement with general relativity is never a result. Where the manuscript and general relativity disagree, the burden is on general relativity's premise: name the premise, and name the observation that could decide.

**No watering down.** Do not write a result as weaker than its mathematics shows. Do not call a result "not derived", "not shown", "unsupported" or "open" when the manuscript derives it: find the place where it is derived first. Do not add a caveat, a softer word or a "but" that no calculation requires. Do not move the burden from general relativity's premise onto the manuscript. Do not leave a derived result out. Legitimate mathematical corrections are welcome: an arithmetic, sign, unit or scope error, a formula used outside its domain, or a test that the manuscript declared in advance and did not meet.

**The manuscript's definitions govern.**

- Conservation of mass-energy means that an observer's complete count of everything inside a closed surface, each kind of energy counted once in that observer's units, does not change (Section 2).
- The premises of Section 3 are the author's, stated with their arguments from the conservation laws. Premises 7 and 8 state what holds at and beyond the event horizon. They are the manuscript's premises; do not replace them by general relativity's continuation.
- The author's terms stay. Where a term differs from standard usage (for example "the curvature between two points is the integral of f dot dr"), propose a one-line definition, never a replacement.
- The author's bold statements are his words. Do not remove, narrow or reinterpret them. If a premise has a mathematical consequence that looks unphysical, state the consequence exactly and leave the decision to the author.
- The first paper ("Why Is It Impossible to Escape from a Black Hole?") is not a source. Passages that still rest on it are flagged in the manuscript by working notes. You may show where they conflict with the premises; they are not the manuscript's position.

**Do not do the following.** Each was done by an earlier run of this prompt, and each would have weakened the paper.

1. Do not use general relativity's causal structure inside the event horizon (its light cones; "every future-directed path has decreasing r") to deny that objects move beyond their event horizon. That structure belongs to the continuation under attack. Premise 8 states what holds there, and Section 3 derives the passage: the speed c·e at L, reached in a finite time of the body's own.
2. Do not judge the manuscript's conservation claims by general relativity's standards (the conservation of a particle's symmetry charge, ∇·T = 0) and conclude that the manuscript "does not prove" that general relativity violates conservation. Use the manuscript's definition (Section 2). Report general relativity's standards on the comparison side, labelled.
3. Do not recast the manuscript's thesis as "adopted postulates", and do not write replacement text for its summaries of what it derives. You may name an import (special relativity at one place, Planck's relation, Newton's law far away), as the manuscript itself does in Section 4.
4. Do not cut or narrow a premise by reading it as a claim about a different quantity, for example premise 4 read as a claim about light exchanged between two distant events. Premise 4 concerns a frame's own clock, rulers and mass; Section 4 derives it (statements 3 and 4).
5. Do not repair the manuscript with relations of general relativity: its interior ruler 1 − 2Gm(r)/(c²r), the lapse of its constant-density interior, geodesic motion. They are imports. With the interior ruler, for example, the 73.2 percent limit of Section 17 would become general relativity's 200 percent. If you find a real problem in a premise (for example, premise 5 continued to the centre of a body makes the centre a conical point), report it as a finding, and derive repairs from the manuscript's own premises only. A repair taken from general relativity, if you give one, is labelled as the comparison and is never offered as replacement text.
6. Do not present a law of motion, for example the Hamiltonian of a static metric (straightest-path motion, Einstein's assumption A6), as a derived result of the manuscript. Label it as an import.
7. Do not state as a general rule that a change of reference frame "does not relocate a causal boundary". For frames at rest the boundary is the one circle L (Section 3). The manuscript's frame-dependence of the causal boundary concerns frames in motion (Section 9, statement 3).
8. Do not write a verdict on whether general relativity is correct in general. State what the manuscript's derivations establish on its own definitions and premises, and what the comparison with general relativity shows, each at its demonstrated strength.

**Objections that do not count, with the place in the manuscript that answers each.** An objection of one of these kinds is not a finding.

1. The result agrees with general relativity, so general relativity is confirmed. Agreement is never a result. Section 6 names where the two derivations part.
2. A change must move at the speed of light. That is general relativity's premise. Premise 6 states the opposite, and Section 3 gives its mathematics.
3. An event horizon is the same surface for every frame and is crossed one way only. That is the step under attack. Premises 7 and 8 (Section 3) stand in its place.
4. No frame can be held at rest below L, so nothing can be computed there. That is general relativity's premise about its own inside. An objection counts only if a step of the manuscript's mathematics is shown wrong.
5. The premises do not follow from the conservation laws alone. The premises are stated as premises in Section 3. An objection counts only where a step uses something that is in neither Section 2 nor Section 3 nor the derivation's own list of what it uses.
6. The sum over point masses cannot be exact because Einstein's equations are not linear. Einstein's equations are on the comparison side. Section 4, statement 7, derives the sum from premises 1, 3 and 5 in the frame of the calculation.
7. Inside the event horizon every future-directed path moves inward, so an outward solution is no escape. That is general relativity's continued causal structure, the step under attack (item 3). Section 3 derives the passage under premise 8.
8. General relativity conserves its symmetry charge and ∇·T = 0, so the manuscript shows no violation of conservation. Those are general relativity's standards. On the manuscript's definition (Section 2), general relativity's continuation inside the event horizon keeps no count of mass-energy: no observer at rest is left there, and the conserved e is a momentum (Section 9, statement 3).
9. A change of the reference clock does not move the zero of f, so causal boundaries do not depend on the frame. For frames at rest the zero is the circle L, as Section 3 states. The frame-dependence concerns frames in motion (Section 9, statement 3).
10. The interior of a body should be made regular with general relativity's interior ruler. That is an import, and it removes the manuscript's result of Section 17.

## 1. Fix the Question, Physical System and Original Premises

State the precise question being investigated and the result the author intends to establish. Preserve the distinction between:

- Deriving the proposed gravitational interaction from the manuscript's ideas.
- Establishing whether that interaction conserves mass-energy and momentum.
- Establishing agreement or disagreement with GR.
- Establishing whether a particular GR prediction violates a specified conservation law.

Record the original physical system: objects, observers, frame relationships, boundaries, initial conditions, permitted transfers, definitions of energy and momentum, and relevant domains. Retain the manuscript's meaning of waves, amplitudes, probabilities, overlaps, distance, time and curvature.

Identify which statements are definitions, physical postulates, supplied observations, derived results or proposed conclusions. Accept declared postulates provisionally for the internal mathematical investigation; assess their empirical support separately.

Do not silently change the thought experiment, replace an observer, introduce a different boundary, or substitute an easier physical question. If a repair requires changing a physical premise, identify that change explicitly and treat the repaired model as a distinct branch of the original investigation.

## 2. Track the Origin of Every Material Assumption

Give each material premise or added rule an identifier and classify it:

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Definition | A quantity or convention explicitly defined in the manuscript. |
| Manuscript premise | A physical assumption explicitly adopted by the manuscript. |
| Mathematical result | A theorem or identity whose hypotheses have been checked. |
| Derived result | A consequence established from identified earlier premises. |
| Provisional addition | A new assumption introduced to complete or repair the model. |
| Empirical input | A measurement, calibration or observational constraint actually supplied or sourced. |
| Comparison assumption | A premise used only to calculate the predictions of GR or another comparison theory. |

Every substantive step must have a traceable origin. Use citations or equation references for supplied material and external results. Do not invent unavailable source content or numerical inputs.

Maintain a compact dependency list. An assumption introduced during a repair must remain identifiable in every result that depends on it; it must not later be described as a result derived from the original manuscript alone.

## 3. Do Not Inherit Requirements from Quantum Mechanics

**No quantum-mechanical requirement may constrain the independent derivation merely because the manuscript uses waves, amplitudes, probabilities, particles or overlaps. A requirement must be explicitly present in the manuscript's stated premises or follow by a demonstrated derivation from those premises.**

In particular, do not automatically impose:

- The Schrödinger equation, Klein–Gordon equation or other conventional quantum dynamics.
- The Born rule or standard measurement and collapse postulates.
- A Hilbert-space interpretation, operator-observable correspondence or canonical commutation relations.
- Unitary evolution, quantum superposition or standard uncertainty relations.
- Quantization, tensor-product composition or conventional quantum-field assumptions.

For each proposed requirement associated with quantum mechanics, identify the exact manuscript premise that supplies it or derive it from the paper's ideas. If neither is possible, it is not an admissible requirement of this independent derivation. A rule explicitly stated by the manuscript remains a premise unless it is independently derived.

The permission to add provisional assumptions is not permission to import quantum mechanics under another name. Any proposed dynamics, probability rule or coupling must have an explicit motivation in the manuscript's mechanism and must be labeled as an addition when the manuscript does not supply it. For each addition, check that its justification and imposed constraints do not depend on accepting quantum mechanics. Resemblance or mathematical equivalence to a conventional quantum equation neither justifies nor disqualifies it; justify it from the manuscript's mechanism and explicitly declared independent assumptions.

Ordinary mathematics still applies to the structures actually defined. For example, a quantity defined as a normalized probability density must satisfy its stated nonnegativity and normalization conditions relative to its specified measure. These follow from that definition, not from an automatic adoption of the Born rule. Mathematical tools may be used when their hypotheses hold, without importing their usual physical interpretation. If supplied observations are part of the target, compare with those observations without treating their conventional quantum interpretation as an additional axiom.

Apply the same separation to GR: do not import the Einstein field equations, Einstein–Hilbert action, Schwarzschild metric or conventional matter model into the independent derivation unless the manuscript explicitly supplies them. They may be used in the separately identified GR comparison. Using GR to calculate its own predictions does not establish those premises for the independent model.

A provisional addition that reproduces a relation of general relativity, such as the interior ruler 1 − 2Gm(r)/(c²r), the lapse of its constant-density interior, geodesic or straightest-path motion, or the causal cones of its continued metric, is an import of general relativity. Label it so, never call it a repair of the manuscript, and state which of the manuscript's results it would change.

Before extensive calculations, give a finite sequence of stages leading from the available premises to the requested result. For each stage state:

1. Its inputs and dependencies.
2. The equation, operation or construction to perform.
3. The result that would complete the stage.

Perform the immediate consistency checks available before calculation, then establish further consistency through construction and verification of the solution. Neither advance knowledge of the final result nor a general existence theorem is required before attempting a repair.

Add a new stage only when a specific equation or requested conclusion actually depends on it. A complete theory of all physics is not a prerequisite for a result about the bounded system under investigation.

## 5. Diagnose Every Error Precisely

For every material issue, provide:

Disagreement with an established theory is not, by itself, a mathematical error. A missing specification is not the same as an inconsistent specification. Failure of one attempted proof does not establish that its conclusion is false.

State exactly what is conserved, how it is measured, which system is included and how quantities at different locations or times are compared. Distinguish total energy conservation from constancy of the individual rest masses.

Where the chosen framework defines comparable total energy and momentum, calculate the balances

\[
\mathcal R_E=\Delta E_{\mathrm{system}}+E_{\mathrm{net,out}},
\]

\[
\boldsymbol{\mathcal R}_P=\Delta\mathbf P_{\mathrm{system}}+\mathbf P_{\mathrm{net,out}}.
\]

Net transfer out includes relevant boundary transport and work; an isolated system has zero external transfer under its stated conditions. If a different local or covariant balance is appropriate, define it and show how it answers the requested conservation question. Do not assume a global momentum vector exists without the structure needed to compare its components.

Defining a quantity to be constant, imposing a compensating term or restating the conservation postulate does not independently verify the proposed dynamics.

Then verify that the completed equations realize the stated balance and identify their additional consequences. Do not demand an independent derivation of conservation when it was openly adopted as an input. Distinguish that construction from evidence that the original, unrepaired dynamics already conserved the quantity.

For a violation, identify the nonzero residual, its sign, magnitude, domain and physical interpretation, and establish that it survives the model's complete accounting. For conservation, calculate the cancellation or identity under the stated conditions.

In this manuscript, conservation of mass-energy is the statement that an observer's complete count of everything inside a closed surface does not change (Section 2). Use that definition for every conservation question, about the manuscript and about general relativity's continued solution alike. General relativity's local conservation (∇·T = 0) and the conservation of a particle's symmetry charge are general relativity's own standards: report them on the comparison side, and do not offer them as the answer to the manuscript's question.

Keep mass-shell relations, local conservation equations, global charges and total momentum balances distinct. If the manuscript has not defined the requested total, identify and repair that missing definition where possible; absence of a definition alone is not a measured loss or gain.

## 10. Compare with GR Under the Same Physical Conditions

Keep the independent derivation and the GR calculation distinguishable. General relativity's continuation of one metric across the event horizon for all observers, and every consequence of it (one horizon for every frame, crossed one way only; its causal cones inside; no frame at rest inside), is the premise under attack. Do not use it to judge the manuscript's statements about what holds at and beyond the event horizon; the manuscript's premises 7 and 8 stand in its place (Section 3). You may calculate what general relativity predicts there, labelled as the comparison. Apply GR's own equations to calculate its predictions; do not use them to impose hidden constraints on the alternative model.

Compare equivalent source configurations, boundary conditions, initial data, observer measurements, units and physical quantities. Show the conversion explicitly when comparing local quantities, coordinate quantities or symmetry charges. Do not substitute a different observer or experiment to remove a discrepancy.

If the requested configuration cannot be realized under GR's assumptions, identify the exact incompatibility and derive it. Report that result directly. A calculation for a different configuration may not be presented as resolving the original one.

For each claimed agreement or violation, identify the conservation requirement, the model prediction, the GR prediction and the equation that establishes their relationship. A proposed reconciliation must be calculated for the specified system before it can count as a result.

Distinguish a demonstrated conservation violation from a disagreement with an added measurement rule, geometric postulate or physical premise. If the contradiction has the form

\[
\mathrm{GR}+C+P\Longrightarrow\bot,
\]

where \(C\) is the conservation requirement and \(P\) is an additional physical premise, establish the role of \(P\). The contradiction demonstrates joint incompatibility; an unqualified claim that GR violates \(C\) requires the further argument showing why the conclusion does not depend on an optional addition in \(P\).

Do not infer that GR has been vindicated from a failed attempt to prove a violation. Do not infer a violation from the absence of a calculated reconciliation. State every established agreement and disagreement at its demonstrated strength.

## 11. Verify the Completed Derivation and Prevent Endless Expansion

Check the repaired equations by substitution into the retained system. Verify relevant dimensions, signs, boundary conditions, domains, limiting behavior and conservation balances. Where the claim requires an admissible solution, provide at least one nontrivial solution or an adequate existence argument; a formal conditional statement with no admissible realization is not a constructed physical model.

Use independent symbolic or numerical checks when they resolve a concrete mathematical risk. Distinguish exact derivations from approximation results and numerical evidence. State the regime and errors of an approximation where they affect the verdict.

Maintain a finite list of outstanding obligations. For each, record the exact missing equation or inference, the result it affects, and whether it is resolved, assumed for the conditional branch, or a demonstrated obstruction.

Do not reopen a resolved obligation without a specific newly identified error. Do not demand experimental validation, a complete quantum theory, a universal spacetime theory or unrelated predictions as a prerequisite for completing the narrower conditional result.

A new requirement must identify the precise failed inference it repairs and why it is necessary for the current claim. Do not expand the investigation merely because another question could be asked.

If a genuine remaining obstruction prevents the full target, finish the strongest supported partial theorem and identify the exact uncompleted step. Keep mathematical validity, physical interpretation and empirical support separate. An execution limit is not a mathematical disproof.

## 12. Deliver the Repaired Work, State the Verdict and Stop

Present the final work in this order:

1. **Scope and finite plan:** the original question, fixed physical system and calculation route.
2. **Exact error register:** every material error or missing specification, with its demonstration and correction.
3. **Conditions and assumptions:** necessary conditions, sufficient sets, selected additions, their provenance and their empirical status. State material limitations here once.
4. **Completed repaired derivation:** explicit equations, essential intermediate steps and replacement passages, with additions identified by their assumption labels.
5. **Verification:** substitution checks, an admissible worked solution or existence result where needed, and the calculated conservation balances.
6. **GR comparison:** the matched predictions and every established agreement, discrepancy or conservation violation, with its responsible equation.
7. **Final verdict:** what the original manuscript establishes, what the repaired model establishes, and what the calculation establishes about GR.

Use the strongest wording justified by the mathematics. If a result is proved, say so. If its proof uses named additional assumptions, state them as part of the theorem. If a conservation violation is established, explain precisely what fails and by how much. If only incompatibility with an added premise is established, state that incompatibility explicitly. Conditions essential to the theorem's truth belong in its statement; unrelated or repeated caveats do not.

State the verdict about general relativity in the terms of the manuscript's own definitions and premises. Where general relativity's own standards give a different reading, report both, each labelled. Do not say that the manuscript "does not prove" a claim that it derives on its stated definitions; name the definition instead. Do not weaken a valid result because it challenges an established theory. Do not strengthen a result beyond what was demonstrated because it matches the author's intended conclusion.

**Stopping rule:** Once the specified calculations and checks establish the verdict, state it precisely and terminate. Do not append speculative reconciliations, alternative thought experiments, new proof obligations, repeated qualifications or recommendations for further research.

**Governing instruction:** Identify the exact error; determine what must be true or what consistent completion can be chosen; state and provisionally adopt those assumptions; repair and complete the derivation; verify the result; and report exactly what it establishes. Quantum mechanics supplies no automatic requirements, and every substantive addition must remain visible.

## 4. Completed derivation

### The exterior field and the observer’s count

**DERIVED on C, P1–P5 and I.** Use the positive outward holding acceleration \(g\). Local work on the body’s current energy gives \(dm/m=\mathbf g_{\rm pull}\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell/c^2\). The cancellation in P3 therefore gives
\[
\frac{m_B}{m_A}=\frac{f_A}{f_B},\qquad
d\ln f=\frac{g\,d\ell}{c^2},\qquad f\gamma=e .
\]
Counting a held probe gives \(dE_\infty=mc^2\,df=mf g\,d\ell\). The counted holding force is defined per unit of **local** displacement. Spherical symmetry and the areal-radius definition give
\[
4\pi r^2 f g=4\pi G\mathcal M,\qquad
d\ell=\frac{dr}{f},\qquad
fg=c^2 f\frac{df}{dr}=\frac{c^2}{2}F'(r).
\]
Integrate with \(F(\infty)=1\):
\[
\boxed{F=f^2=1-\frac Lr,\qquad L=\frac{2G\mathcal M}{c^2}.}
\]
The inverse square comes from the area and the flux law. Its attractive sign comes from the inward pull opposite the holding force. \(G\) is calibrated far away. The far-counted pull per unit rest mass is \(G\mathcal M/r^2\); the exterior held frame measures \(G\mathcal M/(r^2f)\). It weighs the source at \(\mathcal M/f\).

For the freely falling frame released from rest far away, \(e=1\), so its relative \(\gamma=1/f\). P4 and local SR give the §4 comparison of the held clock and longitudinal ruler; transverse rulers retain the stated scale. A common transition and \(E=h\nu\) give \(\nu_\infty=f\nu_{\rm own}\). In a static arrangement successive crests traverse the same path. For emission at \(a\) and reception at \(b\),
\[
\frac{\nu_b}{\nu_a}=\frac{E_b}{E_a}=\frac{f_a}{f_b},
\qquad 1+z=\frac{f_b}{f_a}.
\]
This checks the clock, ruler, frequency, photon energy and massive-body entry separately. The exact cancellation can be seen directly:
\[
K_\infty=f(\gamma-1)mc^2=(e-f)mc^2,\qquad
U_\infty=(f-1)mc^2,\qquad
mc^2+K_\infty+U_\infty=e\,mc^2 .
\]
In the weak, slow regime,
\[
e=1+\frac{v^2}{2c^2}-\frac{G\mathcal M}{rc^2}
+O\!\left((v^2/c^2+L/r)^2\right).
\]
Multiplication by \(mc^2\) gives the energy expansion needed in §13. Section 4 derivation

### Curvature, extended sources and overlap

**DERIVED on P1, P3, P5, with M where several sources are used.** On the three-dimensional calculation grid the flux equation is
\[
\frac{c^2}{2}\oint\nabla F\cdot d\mathbf A=4\pi G M_{\rm inside}.
\]
For assigned point counts \(\mathcal M_a\), the distributional equation is
\[
\nabla^2 F=\frac{8\pi G}{c^2}\sum_a\mathcal M_a\delta_{\mathbf x_a}.
\]
Integrating the radial vacuum equation gives a constant plus \(b/r\); the small-sphere flux fixes \(b=-2G\mathcal M_a/c^2\). Superposition, \(F\to1\), and absence of other sources then give
\[
\boxed{F(\mathbf x)=1-\sum_a\frac{2G\mathcal M_a}{c^2|\mathbf x-\mathbf x_a|}.}
\]
This is exact in the calculation frame specified in §4, statement 7, for the **assigned complete counts**. Determining the counts of interacting pieces is a further physical operation.

With primes denoting derivatives along the local radial ruler, \(r'=f\), \(f'=L/(2r^2)\), and \(f''=-Lf/r^3\). Put \(Q=L/r^3\). In the order time–radius, time–sphere, radius–sphere and within-sphere, the exterior curvatures are
\[
\left(\frac{f''}{f},\,\frac{f'r'}{fr},\,-\frac{r''}{r},\,\frac{1-r'^2}{r^2}\right)
=(-Q,Q/2,-Q/2,Q).
\]
Their contraction gives \(R_{abcd}R^{abcd}=12Q^2\). A held standing wave with \(\nu=f\nu_0\) measures the same \(f''/f\) by \(\nu''/\nu\). The manuscript’s “curvature between two points” can retain its name with the definition in Part III. The local curvature reconstructs the clock by the different, exact identity
\[
f(D)=f(0)+Df'(0)+\int_0^D(D-s)\,C_t(s)f(s)\,ds.
\]
With the companion equation \(r''=-C_s r\), §10’s data at \(r_A=2000\), \(D=9000\), yield \(r_B=9990.80532\), \(f_B=0.948634792\), and \(c\Delta t=10187.00775\). These agree with the draft.

**DERIVED on W and the field just obtained.** The first overlap is a probe’s **energy distribution averaged against a clock shift**:
\[
dP_B=|\psi_B|^2dV_h,\quad \int dP_B=1,\qquad
U_{A\to B}=m_Bc^2\int(f_A-1)\,dP_B .
\]
Here \(dV_h=\sqrt{\det h}\,d^3x\); the reference density is \(p_B=|\psi_B|^2\sqrt{\det h}\). In the round geometry \(p_B=|\psi_B|^2/f\) in areal Cartesian volume coordinates. Using the same numerical density against both measures would change the source. For a probe wholly in the exterior of A the first two terms are
\[
U_{A\to B}
=-G\mathcal M_A m_B\langle r^{-1}\rangle_B
-\frac{G^2\mathcal M_A^2m_B}{2c^2}\langle r^{-2}\rangle_B+\cdots .
\]
The unexpanded square-root average is exact for that fixed field. The truncation requires \(L_A/r\ll1\) throughout the sampled region.

For **two responding, fixed-shape distributions**, linearize \(f\) and use W’s once-per-pair rule. The \(1/s\) kernel just derived gives
\[
U^{(1)}(\mathbf d)=-Gm_A m_B
 \iint\frac{dP_A(\mathbf x)dP_B(\mathbf y)}
 {|\mathbf d+\mathbf y-\mathbf x|}.
\]
Writing \(\mathbf z=\mathbf d+\mathbf y-\mathbf x\), §2’s work relation gives
\[
\mathbf F_B=-\nabla_{\mathbf d}U^{(1)}
=-Gm_A m_B\iint\frac{\mathbf z}{|\mathbf z|^3}\,dP_A dP_B,
\qquad \mathbf F_A=-\mathbf F_B .
\]
Thus even two disjoint spherical supports interact. Their first-order mutual energy is exactly \(-Gm_A m_B/d\). The different, *local product* overlap enters the trace of the separation Hessian:
\[
\frac{\Delta_{\mathbf d} U^{(1)}}{m_Bc^2}
=\frac{4\pi Gm_A}{c^2}\int p_A(\mathbf d+\mathbf y)p_B(\mathbf y)\,d^3y .
\]
That trace vanishes when their densities have disjoint supports. The energy and force still have their finite values there.

For two equal Gaussians of coordinate standard deviation \(\sigma\), the difference distribution has variance \(2\sigma^2\) per axis. Radial integration gives
\[
U^{(1)}=-\frac{Gm^2}{d}\operatorname{erf}\!\left(\frac d{2\sigma}\right),\quad
U^{(1)}(0)=-\frac{Gm^2}{\sqrt\pi\,\sigma},\quad
|\mathbf F_B|=\frac{Gm^2d}{6\sqrt\pi\,\sigma^3}+O(d^3).
\]
The central pull goes to zero. At the midpoint of two equal disjoint spherical bodies the pull also vanishes, while the three time-curvature components there are \((-32,16,16)Gm/(c^2d^3)\). They follow by differentiating the two \(1/r\) fields at distance \(d/2\). For a point probe in any fixed smooth static geometry with \(N>0\), the exact relation is \(D_iD_jU/(E+U)=D_iD_jN/N\). These results distinguish force, energy, local curvature and curvature as separation changes. Section 10, Parts 12–16

**Section 11.** There is a valid conditional exponent theorem. In its flat reference measure, a normalized Gaussian intensity has the form \(s^{-3}n_1(\mathbf x/s)\). For a power of amplitude \(A^\alpha\), the volume therefore scales as \(s^{3-3\alpha/2}\), selecting \(\alpha=2\). ### A material interior and the surface bound

**DERIVED on P1, P3, P5 and S.** Write \(u\) for areal radius and \(\ell_m(u)=2G\mathcal M(u)/c^2\) for enclosed count in length units. The paper’s interior ruler and flux give
\[
F'(u)=\frac{\ell_m(u)}{u^2},\qquad
1-F(0)=\frac LR+\int_0^R\frac{\ell_m(u)}{u^2}\,du .
\]
For outward-nonincreasing grid density, the mean density within \(u\) is at least the mean within \(R\). Hence \(\ell_m(u)\ge L(u/R)^3\) and \(1-F(0)\ge3L/(2R)\). Equality is attained for uniform count, with
\[
F(u)=1-\frac{L}{2R}\left(3-\frac{u^2}{R^2}\right).
\]
For \(L<R<3L/2\), \(F(R)>0>F(0)\). A zero inside matter with positive enclosed count requires unbounded holding force. Under S’s no-holding condition the result is
\[
R\ge\frac32L,\qquad z_{\rm surface}\le\sqrt3-1=0.73205081\ldots .
\]
The uniform threshold is a limiting geometry. At \(R=3L/2\) put \(a=\sqrt{L/(2R^3)}\). Then
\[
f=au,\qquad d(u,u_*)=a^{-1}\ln(u_*/u),\qquad
4\pi u^2=4\pi u_*^2e^{-2ad},\qquad g_{\rm hold}=c^2a .
\]
For \(0<F(0)<1\) the finite-distance area deficit is instead \(1-F(0)\), and \(K_{\theta\varphi}=(1-F)/u^2\) diverges. Both are exact consequences of the author’s interior ruler. The density condition for vanishing counted pull is independently checkable: \(\ell_m=L(u/R)^{3/2}\) is outward-nonincreasing in density, yet \(F'\propto u^{-1/2}\). At \(R=6L\) it has \(F(0)=1/2\). This proves the need for the central-density qualification in E14. No change to P5 is needed to report either consequence.

**Constructed solution on B and W.** Use a common leading-order Euclidean frame, two translating spherical compact distributions, a fixed surface enclosing their entire orbit, and the pair interaction above counted once. Dot the two force equations with their respective velocities and add:

+\dot U^{(1)}+\sum_a\mathbf F_a^{\rm ext}\cdot\mathbf v_a

The net-out terms are minus the integrated external power and impulse. **Both residuals vanish identically in the completed leading-order model.** This uses an independently specified force and inertia, so it also tests the evolution.

# Part II. The inward body, the light and A’s time

## A. Worked example for §14 — a body falling in

**Premises of the step that tests the author’s hint.** P3 supplies \(e=\gamma f\). P8 supplies a real increasing body time \(\tau\), the radial law in both directions, the far-time passage integral and the specified inward initial direction. P7 supplies the two roots for a held-frame comparison. §4 supplies \(F=1-L/r\) and the reciprocal radial ruler. No GR interior law enters. **HINT, 26 November, C2:** “What happens is that once it hits the causal boundary, time flips. It also move in the complex dimension. This is REALLY important because it explains why there are two solutions.”

**1. DERIVED on P8 — the body’s own clock.** Put \(q(r)=\sqrt{e^2-F(r)}\), \(e>0\). Keeping the sign selected by an inward initial velocity gives
\[
\dot r\equiv\frac{dr}{d\tau}=-cq,\qquad
\dot r(L)=-ce,\qquad
\ddot r=-\frac{c^2}{2}F'(r)=-\frac{c^2L}{2r^2}.
\]
Near \(\tau_L\), \(r=L-ce(\tau-\tau_L)+O((\tau-\tau_L)^2)\). The body crosses \(L\). At every \(0<r<L\), \(q^2=e^2+(L/r-1)>e^2\). An inward body continues inward with increasing \(|dr/d\tau|\). A differentiable reversal requires \(\dot r=0\). The only positive solution of that equation is
\[
r_{\rm turn}=\frac{L}{1-e^2}>L,\qquad 0<e<1.
\]
It is the **outer** turning point reached by an initially outgoing body. Switching the inward root to the outward root at \(L\) would change \(\dot r\) by \(2ce\) instantaneously, in conflict with the finite \(\ddot r\) above. Thus the body falling in does not turn back on its own clock. Premise 8 gives both directions of passage; initial conditions distinguish their trajectories.

For \(e=0.5\) an explicit proper-time primitive is available. Set \(k=1-e^2\), \(r=(L/k)\sin^2\theta\). Then
\[
c\int\frac{dr}{q}
=\frac{L}{k^{3/2}}(\theta-\sin\theta\cos\theta).
\]
For \(L=1000\), the inward intervals \(c\Delta\tau\) are \(223.3013\) from D to C, \(676.2692\) from C to 500, and \(883.0485\) from C to A. The mathematical limit from C to \(r=0\) is \(945.5994\). At zero radius the equation itself is singular. The calculation gives no outgoing continuation from that endpoint.

**2. DERIVED on P3, P8 and §4 — the far clock and ruler.** In the exterior \(d\tau=f\,dt/\gamma\), giving \(dt/d\tau=e/F\). The signed form of the manuscript’s passage integral gives, on the two open radial intervals,
\[
\frac{dt}{d\tau}=\frac eF,\qquad
\frac{c\,dt}{dr}=-\frac e{Fq},\qquad
\frac1c\frac{dr}{dt}=-\frac{Fq}{e}.
\]
Near \(L\), \(F=(r-L)/L+O((r-L)^2/L^2)\), \(q\to e\). Consequently
\[
ct=-L\ln\left|\frac{r-L}{L}\right|+O(1).
\]
For inward passage, \(t\to+\infty\) on approach to \(L\) from either side, with separately selectable finite integration constants. Outside, \(dt/d\tau>0\); inside, its inferred value is negative. **This is the time derivative that flips.** The body’s own \(\tau\) continues forward. The far signed \(dr/dt\) is negative outside and positive inside, even though \(dr/d\tau\) is negative throughout. No finite tick of the far clock records the body turning and coming back out.
